days.title: Storing water: then and now
days.goal: Learn why and how people store water, interview an elder about the past, start a vessel exhibition and test why a clay matka keeps water cool.

steps.title: No water today! (pages 92–93)
steps.do: Read the comic 'Storing water' at the bottom of page 92 together: the society pipeline burst and there is no water today, but the family has stored two buckets. Ask: 'Have you ever had a day with no water? What did we do?' Then read page 93 aloud. Ask: 'Why do people store water?' (Because water does not come all the time; pipes burst, supply comes only some hours a day, or it has to be carried from far.) 'Long ago there were no pipes or taps anywhere. What did people do?' (They made vessels to store water.)

steps.title: Why is matka water cool?
steps.do: Set up Experiment e4. Fill a clay pot (matka or surahi) and a steel vessel of a similar size with water from the same jug. Put both in the same shady, airy spot. Ask your child to predict: 'After 3 hours, which water will be cooler?' Ask them to touch the outside of both pots now, and again after an hour: the clay pot feels damp on the outside. Check after 3 hours by dipping a finger in each, or with a kitchen thermometer if you have one. Then explain using the 'why' of e4: water seeps through tiny holes in the clay and evaporates from the outside, and evaporation takes heat away, just as you feel cool when you come out of a bath. Link back to Day 1: 'Where did the water in our sunny plate go?' (It evaporated.)

steps.title: Book Activity 3: Vessel hunt (pages 93–94)
steps.do: Start Activity a3, based on Activity 3 on page 94. Look at the vessels on page 93 (clay pot, clay surahi, copper, brass, steel and aluminium pots, glass and plastic bottles, plastic bucket). Then your child goes round the house and finds every vessel used to keep water: the matka, the steel drum, the copper lota in the puja room, the water bottle, the bucket in the bathroom, the overhead tank. For each, write: what it is made of, where it is kept, what the water in it is used for, and its name in your home language (matka, ghada, kalash, kudam, lota, handa). Your child chooses the most interesting one and draws it on a sheet with its patterns (many brass and copper pots have engraved lines or flowers, as the book asks).

steps.title: Interview an elder (page 93)
steps.do: Do the 'Ask your grandparents' task at the top of page 93. Call a grandparent or ask an older neighbour these questions, and your child writes the answers: 'How did you get water when you were my age? Who fetched it? Did you use water the same way as we do? How did you store it? Did your vessels have special names?' Many will remember drawing water from a well with a rope and bucket, a village pond or temple tank, a pital (brass) handa, or bathing in a river. Afterwards your child writes a 5-line story beginning 'When Nani was little…'. Ask: 'Who used less water, them or us? Why?'

need: a clay matka or surahi and a steel vessel of similar size
a kitchen thermometer if you have one
a phone to call a grandparent

prep.task: Fix a time to call a grandparent or elder for the interview

days.title: After we use it: dirty water, reuse and safe water
days.goal: Learn that used water becomes dirty, what it can be reused for, why clear-looking water may still be unsafe, and how John Snow's map proved that dirty water spreads disease.

steps.title: Stop for a moment and think! (page 95)
steps.do: Read the 'Stop for a moment and think!' list on page 95 aloud, pointing to each picture: rain, sources, bringing water home, storing it, using it, and the last question, 'What happens to water after we use it?' Let your child guess. Then read the paragraph below. Ask: 'Why can't we drink water used for washing?' (It has dirt, soap and germs in it.) 'What can we reuse it for?' (Watering plants, flushing toilets.) Ask: 'Why does the book say not to add too much soap and chemicals?' (Soapy, chemical water goes down the drain into rivers and lakes and harms the fish and plants there; and soapy water can harm garden plants too.)

steps.title: Reuse sort at the kitchen sink
steps.do: Stand at the kitchen sink with your child. Show three bowls: water from washing vegetables or rinsing rice and dal, soapy water from washing a plate, and oily water from rinsing a kadhai. Ask for each: 'Plants, flushing or mopping, or only the drain?' Good answers: vegetable and rice water is fine for plants; light soapy water can be used for flushing or mopping; oily, greasy water goes to the drain (oil harms plants and soil). Choose one reuse habit for the family this week, like keeping a 'plant bucket' next to the sink, and write it on the fridge.

steps.title: The bottle filter
steps.do: Do Experiment e5. Cut a plastic bottle in half and put the top half upside down into the bottom half like a funnel. Inside the funnel your child layers: a plug of cotton wool, then crushed charcoal (from a used angithi or a pharmacy charcoal tablet crushed), then fine sand, then coarse sand, then small gravel on top. Make muddy water in a glass by stirring in a spoon of soil. Ask: 'When we pour it through, what will come out? Will it be safe to drink?' Pour slowly and compare the before and after glasses. It comes out much clearer. Then ask again: 'Is it safe to drink now?' The answer is no: germs are far too small to see and can pass through. Water must be boiled for a few minutes, or cleaned with a proper filter, to be safe. Pour the filtered water on a plant.

steps.title: John Snow and the Broad Street pump
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v1. Draw a simple street map on paper with a pump in the middle, and let your child put a dot for each 'house where people fell sick' as you call out: most dots near one pump, a few far away. Ask: 'Where do you think the sickness was coming from?' Then ask the voice question. Link to the filter: 'Did the Broad Street water look dirty?' (It probably looked clear, which is why people kept drinking it.)

steps.title: Stretch worksheet (part 1)
steps.do: Start Worksheet ws2 (stretch): do section A now while the reuse sort and filter are fresh. Keep sections B and C for bedtime or tomorrow morning. For the 'only the drain' items, ask your child to give the reason each time.

need: 3 bowls of used water from the kitchen
a plastic bottle, scissors (adult), cotton wool, crushed charcoal, fine sand, coarse sand, small gravel
a spoon of soil and 2 glasses
paper and pencil for the street map

prep.task: Wash sand and gravel and collect a little charcoal for the filter
Keep aside vegetable-washing water, soapy dish water and kadhai-rinse water in three bowls

days.title: Every drop counts: sharing water
days.goal: Learn that clean water is not easy for everyone, take action by offering water to people and building a birdbath, and look at how Indian communities have cared for water.

steps.title: Every drop counts (page 96)
steps.do: Read 'Every drop counts' on page 96 aloud. Ask: 'Why do some people walk long distances for water?' (It rains very little where they live and there are no big rivers or lakes nearby.) Ask the book's question: 'Don't you think everyone must get clean drinking water anywhere, anytime?' Then look at the three pictures: a water tank for animals, free drinking water for people (often called a pyaau or piyau in North India, or a thanneer pandal in Tamil Nadu) and a birdbath. Ask: 'Have you seen any of these near us?'

steps.title: Book Activity 4: Make a birdbath (page 97)
steps.do: Do Activity a4, following Activity 4 on page 97. Choose a shallow, wide container less than 10 cm deep (an old wide bowl, a plant-pot saucer or the bottom of an old bucket). Your child measures the depth with a ruler. Place a few flat stones inside for birds to perch, and small pebbles on one side to make a sloping edge so that insects can drink without drowning. Fill with fresh water and place it on the balcony, terrace or yard, in partial shade, where cats cannot hide nearby. Set the cleaning rule: change the water every day, scrub it twice a week with a scrubber kept only for the garden, never one from the kitchen. Start a list in the notebook: 'Visitors to my birdbath' (crows, mynas, sparrows, bulbuls, pigeons, bees, butterflies).

steps.title: Take action: water for whoever comes (page 96)
steps.do: Read the 'Take action' box on page 96. Together, fill a clean steel jug and two glasses and keep them by the door. Decide with your child to offer water to the next person who comes: the postman, the garbage collector, the delivery person or the vegetable seller. Practise the words: 'Bhaiya/Didi, would you like some water?' Ask: 'Why is this tradition strongest in the hot summer months?' (People sweat and lose water; working outside in the heat is dangerous without drinking water.)

steps.title: Anupam Mishra: the ponds are still standing
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v3. If you can, show a photo on the phone of a stepwell such as the Rani ki Vav in Patan, Gujarat (built in the 11th century, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site) or the Chand Baori in Abhaneri, Rajasthan, and a village pond. Ask the voice question and listen for a reason, not just 'yes' or 'no'.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 (challenge), and finish sections B and C of ws2 if they were not done last night. In ws3, your child can answer the write items aloud while you write. For the 'comparing views' section there is no single right answer; praise answers that give evidence ('because in the filter test…', 'because Snow's map showed…').

need: a shallow wide container less than 10 cm deep, flat stones, small pebbles, a ruler
a phone for photos of stepwells

prep.task: Find a shallow container and collect flat stones and pebbles for the birdbath

days.title: Let us reflect, check and teach it back
days.goal: Finish the Sky Diary and water audit, answer the book's reflection questions, find three ways to stop wasting water, check understanding and teach the chapter back.

steps.title: Sky Diary score and audit total
steps.do: Close the Sky Diary (Activity a1): count how many rain guesses were right this week and which clue worked best. Read the rain gauge one last time. Then add up the water audit from Activity a2: how many mugs did the family use in one day? (A mug is about 1 litre, so 100 mugs is about 100 litres.) Ask: 'Which job used the most water? Where could we save?' Check the birdbath (Activity a4): change the water and add any new visitors to the list.

steps.title: Let us reflect: Write and Draw (page 98)
steps.do: Do question A1 on page 98 aloud first, then your child writes 3–4 lines: what the rain looked like, whether the collected rainwater was clean, and what happened to it on soil and on cement. Then question A2: write a few lines about the water body you found on Day 3. Ask: 'Is this water used for drinking? If yes, how does it reach homes? If not, why not? Was it used in the past?' (Many city lakes and tanks were once used for drinking and are now too dirty.) For B, your child draws the birdbath and writes the names of birds and insects that came.

steps.title: Discuss: three solutions (page 99)
steps.do: Do Discuss question C on page 99. First list together the things in and around the house that waste or pollute water: a dripping tap, an overflowing roof tank, brushing with the tap running, washing the car with a pipe, too much detergent, throwing garbage or oil into drains, puja flowers and plastic thrown into the lake. Then your child chooses three solutions and writes them in the notebook, for example: '1. Turn off the tap while brushing. 2. Put a bucket under the AC drip and use it for plants. 3. Tell the watchman when the tank overflows.'

steps.title: Chapter check
steps.do: Ask the 8 check questions aloud, one at a time, without the book. Tick the ones answered well. For each one missed, open the right page (rain p87–89, groundwater p89, pipes p90–91, storing p93, reuse p95, sharing p96) for one minute and ask again in different words. Six or more right is good; fewer than five means repeat the groundwater jar and the pipe trail next week.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is now the teacher, and you (or a grandparent or sibling) are the student. Using the pipe map, the groundwater jar, the filter and the matka, they teach in 5 minutes: where water comes from (rain), where rainwater goes (soil, groundwater, streams, rivers, ponds, the air), how it reaches our tap, how we store it, and how we can reduce, reuse and share it. Ask two 'student' questions: 'If the filtered water looks clean, can I drink it?' and 'Why is matka water cold without a fridge?' End by putting the rain gauge somewhere safe for the next rainy season.

need: Sky Diary, water audit, pipe map
the groundwater jar, the bottle filter and the matka

worksheets.title: Where water comes from and where it goes
sections: A. Rain and where it goes

sections.p: Rain falls on a cement road. What mostly happens to it?
opts: It soaks deep into the road
It collects in puddles and flows away to the drain

sections.p: When the sun comes out, water in puddles dries up because it ____ into the air.
The water in our wells comes from water stored ____ the ground.
Sort these sources of water.
Match each thing to its job.
pairs: Stores water high up and sends it down to the taps
Carries water from one place to another
Brings water by truck from a well, river or lake

sections.p: Write where the water in your home comes from and how it reaches your tap.
Which used water is best for watering plants?
opts: Oily water from washing a kadhai

sections.p: We can reuse waste water for watering plants or for flushing ____.
Draw rain falling on soil and on a road. Use arrows to show where the water goes in each place.

worksheets.title: Store it, reuse it, keep it safe

sections.p: Where should each kind of used water go?
items: Water left in your school bottle
Light soapy water from washing clothes
Waste water from the RO purifier
Oily water from washing a kadhai

sections.p: Muddy water came out clear from your bottle filter. Is it safe to drink?
opts: No, germs are too small to see and can pass through; it must be boiled or properly purified

sections.p: Match each vessel to what it is made of.
Water in a clay matka stays cooler than water in a steel pot kept beside it. Explain why, using the word 'evaporate'.
Your society gets tap water only from 6 to 8 in the morning. What is the best thing to do?
opts: Leave the taps open all day
Fill and cover buckets and vessels in the morning to use later

sections.p: In a village, the pond was filled with soil to build a shop. A few years later the village well dried up. Why might these two things be connected?
Look at three surfaces after rain (or after you pour a mug of water). Fill the table.

worksheets.title: Water puzzles and people who disagreed

sections.p: Earth looks blue from space because it is covered in water. Yet many cities run short of water. Why?
opts: About 97 of every 100 drops are salty sea water, and most fresh water is frozen as ice, so very little is easy to use
Rain only falls on the sea

sections.p: Your rain gauge showed 2 cm one day and 0 cm the next. Your friend's gauge, 10 km away, showed 5 cm on both days. What does this tell you about rain?
A city paves every open ground with cement. What will happen to its groundwater and to its roads when it rains heavily? Give two effects.
What if no rain fell for a whole year where you live? List four things that would change, from the well to your plate.
What if everyone in your building turned off the tap while brushing? If each person saves 8 mugs a day and 40 people live there, how many mugs are saved in a day?
In 1854 most doctors said cholera came from bad-smelling air. John Snow said it came from dirty water. What evidence did Snow use, and why was it convincing?
Some scientists say that when villages hold back lots of rain in ponds and johads, less water flows on to villages further down the river. How could you check if this is true?
Who owns the rain that falls on your roof? Who owns a river? Write what you think and why.

experiments.title: Sun or shade: where does the water go?
experiments.question: Where does water go when a wet thing dries, and does it dry faster in the sun or in the shade?
need: a sunny spot and a shady spot
steps: Pour exactly 4 tablespoons of water into each plate.
Put one plate in direct sunlight and one in the shade indoors.
Wet two hankies the same amount, wring them, and hang one in the sun and one in the shade.
Check every half hour. Write down the time each plate and each hanky becomes completely dry.
Next day, discuss: where did the water go?
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which plate will dry first? Where will the water go: into the plate, into the floor or somewhere else?
experiments.observe: The plate and hanky in the sun dry much faster, often in under an hour on a hot day; the ones in the shade take several hours. Nothing soaks into a steel plate, so the water must have gone into the air.
experiments.why: Water is made of tiny particles that are always jiggling. At the surface, some of them jiggle free and escape into the air as an invisible gas called water vapour. This is evaporation. Heat from the sun makes the particles jiggle faster, so more escape each minute and the water disappears sooner. Wind also helps by carrying the vapour away. This is what happens to puddles after rain (page 89), and to wet clothes on the line. The water is not destroyed; it is in the air around us, and later it will form clouds and fall again as rain. (The full water cycle comes in Class 5.)
experiments.time: 12 min to set up + checks every half hour for the day

experiments.title: Rain on different surfaces
experiments.question: What happens to rainwater when it falls on soil, cement, grass and sand? (Based on page 89)
need: a cement or tiled floor that slopes to a drain
a heap or tray of sand
steps: Fill four mugs with the same amount of water.
Pour one mug slowly onto each surface from the same height.
Count slowly to 30 and watch: does it soak in, make a puddle or flow away?
Mark the edge of any puddle with chalk.
Come back after 2 hours and look again.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: on which surface will the water disappear fastest? On which will it make a puddle? Where will the puddle water go?
experiments.observe: Sand and loose soil soak the water in within seconds. Grass holds some on its blades and the soil underneath soaks the rest. Cement makes a puddle and the water runs off towards the drain. After 2 hours the cement is dry or nearly dry.
experiments.why: Sand and soil have tiny gaps (pores) between their grains, and water runs down into these gaps. Grass roots loosen the soil and slow the water down so it has time to soak in. Cement has almost no gaps, so the water cannot go down; it can only flow sideways to the lowest point or sit in a puddle until it evaporates. This is why rain on a city of roads and buildings runs into drains and can cause flooding, while rain on fields and forests soaks in and refills the groundwater that wells use.
experiments.safety: Wet cement and tiles are slippery: walk slowly.

experiments.title: Groundwater in a jar
experiments.question: How is rainwater stored under the ground, and how does a well or borewell get it?
need: a clear glass jar or cut transparent plastic bottle
a spoon or a bottle with holes in the cap
steps: Put a 3 cm layer of pebbles at the bottom of the jar (these are the rocks).
Add a 3 cm layer of coarse sand, then a 4 cm layer of soil on top.
Push a straw down the side of the jar until it reaches the pebbles. This is your borewell.
Sprinkle water slowly over the soil like rain, a few spoons at a time.
Watch through the glass as the water moves down and fills the gaps between the pebbles.
Look at the water level inside the straw. Suck a little water up, then 'rain' again and watch the level rise.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: where will the rainwater go? Will we be able to see it at the bottom? What will happen to the water in the 'borewell' if we stop the rain and keep sucking water out?
experiments.observe: The soil darkens as water soaks in, and after a while water collects in the gaps between the pebbles at the bottom. The water in the straw rises to the same level as the water in the pebble layer. When water is taken out and no new 'rain' falls, the level falls.
experiments.why: Underground there is no big lake. Groundwater sits in the tiny gaps between grains of sand and cracks in rocks, like water in a sponge. Layers of rock and sand that hold a lot of water are called aquifers. A well or borewell is a hole that reaches down into this wet layer, so water seeps into it and can be pulled up by a pulley, hand pump or electric pump. Rain that soaks in refills (recharges) the aquifer. If we pull water out faster than rain refills it, the water level drops and wells have to be dug deeper. India uses more groundwater than any other country, and in many districts the water level has been falling for years, which is why soaking rain into the ground matters so much.
experiments.safety: Do not drink the water from the jar.

experiments.title: Why is matka water cool?
experiments.question: Does water stay cooler in a clay pot than in a steel pot, and why?
need: an unglazed clay matka or surahi
a steel vessel of a similar size
steps: Fill both vessels with the same amount of water from the same jug, so they start at the same temperature.
Put both in the same shady, airy place, side by side, with lids on.
After 1 hour, feel the outside of each vessel.
After 3 hours, dip a clean finger in each, or measure the temperature with the thermometer.
Record the results in the notebook.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: after 3 hours, which water will feel cooler? Will the outside of the two pots feel different?
experiments.observe: The outside of the clay pot feels damp and cool. After a few hours the water in the matka is noticeably cooler than the water in the steel vessel, often by several degrees on a hot, dry day. The difference is smaller on a humid, rainy day.
experiments.why: Unglazed baked clay is full of tiny holes (it is porous). A little water seeps through the walls to the outside surface and evaporates. To evaporate, water needs heat energy, and it takes that heat from the pot and the water inside, so the water cools. This is the same reason you feel cold when you step out of a bath, or why sweating cools us down in summer. Steel has no holes, so no water seeps out and this cooling does not happen. In humid weather the air is already full of water vapour, so evaporation is slower and the matka cools less. People in India have used this simple science for thousands of years.
experiments.safety: Handle the clay pot gently; it breaks easily.
experiments.time: 12 min to set up + checks after 1 and 3 hours

experiments.title: The bottle filter
experiments.question: Can sand, gravel and charcoal clean muddy water, and does clear water mean safe water?
steps: An adult cuts the bottle in half. Turn the top half upside down into the bottom half, with the cap removed.
Push a plug of cotton wool into the neck.
Add layers: 2 cm crushed charcoal, 3 cm fine sand, 3 cm coarse sand, 3 cm gravel on top.
Pour some clean water through first to wash the layers, and throw it away.
Stir a spoon of soil into a glass of water. Keep a little of it in the second glass to compare.
Pour the muddy water slowly into the filter and collect what comes out. Compare it with the muddy water.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: what will come out of the bottom? Will it be clear? Will it be safe to drink?
experiments.observe: The water that comes out is much clearer than the muddy water. It may still be slightly cloudy. The top layers of gravel and sand turn brown with trapped mud.
experiments.why: Each layer acts like a sieve with smaller and smaller holes. Gravel catches big bits like leaves and grit, coarse sand catches smaller bits, and fine sand catches fine mud. Charcoal is full of tiny pores that can trap some smells and colours. But disease germs (bacteria and viruses) are thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand and can pass straight through, and you cannot see them. So clear water is not the same as safe water. To make water safe to drink, it must be boiled for a few minutes or cleaned with a proper water purifier. City water works use similar sand filters as one step, and then add a small amount of chlorine to kill the germs.
experiments.safety: Never drink the filtered water. An adult should do the cutting. Wash hands after handling soil.

activities.title: Sky Diary and rain gauge (page 87)
need: a ruler and a paper strip
steps: Make a 'My Sky Diary' page with columns: Date, My guess (rain / no rain), My 2 clues, Did it rain?, Rain gauge (cm).
Each morning, look at the sky and write your guess and two clues, as page 87 asks.
Make the gauge: an adult cuts the top off the bottle; turn the top upside down into the bottom as a funnel and tape it.
Tape a paper strip down the side and mark centimetres from the bottom with a ruler.
Place it in the open, away from roofs and trees, held steady with stones.
Each morning read the water level, write it down, then empty the gauge.
At the end of the week, count how many guesses were right and which clue worked best.
activities.outcome: A week-long weather record with your child's own rain clues, a working rain gauge, and a score for how good a weather forecaster they are.

activities.title: Home water audit (page 92)
steps: Brush your teeth with water in a mug and count the mugs used.
Let the tap run for 2 minutes into a bucket and count how many mugs it fills.
Draw a table: Activity, Mugs or buckets used, Could we use less? How?
Fill in rows through the day: brushing, bath, washing hands, cooking, drinking, dishes, clothes, mopping, plants, flushing.
A bucket is about 15–20 mugs; count buckets as mugs to add them up.
At night, add up the total and circle the job that used the most water.
Choose two changes for the family and write them on the fridge.
activities.outcome: A one-day record of how much water the family uses, the biggest water-using job, and two real changes the family agrees to make.

activities.title: Water vessel exhibition (Book Activity 3, page 94)
need: the water vessels in your home
string and clips to hang pictures
steps: Find every vessel used to keep water at home: matka, bucket, lota, bottles, drum, tank.
For each, note what it is made of and its name in your home language.
Ask elders which vessels they used when they were young and how they were different.
Draw the most interesting vessel on a sheet, with its patterns, and write its name in English and your language.
Add drawings of two vessels the elders remember.
Hang the drawings on a string in the hall as a mini exhibition and invite family members to walk around, as the book suggests.
Count how many kinds of vessels are in the exhibition and how many materials they are made from.
activities.outcome: A small home exhibition of water vessels, old and new, labelled in two languages, and a count of the materials people have used to store water.

activities.title: Birdbath (Book Activity 4, page 97)
need: a shallow, wide container less than 10 cm deep
a scrubber kept only for the garden
steps: Measure the container with a ruler to check it is less than 10 cm deep.
Place some flat stones inside so birds have a place to perch.
Add small pebbles on one side to make a sloping edge for insects.
Fill with fresh water and place it on the balcony, terrace or yard in partial shade, away from where cats can hide.
Change the water every day so mosquitoes cannot breed in it.
Scrub it twice a week with the garden scrubber, never a kitchen one.
Keep a list of every bird and insect that visits, with the date and time.
activities.outcome: A working birdbath, a daily care habit, and a growing list of the birds and insects that come to drink, for the drawing on page 98.

voices.who: John Snow (1813–1858), doctor, London, England
voices.idea: During a terrible outbreak of cholera in the Soho area of London in 1854, Snow marked the home of every person who died on a street map. Most deaths were clustered around one public water pump on Broad Street. He argued that cholera was spread by something in dirty water, not by bad air. He also showed that people who worked in a nearby brewery, who drank beer and not pump water, mostly stayed well. He persuaded the local officials to remove the pump's handle so that no one could use it.
voices.then: Most doctors and officials at the time believed in the 'miasma' theory: that diseases like cholera came from bad-smelling air rising from rotting rubbish. Even after the pump handle was removed, an official inquiry did not fully accept Snow's water explanation, and he died in 1858 before his idea was widely accepted.
voices.now: Snow was right. In 1883 Robert Koch identified the cholera germ (a bacterium, Vibrio cholerae) and showed it spreads through water and food contaminated with sewage. Snow's map is now famous as one of the first uses of mapping in medicine, and he is called a father of epidemiology, the science of how diseases spread. Cholera still kills people where clean drinking water and toilets are not available.
voices.ask: People kept drinking from the Broad Street pump because the water looked fine. What evidence would you need to see before you believed clear water was making people sick?

voices.who: Rajendra Singh (born 1959), India, 'the Waterman of India'
voices.idea: In 1985 Rajendra Singh went to work in the dry Alwar district of Rajasthan with his group Tarun Bharat Sangh. Village elders told him the real problem was water. Following the old local practice, he and the villagers dug and rebuilt johads: curved mud walls across slopes that hold back rainwater in small ponds so it soaks into the ground. Over the years thousands of johads were built, wells filled up again, and small rivers such as the Arvari, which had stopped flowing in the dry months, began to flow all year again.
voices.then: At first government officials objected that the villagers had built the structures without permission, and some engineers saw mud johads as old-fashioned compared with big dams and pipelines. The villagers carried on, and the results in the wells convinced many.
voices.now: His work has been widely praised: he received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2001 and the Stockholm Water Prize in 2015, and catching rain where it falls is now part of government water programmes. Water scientists agree that local rainwater harvesting can recharge groundwater. They also study a fair question: if every village upstream holds back lots of rain, does less water reach villages and rivers further downstream? The answer depends on the place, and it is still being studied.
voices.ask: The wells in Alwar filled up after johads were built. What else could have made them fill up? What would you compare to be sure the johads were the reason?

voices.who: Anupam Mishra (1948–2016), writer and environmentalist, India
voices.idea: Anupam Mishra, who worked at the Gandhi Peace Foundation in Delhi, travelled across India to record how ordinary communities had built and cared for ponds, tanks, kunds and stepwells for hundreds of years, without engineers from outside. His Hindi book 'Aaj Bhi Khare Hain Talaab' (1993; 'The ponds are still standing') showed that these systems were clever science: they were placed where rain naturally collected, cleaned every year by the whole village, and refilled the wells. His book 'Rajasthan ki Rajat Boondein' (1995; 'The radiant raindrops of Rajasthan') described how desert people caught every drop of rain.
voices.then: For much of the 20th century, planners thought that big dams, canals and piped water would replace traditional ponds, and many tanks and lakes were filled in, built over or turned into rubbish dumps. Mishra's view that the old systems still mattered was not part of official thinking.
voices.now: His books have been reprinted many times, translated into other languages and used by villages to revive their ponds. Many cities and states now try to protect and restore their old lakes and stepwells to recharge groundwater. Most experts today see traditional harvesting and modern supply as working best together, not one replacing the other.
voices.ask: A city filled up its old lake to build houses, and now it floods every monsoon and its borewells are drying. Was the old lake 'old-fashioned' or was it doing a job? How could you prove it?

check.q: Give two clues that tell you it might rain soon.
check.a: Any two of: dark grey clouds, tall piled-up clouds, the sky turning dark in the day, a sudden cool wind, the air feeling heavy and sticky, thunder, ants or birds behaving differently.

check.q: What happens to rain that falls on soil, and to rain that falls on a cement road?
check.a: On soil it soaks in, and some goes down to become groundwater or flows under the soil into streams. On cement it cannot soak in, so it collects in puddles or flows away into drains, and the puddles dry up in the sun.

check.q: Where does the water in a well or borewell come from?
check.a: From groundwater: rainwater that soaked into the ground and is stored in the gaps between soil, sand and rocks.

check.q: How does water reach the tap in our home?
check.a: From a source such as a river, lake, well or borewell, through big pipes or a tanker, into a tank (often on the roof), and then down smaller pipes to the tap. The child should describe their own home's route.

check.q: Why do people store water? Name three vessels used to store it.
check.a: Because water does not come all the time (supply hours, burst pipes, carrying it from far). Vessels: clay matka or surahi, copper, brass or steel pot, plastic bucket, bottle, drum, tank.

check.q: Why does water stay cool in a clay matka?
check.a: Water seeps through tiny holes in the clay and evaporates from the outside; evaporation takes heat away from the pot and the water, so the water cools.

check.q: Muddy water came out clear from our filter. Can we drink it? Why?
check.a: No. Germs are too small to see and can pass through sand. Water must be boiled or properly purified to be safe. John Snow showed that water which looks fine can carry disease.

check.q: Name three ways your family can reduce, reuse or share water.
check.a: For example: turn off the tap while brushing, bathe with a bucket and mug, fix leaks, reuse vegetable-washing water for plants, collect AC water for mopping, offer drinking water to people who come to the door, keep a birdbath.

c.covers: Why food matters for health; foods from many sources; nutrients; traditional knowledge of healthy eating
game: Thali Builder

Food cards carry energy, body-building and protective icons. Race to build a balanced thali from your hand; then a twist card asks for a Kerala, Punjabi or Bengali thali using only local foods. Opponent can challenge a card's region.
exp: Starch test: a drop of iodine (Betadine) on potato, rice, bread and cucumber. Which turn blue-black? (Adult; don't eat after.)
Sprouting chana: weigh 50 g, soak and sprout for 2 days, weigh again. Why heavier?
act: Food-origin trail: pick 5 foods at dinner and trace each back to a farm, a tree or an animal.
Cook a grandparent's recipe together and write it down.
proj: Our Family Cookbook
Collect 5 recipes from relatives with where each comes from, photos, and one dish the child cooks.
A handmade or printed recipe booklet
read: Gregory, the Terrible Eater, Mitchell Sharmat
Eating the Alphabet, Lois Ehlert
links: Maths Mela Ch 10: Fun at Class Party!

learn: Food comes from plants (grains, pulses, vegetables, fruits, spices) and animals (milk, eggs, fish, meat).
Each region eats what grows nearby: coconut and rice in Kerala, wheat in Punjab, fish in Bengal, millets in dry lands.
Millets (ragi, bajra, jowar) grow with little water and are very nutritious; 2023 was the International Year of Millets.
Cooking changes food: taste, softness, colour, and sometimes how easily the body can use it.
A balanced plate has energy foods, body-building foods and protective foods.
think: Is rice better than millet? Better for whom: your body, the farmer, the river?
Why do people in different places eat such different foods?
Two sides: some say vegetarian food is healthiest; others say eggs or fish help growth. Many nutrition scientists say both can be healthy when balanced. What would you need to know to decide?
x.oneness: Sunlight grew the mango, and now the mango becomes you. Where does the food stop and you begin?
jokes: Why did the tomato blush? It saw the salad dressing!
What does a nervous laddoo say? I'm falling to pieces!
Why did the roti go to school? To be well-rounded!
quiz: Ragi and bajra are millets.
So are jowar and foxtail millet.
All food comes from plants.
Milk and eggs come from animals.
Potatoes contain starch.
Iodine turns them blue-black.
People everywhere eat the same food.
Food depends on what grows nearby and on culture.
odd: Moong is a pulse; the others are millets.
ws: Sort 12 foods from your kitchen into plant and animal.
Draw your lunch. Colour energy foods yellow, body-building red, protective green.
Pick 3 foods at dinner and draw where each came from.
Write one reason someone eats vegetarian and one reason someone eats eggs or fish.
cur: Eat a Rainbow lesson and chart
Fill a week's colour chart with Indian foods (ragi, palak, gajar, baingan, banana); invent a rainbow thali.

deep.q: Rice or millet: which is better?
deep.why: Millets like ragi, bajra and jowar were India's main grains for thousands of years. Rice and wheat took over after the 1960s Green Revolution, which helped feed India but used much more water.
views: Nutritionists
Ragi is rich in calcium; bajra in iron. Millets also have more fibre than polished rice.
Farmers and water experts
Rice needs a lot of water; millets grow in dry land with little rain. That's why the UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets.
Cooks and families
Taste, habit and what's in the shop matter too. 'Better' depends on whether you mean for your body, the farmer or the river.
deep.tryit: Taste a ragi roti or ragi porridge and a rice dish. Compare taste, how full you feel, and look up how much water each crop needs.

deep.q: Why do people in different places eat such different food?
deep.why: Food follows land and climate: coconuts and rice in wet Kerala, wheat in Punjab, fish in Bengal and Goa, millets in dry Rajasthan. Trade, religion and history add more layers.
views: Geographers
What grows nearby shapes what people cook.
Historians
Chillies, potatoes and tomatoes came to India from the Americas only about 400–500 years ago; Indian food has always mixed and changed.
Today
Supermarkets bring food from everywhere. Is that good for farmers near you?
deep.tryit: Pick one dish your family cooks. List each ingredient and where it grows. How many came from far away?

deep.q: Vegetarian, eggs, fish or meat: what's healthiest?
deep.why: Families eat differently for reasons of health, belief, culture, cost and care for animals.
views: Many nutrition scientists
Both vegetarian and non-vegetarian diets can be healthy when balanced; pulses, milk, nuts and grains together give good protein.
Ethical vegetarians (and Jain and many Hindu traditions)
Avoiding harm to animals (ahimsa) is the main reason.
Coastal and hill communities
Fish, eggs or meat are local, affordable and traditional.
deep.tryit: Without judging, ask three people why they eat what they eat. Sort the reasons: health, belief, taste, cost, habit.

wsd.p: Sort these foods.
Which of these is a millet?
Draw today's lunch. Colour energy foods yellow, body-building foods red, protective foods green.
Is your plate balanced?
Trace three foods back to where they grew.
Starch test (adult adds iodine).
Rice needs much more water than millets. If your area has little rain, which would you grow? Give two reasons.

x.guide: Food is biology, geography and family history on one plate. Trace food back to farms and grandmothers' kitchens. Use your own regional dishes as the main examples, not textbook ones. Pitfall: iodine stains and isn't food. Use old cut pieces and throw them away after.
prep: Read Chapter 8 yourself first and mark 2–3 places to stop and ask a question (15 min)
Your NCERT book, or the free PDF: ncert.nic.in/textbook.php → Class 3 → Our Wondrous World (also on the ePathshala app)
Read the three big questions and their views. Decide which one you'll open with and what you think (10 min)
In this app: open the chapter → Think
Print the worksheet or keep the app open on a tablet; set out pencils and crayons
In this app (Worksheet), or print it from the worksheet PDF
Betadine (iodine), a dropper; cut potato, rice, bread, cucumber on an old plate (not to be eaten after)
Weigh 50 g of chana and soak it 2 days before the lesson so the sprouts are ready
Ask a grandparent for one recipe and buy its ingredients
Make food cards with energy, body-building and protective icons for Thali Builder
Message 5 relatives asking for a family recipe and a photo

p.title: Food We Eat
p.source: NCERT Our Wondrous World, Class 3, Chapter 8 (pages 100–108), Unit 3 'Gifts of Nature', Reprint 2026-27
p.summary: Starting from your child's favourite dishes and the six tastes of a festive chhappan bhog, this chapter asks why we eat and drink. Through the story of Shirin the runner, your child learns that a strong, healthy body needs a balanced variety of home-cooked food and plenty of water; they then explore seasonal and regional foods, find out which part of a plant or animal each food comes from, and solve the puzzle of salt and water, which come from neither.
goals: By the end your child can explain why we need to eat and drink: food gives energy to move and play, helps the body grow and repair, and keeps it well, and water keeps the body working.
By the end your child can say what a balanced diet is, sort foods into energy-giving, body-building and protective foods, and build a balanced thali from Indian foods.
By the end your child can name the six tastes of Indian tradition, test their own sense of taste, and explain that the old 'tongue map' was wrong.
By the end your child can give examples of seasonal and regional foods and explain why we drink more in summer.
By the end your child can say which part of a plant (root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed) or which animal each common food comes from, and that salt and water come from neither.
By the end your child can suggest ways to share food and reduce food waste at home, and say why people still argue about how India grows its food.
words: meals that have the right mix of different kinds of food (grains, dal, vegetables, fruits, milk, nuts) and water, so the body gets everything it needs
the power our body needs to move, play, think and keep warm; grains like rice, roti and ragi, and fats like ghee, give lots of it
the seed of a grass plant that we eat, like rice, wheat, ragi, jowar and bajra
the dried seeds of bean and pea plants, such as moong, toor, masoor, chana and rajma; we cook them as dal
food that grows and is fresh at a particular time of year, like mangoes in summer and carrots and sarson in winter
a plant grown in large amounts on a farm for food or other uses, like wheat, rice, sugarcane or cotton
salty water that comes out through tiny holes in our skin when we are hot or busy playing; it cools the body as it dries
what the tongue tells us about food; scientists name five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami (savoury)
a kind of stored energy food made by plants; rice, potato, wheat and bread are full of it
a seed that has soaked up water and started to grow a tiny root and shoot, like moong sprouts
a Japanese word for the savoury, meaty taste found in ripe tomatoes, mushrooms, cheese and soups
food that is thrown away instead of being eaten

days.title: My favourite food and the six tastes
days.goal: Begin with the food your child loves, discover the six tastes of chhappan bhog by tasting them, meet the ancient Indian idea of six rasas, and start a sprouting experiment.

steps.title: If you could eat only one dish…
steps.do: Ask: 'If you could choose just one dish for dinner tonight, what would it be?' Then: 'Who makes it best in our family? What does it smell like when it is cooking?' Let your child talk freely. Ask one more: 'Is there any food you do not like? Why?' Note their answers; we will come back to them on the last day.

steps.title: My favourite food (pages 100–101)
steps.do: Open page 100 and do the task: your child draws two or three favourite home-made dishes and writes their names (for example poha, rajma-chawal, idli-sambar, aloo paratha, kheer). Then do Activity 1 on page 101: 'Share your reasons for why you like these foods.' Good reasons: the taste (sweet, spicy, tangy), the smell, the crunch or softness, who cooks it, a festival memory. Read the paragraph on page 101 about sweet, sour, spicy and bitter foods aloud, and ask the book's question: 'Have you wondered why we eat and drink?' Do not answer yet; say 'Let's find out this week.'

steps.title: The six-taste plate
steps.do: Read the chhappan bhog box on page 101 aloud: 56 dishes for festivals, with six tastes: sweet (meetha), spicy (teekha), astringent (kasaila), sour (khatta), salty (namkeen) and bitter (karva). Make a small tasting plate with a pinch or a tiny piece of each: jaggery (sweet), a slice of green chilli touched to the tongue or a pinch of black pepper (spicy; adult supervises, give water after), a slice of raw unripe banana, raw guava skin or a sip of strong black tea (astringent: it makes the mouth feel dry and puckery), lemon (sour), a few grains of salt (salty) and a tiny piece of karela or a methi seed (bitter). Your child tastes each, sips water in between, and names the taste. Ask: 'Which was the hardest to name?' (Usually astringent, because it feels more like dryness than a taste.) Ask: 'Which of these tastes are in our dal-chawal today?'

steps.title: Six rasas or five tastes?
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v3: the Charaka Samhita, an ancient Indian medical book, also names six tastes (rasas), and today's taste scientists count differently. Ask: 'When you tasted chilli, did it feel like a taste, or more like heat or burning?' and 'When you tasted the raw banana, was it a taste or a dry feeling?' Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Start the chana sprouting test
steps.do: Set up Experiment e1. Weigh exactly 50 g of dry kala chana or whole moong on a kitchen scale with your child (if you have no scale, count out 50 seeds and fill a small steel katori level to the top instead). Your child writes the weight and draws one seed actual size. Put the seeds in a bowl and cover with three times as much water. Ask them to predict: 'Tomorrow morning, will the seeds weigh more, less or the same? Will the bowl have more water or less water?' Write down the predictions.

need: tasting plate: jaggery, green chilli or black pepper, raw guava or unripe banana or black tea, lemon, salt, a small piece of karela or a methi seed
50 g dry kala chana or whole moong

prep.task: Buy a small karela, a lemon and a raw guava or banana for the tasting plate

days.title: Shirin the runner: why we need different foods
days.goal: Read Shirin's story, understand why eating only one or two foods is not enough, and sort foods into energy-giving, body-building and protective groups.

steps.title: Weigh the soaked chana
steps.do: Continue Experiment e1. Drain the chana and look at the bowl: is there less water than last night? Weigh the soaked seeds (or see if they still fit in the katori; they won't). A typical result: 50 g becomes about 100 g. Ask: 'Where did the extra weight come from?' Good answer: 'The seeds drank up the water.' Then wrap the chana in a damp cotton cloth or put them in a sprout box, and keep in a warm place. Ask: 'What do you think will happen in one more day?'

steps.title: Story of Shirin, the runner (pages 101–103)
steps.do: Read the story of Shirin aloud from the bottom of page 101 to the top of page 103. Pause after Shirin says 'I like only rice and potatoes' and ask: 'What do you think the champion will say?' Then read on. Ask: 'Was it wrong to eat rice and potatoes?' (No, they are good, but they are not enough on their own.) 'What else did the champion tell her to eat?' (Different vegetables and fruits, grains like rice, ragi, jowar, wheat and bajra, dal and nuts, and food cooked at home.) 'What changed for Shirin after a few months?' (She stopped falling sick, ran faster, felt energetic and won a medal.) Then ask the question on page 103: 'Why do we need to eat healthy food?'

steps.title: Why do we eat and drink? (page 101)
steps.do: Now answer the page 101 question together: 'Why do we need to eat and drink?' Ask an elder in the family too, as the book suggests. Collect three reasons and write them in the notebook: 1. Food gives us energy to move, run, think and stay warm (like petrol for a scooter). 2. Food gives our body the material to grow taller, build muscles and heal a cut. 3. Food helps keep us well and fight off illness. Add: 'And water? Our body is more than half water, and we lose some every day in sweat, breath and urine, so we must keep drinking.'

steps.title: Book Activity 2 and the three-group sort (page 103)
steps.do: Do Activity 2 on page 103: your child ticks the foods they eat regularly (vegetables, sweets, milk, salads, dal, rice, lassi, snacks, fruits, juice, roti, paneer). Then draw three big circles on a sheet: 'Go foods (energy)', 'Grow foods (body-building)' and 'Glow foods (protective)'. From the kitchen, bring real examples and sort them: rice, roti, ragi, potato, ghee, jaggery go in Go; dal, chana, milk, curd, paneer, eggs, nuts go in Grow; vegetables and fruits like palak, carrot, tomato, guava, banana go in Glow. Tell your child honestly: many foods do more than one job (milk gives energy too, and dal also gives fibre), so these groups are a helpful guide, not strict boxes. Finally ask the page 103 question: 'Which of these foods should be part of a balanced diet?' Good answer: 'Some from every circle each day, plus water; sweets and fried snacks only sometimes.'

steps.title: Shirin's new plate
steps.do: Ask your child to plan one day of meals for Shirin using foods from all three circles: breakfast, lunch, snack and dinner. For example: ragi dosa with chutney and milk; rice, dal, palak sabzi and curd; a banana and peanuts; roti, rajma and salad. Ask: 'Which circle was hardest to fill? Why?' Write the menu in the notebook.

need: the soaked chana, a kitchen scale, a damp cotton cloth or sprout box
a big sheet of paper and crayons
real food samples from the kitchen (rice, dal, potato, milk, a vegetable, a fruit, nuts)

days.title: The science of taste
days.goal: Test the old 'tongue map' with our own tongues, learn how scientists corrected it, meet the discoverer of umami, finish the sprouts and play Thali Builder.

steps.title: Sprout check and final weigh
steps.do: Finish Experiment e1. Open the cloth: the chana should have tiny white roots (sprouts). Your child weighs them again and draws one sprout next to the dry seed drawn on Day 1. Fill in the table: dry, soaked, sprouted. Ask: 'Why are the sprouts heavier than the dry seeds?' (They took in water; the seed is now a baby plant starting to grow.) Keep the sprouts in the fridge for a sprout chaat later today or tomorrow (lightly steam or boil them first).

steps.title: Test the tongue map
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Make four small cups: sugar water, salt water, lemon water, and bitter water (soak a few methi seeds or a slice of karela in water for 10 minutes). Draw a big tongue on paper and mark tip, left side, right side and back. First show your child the old 'tongue map' idea: 'Some books used to say sweet is tasted only at the tip, salty and sour at the sides and bitter at the back.' Ask them to predict if this is true. Then, with a fresh cotton bud for each dip, touch each liquid to the tip, the side and the middle of the back of the tongue (not too far back), with a sip of plain water in between. Your child writes on the tongue drawing where they could taste each one. They will find they can taste every taste on every part, though some spots may feel a little stronger.

steps.title: The map that was wrong
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v1 (the tongue map: Hänig, Boring and the scientists who checked). Point out that your child has just done what scientists did to correct it: tested it instead of believing the picture. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Kikunae Ikeda and the fifth taste
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v2. Give your child a small piece of very ripe tomato, and if you have them, a sip of clear vegetable or tomato soup or a bit of cheese. Ask: 'Is this sweet, sour, salty or bitter? Or something else, a full, savoury taste?' That 'something else' is umami. Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Thali Builder
steps.do: Play the DeepKids game Thali Builder. Make about 30 food cards with a picture or name and a symbol: a sun for Go (energy), a brick for Grow (body-building), a star for Glow (protective). Include many Indian foods: roti, rice, ragi mudde, poha, dal, rajma, chana, curd, paneer, egg, fish, palak, bhindi, carrot, guava, banana, mango, peanuts, ghee, jalebi, chips. Deal 5 cards each; take turns drawing and discarding. The first to hold a thali with at least one sun, one brick and two stars, and say why, wins. Then play a twist round: draw a 'region card' (Kerala, Punjab, Bengal, Rajasthan) and build a balanced thali with foods from that place. Other players can challenge a card's region, and the player must explain.

need: the sprouted chana and the kitchen scale
4 small cups: sugar water, salt water, lemon water, bitter methi or karela water
a packet of cotton buds and plain water
a ripe tomato (and clear soup or cheese if available)
card paper and pens for 30 food cards

prep.task: Make the 30 Thali Builder cards (or let your child help as a craft the day before)

days.title: Food changes with the seasons and the place
days.goal: Find out why we eat different foods in summer and winter, and in different parts of India, and start collecting a family recipe.

steps.title: We eat different things (page 104)
steps.do: Read 'We eat different things' on page 104 aloud. Ask: 'What do we like to eat when it is very hot?' (Kulfi, ice-cream, tender coconut water, buttermilk, watermelon, curd rice.) 'And when it is cold?' (Soups, stew, hot drinks, gajar halwa, til laddoo, bajra roti, sarson ka saag.) Ask: 'Why do mangoes come in summer and not in December?' Good answer: 'Each plant flowers and gives fruit at its own time of year; mango trees flower in late winter and the fruits ripen in the summer heat.'

steps.title: Summer and winter list at the sabzi shop
steps.do: Do the summer/winter table on page 104. Visit the local sabzi mandi, vegetable cart or the fruit shop with your child, or ask the vegetable seller when he comes. Ask him: 'Which vegetables and fruits are fresh now? Which ones come only in summer? Which only in winter?' Your child writes them into the two columns in the book. Typical answers: summer: mango, watermelon, muskmelon, lychee, jamun, lauki, karela, bhindi, cucumber; winter: carrot, peas, cauliflower, sarson, methi, radish, oranges, guava, amla. Ask: 'Which is cheaper today: a fruit that is in season or one that is not?' Notice that seasonal food is often fresher and cheaper because it did not travel far or sit in cold storage.

steps.title: Food from other parts of India (page 104)
steps.do: Read the second paragraph on page 104 aloud. Ask: 'Which dishes have you heard about but never tasted?' Then call a relative or friend who lives in another state, or remember a trip, and ask what they eat every day. Your child marks a rough outline map of India (draw it or print it) with at least five dishes: for example, Kashmir: rogan josh or kahwa; Punjab: makki di roti and sarson da saag; Gujarat: dhokla; Rajasthan: dal baati; Bengal: machher jhol; Kerala: appam and stew, puttu; Tamil Nadu: idli, pongal; Assam: masor tenga; Maharashtra: puran poli. Ask: 'Why do you think people near the sea eat more fish, and people in dry Rajasthan eat more bajra?' (People cook what grows or lives near them; bajra grows with little water.)

steps.title: Start the family recipe book
steps.do: Start Activity a1. Your child interviews a grandparent or another elder (in person or by phone) about one dish they grew up eating. Questions: 'What is the dish called? Where did you learn it? What goes into it? Which ingredients come from plants and which from animals? When was it made: every day, a special season or a festival?' Your child writes the answers on the first page of a small notebook titled 'Our Family Cookbook'. Decide together which day this week you will cook it together (Day 7).

need: a shopping bag and a little money for the sabzi shop
a printed or hand-drawn outline map of India
a phone to call a relative
a small notebook for the family cookbook

prep.task: Ask a grandparent or elder to be ready to talk about one family dish on the phone

days.title: Water is life and food grows in fields
days.goal: Understand why we drink more in hot weather, track how much we drink, find out which crops grow in fields, and test foods for starch.

steps.title: Summer drinks and sweat (page 105)
steps.do: Look at the drinks on page 105 (tender coconut water, mango juice, aam panna, orange juice, lime water) and ask your child to name each in your home language (for example, elaneer in Tamil, nariyal pani in Hindi, daab in Bengali). Read the paragraph below aloud. Ask: 'Why do we drink more in summer?' (We sweat more, and sweat is water leaving the body.) 'Where else do we sweat?' (When we run and play.) Ask your child to lick the back of their hand after running around: it tastes a little salty. Explain: sweat is water with a little salt; as it dries on the skin it cools us down. Ask the book's question: 'How often do you drink water?'

steps.title: My water bottle chart
steps.do: Give your child a steel or plastic water bottle and mark its side with tape every quarter. Make a chart for the rest of today and tomorrow: Time, How much I drank, What I was doing. Ask: 'Did you drink more after playing outside?' A child of this age needs roughly 5 to 7 glasses of water a day, more in hot weather or after sport. Ask: 'How do you know when your body needs water?' (Thirst, dry mouth, dark yellow urine, feeling tired or getting a headache.)

steps.title: Where does food come from? (page 105)
steps.do: Read 'Where does food come from?' at the bottom of page 105. Do both tasks. First, your child writes names of crops grown in fields: rice (paddy), wheat, ragi, jowar, bajra, maize, sugarcane, mustard, groundnut, toor, chana, potato, onion, cotton (not a food, but a crop). Then the second task: in what form is each cooked? (Wheat becomes roti, puri, halwa; rice becomes chawal, idli, dosa, poha, kheer; ragi becomes mudde, dosa or porridge; chana becomes dal, besan, chole; sugarcane becomes sugar, jaggery or juice.) Ask: 'Who grows all this for us?' (Farmers.)

steps.title: M.S. Swaminathan and India's wheat fields
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v4. Show the rice and wheat in your kitchen and a bit of ragi or bajra flour. Ask: 'Which of these needs the most water to grow?' (Rice, by far.) Then ask the voice question and let your child weigh both sides.

steps.title: Which foods are full of starch?
steps.do: Do Experiment e3 (adult handles the iodine). On a steel plate, put small pieces of raw potato, cooked rice, bread or roti, cucumber, apple, a pinch of sugar and a pinch of besan or ragi flour. Ask your child to predict which ones will turn blue-black (meaning they contain starch). Mix 5 drops of Betadine or tincture of iodine in a spoon of water and put one drop on each food. Your child records the colour. Potato, rice, bread, roti and flours turn dark blue-black; cucumber, apple and sugar stay yellow-brown. Explain: starch is the energy food plants store in their seeds, roots and stems, so these are our Go foods. Throw everything away afterwards; do not eat it.

steps.title: Core worksheet (part 1)
steps.do: Do section A of Worksheet ws1 (core) now: why we eat and the three food groups. Keep sections B and C for Day 6 after the plant-parts lesson. Read aloud if needed and mark it together.

need: small bowls of rice, wheat and ragi or bajra
raw potato, cooked rice, bread or roti, cucumber, apple, sugar, a flour
Betadine (povidone-iodine) or tincture of iodine, a dropper and a steel plate

prep.task: Buy or find a small bottle of Betadine or tincture of iodine from a chemist

days.title: Which part do we eat? And the salt-and-water puzzle
days.goal: Sort our foods by the part of the plant they come from, list foods from animals, trace dinner back to its origins, and solve the puzzle of salt and water.

steps.title: Parts of plants we eat (pages 106–107)
steps.do: Turn to pages 106 and 107. Read each heading and name each picture together: leaves (spinach/palak, fenugreek/methi, cabbage, mustard, coriander/dhaniya), fruits (guava, sapota/chikoo, apple, mango), roots (carrot, radish, beetroot), stems (potatoes, bamboo shoots, ginger, onion) and seeds (grains, pulses, dry fruits). Your child ticks the ones they eat, as the book asks. Ask: 'Potato grows under the ground. Why is it under stems, not roots?' (It has 'eyes', buds that sprout into new shoots, and only stems have buds.) Tell them honestly: an onion is mostly fleshy leaves wrapped round a very short flat stem, which is why some books call it a stem and others a bulb of leaves.

steps.title: Kitchen plant-part hunt
steps.do: Open the vegetable basket and the masala box. Your child finds one food for each plant part and lays them in a row: root (carrot, radish, beetroot), stem (potato, ginger, sugarcane), leaf (methi, palak, curry leaves), flower (cauliflower, broccoli, banana flower; and from the masala box: cloves are dried flower buds), fruit (tomato, bhindi, brinjal, cucumber; yes, these 'vegetables' are fruits because they hold seeds), seed (rice, dal, jeera, peanuts, rajma). Ask: 'Which part did you find most of?' Then read the line on page 107 about foods from animals: milk, curd, ghee, cheese, paneer, honey, eggs and meat. Ask: 'Which animals do these come from?' (Cow, buffalo, goat; bees for honey; hens for eggs; fish, goat and chicken for meat, for families who eat it.)

steps.title: Food-origin trail
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Choose five things you will eat at dinner tonight (for example roti, dal, aloo sabzi, curd, a banana). For each, your child draws a chain of arrows back to where it came from: roti ← atta ← wheat seeds ← wheat plant in a field in Punjab or Madhya Pradesh ← farmer. Curd ← milk ← cow or buffalo ← grass and fodder ← a plant again! Ask: 'Did every chain end at a plant?' Most will, even the animal foods, because animals eat plants. Ask: 'How many people helped bring this food to our plate?' (Farmer, truck driver, mill, shopkeeper, the cook at home.)

steps.title: Puzzle time: neither plant nor animal (page 107)
steps.do: Read the 'Puzzle time' box on page 107 and let your child guess: 'Two of our most common ingredients come neither from plants nor animals.' Give hints: 'One is in every glass we drink. One is in the namak dabba.' The answers are water and salt. Then set up Experiment e4 to see where salt comes from: stir 2 teaspoons of salt into half a cup of warm water until it disappears. Pour it into a dark-coloured plate or a steel plate and put it in the sun. Ask: 'Where did the salt go? Will we get it back?' Check tomorrow. Tell your child that most of our salt is made exactly like this, in huge flat salt pans by the sea in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, and sendha namak (rock salt) is dug out of the ground.

steps.title: Core worksheet (part 2)
steps.do: Finish Worksheet ws1 (core) sections B and C: parts of plants we eat and foods from animals. Let your child use the food row from the kitchen hunt to check answers.

need: vegetables, masala box, grains and dals from the kitchen
paper and pencil for the food-origin trail
salt, warm water, a cup and a dark or steel plate

days.title: Cooking, sharing and not wasting
days.goal: Cook a family recipe together and write it down, think about sharing food and avoiding waste, see salt crystals appear, and stretch our thinking with worksheets.

steps.title: Salt crystals are back
steps.do: Check Experiment e4. The water in the plate should have evaporated, leaving white crusty salt crystals. Your child looks closely, using a magnifying glass if you have one: many grains are tiny cubes. Ask: 'Where did the water go?' (Into the air; it evaporated in the sun.) 'Where did the salt come from?' (It was in the water all the time, dissolved.) 'So where does sea salt come from?' (Sea water is let into shallow pans and the sun dries it.)

steps.title: Cook the family recipe
steps.do: Continue Activity a1. Cook the dish your child collected on Day 4, or a simple one like sprout chaat (using the sprouts from e1, steamed, with onion, tomato, lemon and salt). Your child washes hands first and does safe jobs: washing vegetables, measuring with spoons and cups, mixing, tearing coriander, setting the plate. As you cook, ask: 'Which ingredients came from plants? Which from animals? Which from neither?' and 'Which tastes are in this dish?' Afterwards, your child writes the recipe in Our Family Cookbook, as question B2 on page 108 asks: name, who taught it, ingredients with amounts, and steps in order.

steps.title: Sharing and food waste (pages 107–108)
steps.do: Ask the question at the bottom of page 107: 'Would you share your food with your friend if your friend did not bring lunch?' Listen, then ask 'Why?' Then ask Discuss question A4 on page 108: 'Why is it important to avoid wasting food? What are ways to reduce food waste at home?' Good answers: farmers worked hard, water and land were used to grow it, many people go hungry; take only as much as you can eat, use leftovers (leftover rice becomes lemon rice or curd rice, stale roti becomes a snack), store food properly, give extra food to someone who needs it, and put peels into compost. Ask your child to watch tonight's dinner and count anything thrown away.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 (stretch) now. For the masala sort, open the masala box so your child can hold each spice: jeera and mustard are seeds, cloves are dried flower buds, cinnamon is the bark of a tree, haldi is an underground stem, curry leaves are leaves, and sugar is made from the sugarcane stem.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Start Worksheet ws3 (challenge) section A now (the nose-holding apple and potato test is fun to do right away), and finish sections B and C at bedtime or tomorrow morning. In section C there is no single right answer: praise reasons that use evidence from this week ('in my tongue test…', 'Swaminathan helped India have enough wheat, but…').

need: the salt plate from yesterday and a magnifying glass if available
ingredients for the family recipe or sprout chaat

prep.task: Buy the ingredients for the family recipe

days.title: Let us reflect, check and teach it back
days.goal: Answer the book's reflection questions, draw our three thalis, make and share a fruit chaat, check understanding and teach the chapter back.

steps.title: Let us reflect: Discuss (page 108)
steps.do: Ask Discuss questions A1 to A3 on page 108 aloud. A1: 'Why do we need different kinds of food?' (Each kind does a different job: energy, growth and repair, keeping well; no single food has everything, as Shirin found out.) A2: 'Why do we eat seasonal foods?' (They are fresh, tasty and cheaper, they suit the weather, like cooling buttermilk in summer, and they did not travel far.) A3: 'How can you tell if a food is healthy or unhealthy?' (Home-cooked, fresh, varied, not too much sugar, salt or oil; very sweet, fried or packaged snacks are fine only sometimes.) Also ask the 'Think' question E: 'A guest arrives suddenly. What would you serve, and why?'

steps.title: Eating together: fruit chaat (page 108)
steps.do: Do Activity a3, based on 'Eating together' (D) on page 108. Your child chooses 3–4 seasonal fruits, washes them, and with you cuts them (a child-safe knife or butter knife for soft fruit like banana and papaya; an adult cuts hard fruit). Add a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chaat masala or black salt. Your child names the plant part (fruit) and the tastes (sweet, sour, salty). Share it with family members or a neighbour. Then do Write question B3 on page 108: name a food with both plant and animal ingredients (for example lassi: curd from milk and sugar from sugarcane; kheer: milk and rice; paneer tikka: paneer and capsicum).

steps.title: Three thalis (page 108)
steps.do: Do Draw questions C1 and C2 on page 108: your child draws three plates or thalis in the notebook, for morning, afternoon and night, and labels each food in them. Then ask them to colour a small sun, brick or star beside each food (Go, Grow, Glow). Ask: 'Is each thali balanced? What would you add?' Also finish Write question B1: list the fruits and vegetables your family eats.

steps.title: Chapter check
steps.do: Ask the 8 check questions aloud, one at a time, without the book. Tick the ones answered well. For each one missed, open the right page (tastes p101, Shirin p102–103, seasons p104, water p105, plant parts p106–107) and look for one minute, then ask again in different words. Six or more right is good; fewer than five means play Thali Builder and the kitchen plant-part hunt again next week.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is now the teacher; you or a grandparent are the student. Using the three-circle chart, the food-origin trail, the tongue drawing and the salt plate, they teach in 5 minutes: why we eat and drink, what a balanced diet is, which part of a plant our foods come from, and why salt and water are special. Ask two 'student' questions: 'If I only eat rice and potatoes, what will happen?' and 'Is it true we taste sweet only on the tip of the tongue?' End by looking back at Day 1's answer about the food they did not like, and ask: 'Would you try it once more, cooked a new way?'

need: 3–4 seasonal fruits, lemon, chaat masala or black salt, a child-safe knife
the charts and drawings from this week

prep.task: Buy 3–4 seasonal fruits for the fruit chaat

worksheets.title: Why we eat and where food comes from

sections.p: Shirin often fell sick. What did the champion say she should change?
opts: Eat many kinds of food: vegetables, fruits, different grains, dal and nuts, cooked at home

sections.p: Sort these foods into the group they mostly belong to.
In summer we sweat a lot and lose ____ from our body, so we must drink more.

sections: B. Parts of plants we eat

sections.p: Which part of the plant do we eat?
Why is a potato called a stem and not a root?
opts: It has 'eyes' (buds) that sprout new shoots

sections.p: Where does each food come from?
Match the drink to the plant or animal it comes from.
pairs: Milk of a cow or buffalo

sections.p: Draw a balanced thali. Label each food and mark it Go, Grow or Glow.
Cauliflower is which part of the plant?
Tomato, bhindi and brinjal are called vegetables in the kitchen. A scientist would call them:
Sort these items from the masala box and kitchen.
When are these usually fresh and plentiful in most of India?
People in coastal Kerala eat lots of fish and coconut, and people in dry Rajasthan eat lots of bajra. Explain why, in two sentences.
Write your sprouting results.
One drop of iodine turned potato and rice blue-black, but cucumber stayed brown. What does this tell you about these foods?
We dissolved salt in water and left it in the sun. What was left behind next day, and where did the water go?

worksheets.title: Taste puzzles and big food questions

sections.p: Green chilli feels 'hot' but it is not hot to touch. Scientists say we feel chilli with the same nerves that feel heat and pain. Is spicy a taste, then? Give your reason.
Hold your nose and eat a small piece of apple, then a small piece of raw potato. Can you tell them apart? What does this tell you about smell and taste?
The fifth basic taste, found in ripe tomatoes and soups, is called ____.
What if you could eat only one food for a whole month? Which would you choose to stay healthiest, and what would your body still be missing?
What if all the bees disappeared? Which foods on your plate might become rare? (Hint: bees help many plants make fruits and seeds.)
For many decades school books showed a 'tongue map'. How did scientists find out it was wrong? What does this teach us about pictures in books?

The Green Revolution helped India grow much more wheat and rice so fewer people went hungry. Others say it used too much water and pushed out millets. Write one good point on each side, and what you would choose for your state.
Ayurveda counts six tastes; modern taste scientists count five basic tastes. Which is the best way to describe this?
opts: They sort the same experiences in different ways; scientists explain spicy and astringent as feelings of heat and dryness rather than taste-bud tastes
Everyone agrees there are exactly six

experiments.title: How much heavier do sprouts get?
experiments.question: What happens to the weight of dry seeds when they are soaked and sprouted, and why?
need: 50 g dry kala chana or whole moong
a kitchen scale (or a small katori to measure volume)
a damp cotton cloth or sprout box
steps: Weigh 50 g of dry seeds and draw one seed actual size.
Soak the seeds overnight in three times their amount of water.
Next morning, drain, look at how much water is left, and weigh the seeds again.
Wrap the seeds in a damp cloth or put them in a sprout box in a warm place.
After one more day, weigh the sprouts and draw one next to the dry seed.
Record all three weights in a table.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: after soaking, will the seeds weigh more, less or the same? Will there be more or less water in the bowl?
experiments.observe: The seeds swell to about twice their size, the skins may wrinkle or split, and there is less water in the bowl. After sprouting, a small white root appears. The weight roughly doubles, for example from 50 g to about 100 g.
experiments.why: A dry seed has very little water in it. When it is soaked, water enters through the seed coat and a tiny hole near the scar of the seed, and the seed swells, just as a dry sponge swells. The water wakes up the baby plant inside, which starts using its stored food to grow a root and shoot. The extra weight is almost all the water the seed drank. This is also why sprouts are soft and easy to cook, and why soaked chana cooks faster than dry chana.
experiments.safety: Rinse sprouts twice a day if you keep them longer. Steam or boil sprouts before eating; raw sprouts can carry germs.
experiments.time: 9 min to set up + 6 min next morning + 5 min the day after

experiments.title: Test the tongue map
experiments.question: Is it true that we taste sweet only at the tip of the tongue, salty and sour at the sides and bitter at the back?
need: 4 small cups: sugar water, salt water, lemon water, bitter water (methi seeds or karela soaked in water)
a big tongue drawing on paper
steps: Draw a big tongue and mark four places: tip, left side, right side, middle of the back.
Your child sticks out their tongue. Dip a fresh cotton bud in sugar water and touch it to the tip.
Ask them to say what they taste before pulling the tongue back in. Sip plain water.
Repeat on each side and on the middle of the back. Use a new cotton bud every time.
Do the same for salt, lemon and bitter water.
Mark on the drawing every place each taste was felt.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first, after you show them the old tongue map: will sugar water taste sweet if we touch it to the back of the tongue? Will bitter be tasted at the tip?
experiments.observe: Every taste can be felt on every part of the tongue that has taste buds. Some children find one area slightly stronger for a particular taste, but no area tastes only one thing. The very middle of the tongue has fewer taste buds, so tastes may feel weaker there.
experiments.why: Your tongue is covered in tiny bumps, and on them are thousands of taste buds. Each taste bud has taste cells for sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami, so every part of the tongue that has taste buds can sense every basic taste. When a taste cell senses a taste, it sends a message along a nerve to the brain, and the brain tells you 'sweet!' The tongue map came from a misreading of an old experiment that found only very small differences in sensitivity. Your own test is the same kind of evidence that showed it was wrong.
experiments.safety: Use a fresh cotton bud for each dip, and do not touch too far back on the tongue. Check for any food allergy first.

experiments.title: Which foods are full of starch?
experiments.question: Which of our everyday foods contain starch, the plant's stored energy food?
need: small pieces of raw potato, cooked rice, bread or roti, cucumber, apple
a pinch of sugar and a pinch of besan or ragi flour
steps: Arrange the foods on the plate, a little apart from each other, and label them.
An adult mixes about 5 drops of iodine into a spoonful of water.
Put one drop of the iodine water on each food.
Wait one minute and look at the colour of each spot.
Record: food, colour, starch yes or no.
Throw away all the tested food and wash the plate and hands.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which foods will turn dark blue-black? Will sugar, which is sweet, turn black?
experiments.observe: Potato, rice, bread, roti and flours turn dark blue-black. Cucumber, apple and sugar stay orange-brown (the colour of the iodine). Ripe apple may show a few dark spots.
experiments.why: Iodine reacts with starch to make a dark blue-black colour, so it is a simple test for starch. Plants make sugar in their leaves using sunlight, then join thousands of sugar pieces together into long chains called starch to store it, mostly in seeds (rice, wheat, dal), underground stems (potato) and roots. Starch is a big energy store, which is why these are 'Go' foods. When we chew and digest starch, our body breaks it back into sugar for energy; chew a piece of plain roti for a long time and it starts tasting slightly sweet, because saliva begins this breaking-up. Sugar itself does not turn black because it is not starch.
experiments.safety: An adult handles the iodine. Iodine stains skin and clothes and must not be swallowed. Do not eat the tested food.

experiments.title: Getting salt back from water
experiments.question: Where does salt go when it dissolves in water, and how do people get salt from the sea?
need: half a cup of warm water
steps: Stir 2 teaspoons of salt into half a cup of warm water until you cannot see any salt.
Ask your child to taste a drop from a fingertip: is the salt still there?
Pour the salty water into the plate.
Leave the plate in a sunny place, away from dust, for a day or two.
Look at the plate with a magnifying glass and draw what you see.
