cols: Who hoists the flag or what people do

sections.p: Sort these festivals by what decides their date.
12 moon-months make about 354 days. A calendar year has 365 days. So Eid comes about ____ days earlier each year.
If Eid was in April this year, in which month will it be about three years from now? Show how you worked it out.
Why does Deepawali stay in October or November even though it follows the moon?
opts: It does not follow the moon
An extra month is added to the Hindu calendar about every three years
The moon is always full in Kartik

sections.p: What if the Earth did not spin? Would we still have day and night? Think about what Aryabhata said.
What if every festival in India were celebrated by only one religion and no one joined anyone else's? What would we lose?
Some people say Eid should begin only when the crescent is seen with the eyes; others say we can calculate it. Write one good reason for each side.
Makara Sankranti is on about 14 January, but the noon sun starts climbing higher from about 21 December. Using your shadow stick results, explain how both can be called the start of Uttarayan.

experiments.title: The noon shadow stick
experiments.question: Does the length of the noon shadow change from week to week, and what does that tell us about the sun's path?
need: a straight stick or 30 cm ruler
clay or a bottle filled with sand to hold it upright
a sheet of paper and tape
steps: Tape the paper flat on a sunny floor and stand the stick upright at one edge of it.
Mark where the stick stands so you can put it back in exactly the same place.
At about 12 noon, mark the tip of the shadow with a dot and write the date.
Measure the shadow length from the stick to the dot.
Repeat at the same time on Days 2, 5 and 6 (and if possible again a month later).
Compare the dots: are they moving towards the stick or away from it?
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: in a week, will the noon shadow be longer, shorter or the same? Why?
experiments.observe: Record the date and shadow length each time. Between late December and late June the noon shadow gets shorter; between late June and late December it gets longer. The change is fastest in March and September and very slow near 21 June and 21 December.
experiments.why: The Earth's spin axis is tilted, so as the Earth goes round the sun during the year, the sun at noon stands higher in our sky in summer and lower in winter. A higher sun casts a shorter shadow. The lowest noon sun, and the shortest day, comes at the winter solstice around 21–22 December; after that the sun climbs higher and rises further north each day: this is Uttarayan, the sun's northward journey. Makara Sankranti on about 14 January is fixed by the sun's position among the stars (entering Makara, Capricorn), not by the solstice. Because the Earth's axis wobbles slowly like a spinning top (once in about 26,000 years), the star date and the solstice have drifted about three weeks apart over roughly 1,700 years.
experiments.safety: Never look straight at the sun. Look only at the shadow.
experiments.time: 12 min to set up + 3–8 min checks on Days 2, 5 and 6

experiments.title: Natural Holi colours and the turmeric surprise
experiments.question: Can we make safe colours from kitchen things, and are colours just colours, or are they chemicals that can change?
need: plates, spoons, a paintbrush, white paper
steps: Mix 1 spoon of haldi into 4 spoons of besan or cornflour for yellow.
Rub beetroot juice into cornflour and let it dry on a plate for pink.
Mix spinach paste or mehendi powder into cornflour for green.
Stir a pinch of haldi into a little water and paint three spots on paper.
Touch one spot with soapy water or baking soda water, one with lemon juice, and leave one alone.
Compare the three spots after one minute.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: what will happen to the yellow haldi spot when soapy water touches it? When lemon juice touches it?
experiments.observe: The soap or baking-soda spot turns red-brown; the lemon spot stays bright yellow; the untouched spot stays yellow. The kitchen colours rub off easily and smell of food.
experiments.why: Every colour, natural or factory-made, is a chemical. The yellow in turmeric is a chemical called curcumin. Soap and baking soda are bases (the opposite of acids), and curcumin changes shape in a base so it reflects red light instead of yellow; lemon is an acid, so curcumin stays yellow. Scientists call a colour that changes like this an indicator. The point is not that 'natural' means 'no chemicals', but that kitchen colours are chemicals we already eat safely. Cheap factory Holi colours can contain chemicals never meant for skin, such as industrial dyes, powdered glass for shine, or heavy metals, which can cause rashes, eye injuries and breathing trouble.
experiments.safety: Keep colours away from eyes. Haldi and beetroot can stain clothes and hands for a while. Do not use any colour that smells of petrol or has shiny particles.

experiments.title: Phases of the moon with a ball and a lamp
experiments.question: Why does the moon change shape through the month, from Amavasya to Purnima?
need: a lamp without a shade, or a phone torch on a pile of books
a ball or an orange stuck on a pencil
a room that can be darkened
steps: Darken the room and switch on the lamp on one side: this is the sun.
Your child holds the ball at arm's length, slightly above their head: their head is the Earth, the ball is the moon.
Face the lamp with the ball in front of it: see the dark side of the ball (new moon, Amavasya).
Turn slowly to the left, keeping the ball in front of your face. Watch a thin crescent appear.
Keep turning: half-lit (quarter moon), then fully lit when the lamp is behind you (full moon, Purnima). Keep the ball just above your head's shadow.
Continue round to come back to the dark new moon. Compare each shape with the moon diary.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: as you turn round, will the ball always look fully lit, or will its shape change? Why does the real moon change shape?
experiments.observe: Record the shape of the lit part at each quarter turn. The lit part grows from a thin crescent to a full circle, then shrinks again.
experiments.why: The moon makes no light of its own: one half of it is always lit by the sun, like the ball by the lamp. As the moon travels round the Earth once in about 29 and a half days, we see different amounts of its lit half. When it is between us and the sun, we face its dark half: Amavasya. When it is on the far side of the Earth from the sun, we see the whole lit half: Purnima. The first thin crescent after the new moon, seen just after sunset, starts each month of the Islamic calendar, which is why Eid begins with a moon sighting. Holi and Guru Nanak Jayanti fall on Purnima, and Deepawali on Amavasya.
experiments.safety: Do not touch a hot bulb. Keep the room clear so no one trips while turning in the dark.

experiments.title: The soot test: what is smoke?
experiments.question: Is smoke only a gas, or does it carry tiny solid bits that can get into our lungs?
need: a diya or candle and matches (adult use)
steps: An adult lights the diya and holds a steel spoon about 2 cm above the flame for 10 seconds.
Let the spoon cool for a minute, then your child wipes the bottom with a white tissue.
Blow out the candle or agarbatti and hold a white tissue near the rising smoke for 30 seconds (not in the flame).
Look at both tissues closely.
Talk about how many crackers burn in one city on one night.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: will the tissue stay white, or will something black come off the spoon? Is smoke just air?
experiments.observe: Black soot comes off the spoon onto the tissue. The tissue held in smoke turns slightly grey or yellow and smells smoky.
experiments.why: A flame burns oil or wax, but not every bit burns completely. The unburnt bits of carbon float up as soot, too small to see one by one. Smoke is a mix of hot gases and these tiny solid and liquid particles. The smallest ones (scientists call them PM2.5, finer than a thirtieth of a hair's width) go deep into our lungs and can make asthma and coughs worse. Firecrackers burn gunpowder and metal salts (which give the colours) all at once, so they release far more smoke and harmful gases in a few hours, and their bangs can be loud enough to damage hearing. That is why the book says children, old and sick people suffer most.
experiments.safety: An adult handles the flame and the spoon. Tie back long hair and keep tissues away from the flame. Do this near an open window and only for a short time.

activities.title: Our festival calendar wheel
steps: Draw a big circle and divide it into 12 slices, with January at the top.
Write each festival from the lesson in its month, with a small drawing (a kite, a diya, a star, a crescent).
Add your family's own festivals and birthdays.
Circle festivals whose date moves each year.
Colour the three national festivals in saffron, white and green.
Hang it on the wall and add to it during the year.
activities.outcome: A wall calendar of India's festivals that shows which come with the harvest, which follow the moon and which are national.

activities.title: Til-gud laddoos for Makara Sankranti
need: half a cup of white til
steps: An adult dry-roasts the til on low heat until it smells nutty, then sets it aside.
An adult melts the jaggery with the ghee and a spoon of water until it bubbles.
Mix in the til and take it off the heat.
When it is warm but not hot, your child greases their palms and rolls small laddoos.
Say 'Tilgul ghya, goad goad bola' (take til-gud and speak sweetly).
Share some with a neighbour.
activities.outcome: A plate of home-made til-gud laddoos, and the idea that harvest foods are shared to make relations sweeter.

activities.title: Moon diary
need: a calendar showing Purnima and Amavasya
steps: Each night at about the same time, find the moon from a window or outdoors.
Draw its shape in a small box with the date and time.
If it is cloudy or you cannot find the moon, write that down too.
Mark this month's Purnima and Amavasya from the calendar.
After a week, see whether the moon is growing (waxing) or shrinking (waning).
Continue until the next Purnima if you can.
activities.outcome: A diary of real moon shapes that matches the ball-and-lamp model and explains why moon-based festivals move.

activities.title: A paper Tiranga with the right proportions
steps: Cut paper to 15 cm long and 10 cm high (3 to 2).
Draw two lines to make three equal stripes, each about 3.3 cm high.
Colour the top saffron and the bottom green; leave the middle white.
Draw a navy-blue circle in the centre of the white stripe and 24 spokes.
Glue it to a straw or stick.
Keep it safely after the day; never throw it on the ground.
activities.outcome: A correctly proportioned paper national flag with a 24-spoke Ashoka Chakra.

voices.who: Aryabhata (476–about 550 CE), India
voices.idea: In his book the Aryabhatiya, written in 499 CE when he was 23, Aryabhata said that the Earth spins on its own axis, and that the stars only appear to move across the sky each night, just as a person in a moving boat sees the trees on the bank moving backwards. He also explained that the moon shines by reflecting sunlight and that eclipses are caused by shadows of the Earth and moon, not by demons swallowing the sun.
voices.then: Many later Indian astronomers, including the great Brahmagupta, rejected the spinning Earth, asking why things on it are not flung off. Some later copyists and commentators even changed his words so that the stars moved instead of the Earth.
voices.now: Aryabhata was right that the Earth spins, once a day, which gives us day and night. This was fully proved only much later, for example by Foucault's swinging pendulum in Paris in 1851. India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named Aryabhata after him.
voices.ask: Sitting still, you cannot feel the Earth spinning, and the sun seems to move across the sky. What evidence would make you believe the Earth is the one moving?

voices.who: Moon-sighting committees and astronomers: a live debate about Islamic calendars
voices.idea: The Islamic calendar is purely lunar: each month starts with the new crescent moon, and Eid-ul-Fitr begins the day after the crescent that ends Ramazan is seen. Traditionally, people must see it with their own eyes, and in India local moon-sighting committees (Ruet-e-Hilal committees) announce when it has been seen. Astronomers can now calculate the moment of the new moon, and roughly when a crescent becomes visible, years in advance.
voices.then: For centuries, sighting by eye was the only method. As astronomy improved, some Muslim scholars argued that reliable calculations should be accepted; others replied that the tradition asks for an actual sighting.
voices.now: Both views are held today. Some councils, such as the Fiqh Council of North America, decided in 2006 to use astronomical calculations; many scholars and committees, including most in India, still require a local sighting. So Eid can fall on different days in different countries, or even different cities. This is a debate about tradition and method, not about the moon itself, which both sides agree on.
voices.ask: If clouds hide the crescent but the calculation says it is there, has the new month begun? What would you trust more, your eyes or a calculation, and why?

voices.who: Guru Nanak (1469–1539), Punjab
voices.idea: Guru Nanak, born in Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan), taught that all people are equal before God, whatever their caste, religion or whether they are a man or a woman. The langar, the free community kitchen where everyone sits together in rows (pangat) on the floor and eats the same food, became a way of practising this equality; later Sikh Gurus made it a central part of every gurdwara.
voices.then: In his time many people believed that eating with people of other castes made them impure, so sitting together in one row was a bold challenge to the custom. Some people, both rich and poor, refused at first.
voices.now: Langar is served in gurdwaras across the world; the Golden Temple in Amritsar serves free meals to tens of thousands of people every day, cooked and served mostly by volunteers. The idea that people must not be treated differently by caste is now part of India's Constitution, though caste discrimination still exists in some places.
voices.ask: Why do you think eating the same food, sitting in the same row, makes people feel equal? What would you need to see to know that a custom has really changed people's minds?

check.q: What does 'unity in diversity' mean, and how do festivals show it?
check.a: People of many religions, regions and languages live as one country. Festivals show it because people of other religions join each other's celebrations, such as Eid seviyan, Christmas cake and Diwali sweets shared among neighbours.

check.q: Give three names of Makara Sankranti in different states, and say why it is celebrated.
check.a: Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Bihu in Assam, Lohri in Punjab, kite-flying Uttarayan in Gujarat, Khichadi Sankranti in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. It is a harvest festival when new crops like rice, til and sugarcane are in.

check.q: What is the story behind Holika Dahan, and what does the book say spoils Holi?
check.a: Holika, who could not be burnt, sat in a fire with Prahlad, but Prahlad was saved and Holika burnt: good over evil. Holi is spoiled by mud, coal-tar, chemical colours, drunkenness and taking revenge.

check.q: Why does Eid come about 11 days earlier every year?
check.a: The Islamic calendar follows the moon: 12 moon-months are about 354 days, 11 days fewer than a 365-day year. Each month begins when the new crescent moon is seen.

check.q: What is langar and what does it teach?
check.a: Langar is the free community meal in a gurdwara, served to everyone, whatever their caste, religion or status, sitting together. It teaches equality, sharing and service.

check.q: Name the five days of Deepawali and say why too many crackers are harmful.
check.a: Dhanteras, Narak Chaturdashi (Choti Diwali), Deepawali with Lakshmi Puja on Amavasya, Govardhan Puja, Bhai Dooj. Crackers make smoke full of tiny particles and harmful gases, and loud noise, which hurt children, old and sick people most.

check.q: What are our three national festivals and what does each mark?
check.a: Independence Day, 15 August, freedom from British rule in 1947; Republic Day, 26 January, the Constitution coming into force in 1950; Gandhi Jayanti, 2 October, Mahatma Gandhi's birth in 1869.

check.q: Why does the moon look different on Amavasya and Purnima?
check.a: The moon is lit by the sun. On Amavasya it is between the Earth and the sun, so we see its dark side; on Purnima it is on the far side of the Earth, so we see its whole lit face.

p.title: Our Basic Needs
p.source: NIOS Open Basic Education, Environmental Studies Level A (A 102), Lesson 7 (pages 92–99), 2016
p.summary: Some things we cannot live without: air, water and food. Two more, clothing and shelter, protect us and keep us well. Your child finds out what is in air that we need (oxygen) and what we breathe out (carbon dioxide), why our body is mostly water, how food gives us energy, why cotton keeps us cool and wool keeps us warm, and what makes a good, healthy house, along with how to keep each of these needs clean and safe.
goals: By the end your child can name the five basic needs (air, water, food, clothing, shelter) and explain which three we cannot survive without at all, and why.

By the end your child can explain that we breathe in air for its oxygen, that blood carries oxygen and food to every part of the body, and that we breathe out carbon dioxide, and can show carbon dioxide in their own breath with lime water.
By the end your child can say that about two-thirds of the body is water, list three jobs water does in the body, and give three ways to keep drinking water clean and stop mosquitoes breeding.
By the end your child can explain why cotton feels cool and wool keeps us warm (air passing through versus air trapped between fibres), after testing it themselves.
By the end your child can describe a good house (airy, with drainage, a ventilated kitchen, rubbish put in the right place) and explain why houses in snowy places have sloping roofs.
By the end your child can tell a need from a want and discuss whether people's needs really come in a fixed order.
words: the things every person must have to live and stay well: air, water, food, clothing and shelter
the gas in air that our body needs to live; the book calls it 'pran vayu' (Sanskrit for 'the air of life')
the waste gas our body makes and we breathe out
the two soft, spongy bags in the chest that fill with air when we breathe in
the red liquid, mostly water, that flows all round the body carrying oxygen and food and taking away waste
the power our body gets from food (with the help of oxygen) to move, think, grow and work
fresh air coming in and stale air going out of a room through windows, doors and vents
water that is clean and safe to drink
water that stays still in one place, like in a pot, tyre or cooler, where mosquitoes lay eggs
a very thin thread; cloth is woven or knitted from fibres of cotton, wool, silk or polyester
pipes and channels that carry used and dirty water away from a house
a house or any place that protects us from heat, cold, rain, wind and wild animals

days.title: What can't we live without?
days.goal: Find out from our own day what a person truly needs, meet the five basic needs from the book, and start a family water diary.

steps.title: The desert island game
steps.do: Say: 'Imagine you are going to live on an empty island for one month. You may take only five things. What will you take?' Write down your child's list without comment. Then ask about each item: 'Would you die without it, or would life just be less fun?' Many children list a phone, a toy or a favourite snack. Do not correct them yet; you will come back to this list at the end of today. If they are stuck, ask: 'What do you do every minute of the day without even thinking?' (Breathe.)

steps.title: The five basic needs (page 92)
steps.do: Read aloud the opening paragraphs of Lesson 7 on page 92, from 'Certain things are very essential for our life' to 'cyclones, dust storms, etc.' Stop after each need and ask: 'Air: why do we need it?' (To breathe.) 'Water?' (Two-thirds of our body is water; we drink it.) 'Food?' (It gives energy to work.) 'Clothes?' (They cover us and protect us from heat and cold.) 'House?' (It protects us from heat, cold, cyclones and dust storms.) Ask: 'Which three does the book say we cannot survive without at all?' (Air, water, food.) Write the five needs in big letters on a sheet and stick it on the wall.

steps.title: Needs or wants sort
steps.do: Do Activity a3. Write these on small slips of paper: air, drinking water, roti or rice, a TV, a shirt, a sweater in winter, a roof, a bicycle, chocolate, a bath, a mobile phone, a blanket, a fan, toys, fruit. Your child sorts them into two piles: 'Need' (we must have it to live and stay well) and 'Want' (nice to have). Ask them to give a reason for each. Expect arguments on the fan and the bath: a good answer is 'We don't die without a fan, but in Chennai in May it helps us stay healthy, so it is close to a need.' Praise any answer that uses a reason. Then look back at their desert-island list and ask: 'Which of your five things were needs?'

steps.title: Basic needs treasure hunt
steps.do: Give your child 5 minutes to walk around the house and bring back (or point to) one thing for each basic need: something that gives us air (an open window, a fan, a plant), something that holds drinking water (matka, bottle, RO tap), some food (a dal packet, a banana), a piece of clothing, and one part of the house that protects us (the roof, a wall, a door). For each, ask: 'How does this help us live?' A good answer for the window: 'It lets fresh air in, so we can breathe clean air.'

steps.title: Start the family water diary
steps.do: Start Activity a1. Draw a table in a notebook with columns: Use, How many buckets or mugs, Who. Explain that one ordinary bucket holds about 15–20 litres (check the number printed on yours, or fill it with a 1-litre bottle and count). Ask your child to guess first: 'How many buckets of water does our whole family use in one day?' Write the guess at the top. From now until tomorrow evening, your child asks each family member and records every use: drinking, cooking, bathing, flushing, washing clothes and dishes, mopping, watering plants. Stick the diary on the fridge with a pencil tied to it.

need: 15 small paper slips and a pencil
a large sheet of paper for the wall

prep.task: Write the 15 need-or-want slips and check how many litres your bucket holds

days.title: Air: the gas of life
days.goal: Learn that we breathe in air for its oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide, measure our breathing, see carbon dioxide in our own breath, and check our home's ventilation.

steps.title: Count your breaths
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Your child sits quietly for one minute while you count their breaths (watch the chest or tummy rise; one rise and fall is one breath). Write the number. Then they do 30 jumping jacks or run up and down the stairs twice, and you count again for one minute. Before the jumping, ask them to guess: 'Will you breathe faster, slower or the same?' Most 8-year-olds breathe about 18–25 times a minute at rest and much faster after running. Ask: 'Why does your body want more air when you run?' Listen for: 'My muscles are working harder and need more oxygen.' Read the 'why' of e1 aloud.

steps.title: 7.1 Air (page 93)
steps.do: Read section 7.1 'Air' on page 93 aloud, up to 'plant more and more trees'. Look together at the picture 'Use of Oxygen and Carbon dioxide'. Your child traces the path with a finger as you say it: nose, windpipe, lungs; oxygen goes into the blood; blood carries oxygen and food all round the body; blood brings carbon dioxide back to the lungs; we breathe it out. Ask: 'What is the special gas in air that we need?' (Oxygen, pran vayu.) 'What gas do we breathe out?' (Carbon dioxide.) 'What carries oxygen to your toes?' (Blood.) If they think we breathe out 'no air', tell them our out-breath is still mostly air, just with less oxygen and more carbon dioxide.

steps.title: Lime water: catch the carbon dioxide
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. You (the adult) prepare clear lime water from a little edible chuna (the white lime paste sold for paan) the night before, as described in e2. Pour clear lime water into two glasses. Your child uses a straw to blow gently into glass 1 for about a minute (blow out only, never suck). Use a bicycle pump or a squeezed empty plastic bottle to push ordinary room air into glass 2 for the same time. Ask first: 'Which glass will change?' Glass 1 turns milky white; glass 2 stays clear or changes only very slightly. Ask: 'What does this prove about our breath?' (It has much more carbon dioxide than room air.)

steps.title: Joseph Priestley and the mouse in the jar
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v1 in your own words: Priestley made a new gas in 1774 that made a candle flame blaze and kept a mouse alive longer; he thought it was air with no 'phlogiston' in it, but Lavoisier showed it was a gas of its own and named it oxygen. Tell them Priestley also found that a sprig of mint could 'refresh' air that a candle had used up, which links to the book's line about planting more trees. Ask the voice question and let your child answer fully.

steps.title: Ventilation check at home
steps.do: The book says our house should be well ventilated and we must not sleep in fully closed rooms. Go room by room with your child. In each room ask: 'Where can fresh air come in? Where can stale air go out?' (Windows, doors, a vent above the door, an exhaust fan, jaali.) Hold a strip of tissue or a thread near a slightly open window to watch it flutter. Your child draws a quick map of the house and marks each window and vent with an arrow. Ask: 'Which room has the least fresh air? What could we do about it?' Also remind them to fill in the water diary (Activity a1) today.

need: a bicycle pump or empty plastic bottle

prep.task: Make lime water: stir half a teaspoon of edible chuna into a glass of water, cover, and leave overnight to settle; next day pour off only the clear top part

days.title: Water: two-thirds of you
days.goal: Learn why our body needs water and how much, add up the family water diary, hunt for stagnant water, and hear how John Snow traced a disease to one water pump.

steps.title: 7.2 Water (pages 93–94)
steps.do: Read section 7.2 'Water' aloud, from 'Human body is two third water' to the end of the section about mosquitoes breeding in stagnant water. Ask: 'What does water do inside the body?' Good answers: 'Most of our blood is water, so it can flow easily', and 'It carries wastes out as urine and sweat.' Ask: 'Who else needs water?' (Animals and plants.) Two honest corrections to tell your child: the book says to drink 8 to 10 glasses a day; for a child of 8, about 6 to 8 glasses is usual, more on hot days or after playing. The book says our electricity is mostly made with water; in India today most electricity is made by burning coal, and only a smaller part comes from water flowing through dams.

steps.title: How much of you is water?
steps.do: Take a 1-litre water bottle and a marker. Ask your child to fill it to show 'two-thirds full' (divide the bottle into 3 equal parts with two marks and fill to the second mark). Say: 'If you were this bottle, this much of you would be water.' If you have a bathroom scale, weigh your child; about two-thirds of that number is roughly the kilograms of water in them (for 24 kg, about 16 kg, which is 16 litres, or 16 one-litre bottles). Line up the bottles you have to help them picture it. Ask: 'Then why don't we slosh when we walk?' (The water is held inside our body's tiny cells and in the blood.)

steps.title: Add up the water diary
steps.do: Finish Activity a1. Your child adds up the buckets or mugs in the diary and multiplies by the litres in one bucket (help with the multiplication). Compare with the guess written on Day 1. Ask: 'Which use took the most water?' (Usually bathing, flushing or washing clothes.) 'Which use is the only one we must have to stay alive?' (Drinking, and some for cooking.) Then together choose two ways your family can save water this week, such as a mug-and-bucket bath instead of a shower, turning the tap off while brushing, or using rice-washing water for plants. Write them on the diary.

steps.title: Stagnant water patrol
steps.do: Walk around the house, balcony, roof and compound with your child, looking for any still water where mosquitoes could breed: the air-cooler tray, flower-pot saucers, an old tyre, coconut shells, a bucket left uncovered, the fridge's drip tray, a blocked drain. Your child counts each one found. Empty or cover what you safely can (the adult should handle cooler water and drains). Explain: 'Mosquitoes lay eggs on still water, and in about a week the eggs become new mosquitoes. Some mosquitoes spread dengue and malaria.' Then check: is your drinking water kept covered? Is the matka or filter tap clean?

steps.title: John Snow and the Broad Street pump
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v2: in London in 1854 many people died of cholera, and most doctors blamed 'bad air'. John Snow marked each death on a map and found they clustered around one street pump. Draw a quick map with your child: a cross for a pump in the middle, dots for houses with sick people mostly around it. Ask: 'What does the map tell you?' Then ask the voice question. Link it to the book: 'This is why the book says keep filth away from water sources.'

need: a bathroom scale if you have one
paper and pencil for a map

days.title: Food: our body's fuel
days.goal: Learn that food gives us energy for physical and mental work, practise clean cooking habits, and check the main ideas so far with the core worksheet.

steps.title: How do you feel when you're hungry?
steps.do: Ask: 'Think of a day you missed breakfast or had to wait a long time for lunch. How did you feel?' Good answers: tired, cranky, could not think, tummy hurt. Tell them the book uses an old saying, 'you cannot worship God on an empty stomach' (in Hindi, 'bhookhe bhajan na hoye Gopala'), which means it is hard to do anything well when you are hungry.

steps.title: 7.3 Food (pages 94–95)
steps.do: Read section 7.3 'Food' aloud, from 'Food is also very essential for our life' to 'Avoid eating stale and rotten food', and the summary box after it. Ask: 'The book says we do two kinds of work. What are they?' (Physical work like running and carrying, and mental work like thinking and reading.) 'Where does the energy for both come from?' (Food.) Remind them of Day 2: 'Food alone is not enough; the body also needs oxygen from air to get the energy out of food, a little like a fire needs both wood and air.'

steps.title: My energy day
steps.do: Your child draws a long line across a page for 'yesterday', from waking up to bedtime. Above the line they draw every meal and snack they ate (for example poha, a banana, dal-chawal, a biscuit, roti-sabzi, milk). Below the line they draw what they did (playing, studying, walking to the park, helping). Ask: 'When did you have the most energy? Did it come after a meal?' Then ask them to mark one 'physical' job and one 'mental' job. Keep this page for the next lesson on food.

steps.title: Clean-cooking helper
steps.do: Do one real kitchen job together, following the book's rules. Your child washes their hands with soap for 20 seconds (sing 'Happy Birthday' twice), then washes vegetables such as tomatoes, potatoes or palak leaves in a bowl of water before you cut them. Ask: 'Why wash before cutting and not after?' (If we cut first, the dirt and germs on the skin get on the cut pieces, and washing cut pieces also washes away some of the goodness.) Then check the kitchen together: is any food stale, smelly or mouldy? Is cooked food kept covered? Throw out anything spoiled (the adult decides).

steps.title: Core worksheet: our basic needs
steps.do: First ask the three 'Let's see, what you have learnt 7.1' questions on page 95 aloud: Which gas is called 'pran vayu'? (Oxygen.) What proportion of our body is water? (Two-thirds.) What care must be taken while cooking? (Cook food hygienically and wash vegetables well before cutting.) Then do Worksheet ws1 (core). Read items aloud if needed. For each wrong answer, go back to the section in the book (7.1, 7.2 or 7.3) and read the line together.

need: soap, a bowl of water and some vegetables

days.title: Clothing: cool cotton, warm wool
days.goal: Learn why we wear clothes and what different fabrics are good for, and test for ourselves whether wool really keeps things warm.

steps.title: Set up the warm-bottle test
steps.do: Set up Experiment e3 now so it runs while you read. Fill two identical steel or glass bottles with warm water from the same jug (warm to touch, not too hot). Your child wraps one bottle in a woollen sweater or shawl and the other in a thin cotton dupatta or handkerchief, tying both with rubber bands. Leave a third bottle bare. Ask them to guess first: 'After 30 minutes, which bottle will be warmest? Which will be coolest?' Write the guesses down and note the time.

steps.title: 7.4 Clothing (pages 95–96)
steps.do: Read section 7.4 'Clothing' aloud, from 'We need clothes to cover our body' to 'may cause skin diseases'. Ask: 'Why are cotton clothes good in summer?' (Air can pass through them easily, so we feel cooler, and cotton soaks up sweat.) 'How does wool keep us warm?' (Air gets trapped between the woollen fibres and stops the body's heat escaping.) 'What does the book say about polyester?' (It does not crush easily and its colours do not fade in sunlight.) 'Why must we wear washed clothes?' (Dirty clothes worn for a long time can cause skin diseases.) Point out that wool does not make heat itself; it only stops our body's own heat from escaping.

steps.title: Wardrobe fabric hunt
steps.do: Open the cupboard together. Find the small label inside the collar or seam of 6 to 8 clothes and read out what each is made of: cotton, wool, silk, polyester, or a mix like 'polycotton'. Your child sorts them into piles. Then do the crush test: scrunch a cotton handkerchief and a polyester one (or a polyester shirt sleeve) tightly in the fist for 30 seconds and open them. Ask: 'Which one stayed wrinkled?' (Usually cotton.) Ask: 'Which would you wear for a cricket match in May, and which in a Delhi winter?' Ask the reason each time.

steps.title: Warm-bottle results
steps.do: After 30 minutes, unwrap the three bottles from Experiment e3. Your child touches each with the inside of the wrist (or use a kitchen thermometer if you have one) and puts them in order from warmest to coolest. Usually the wool-wrapped bottle is warmest, the cotton one is in between and the bare bottle is coolest. Compare with the guesses. Read the 'why' of e3 aloud and ask: 'So does a sweater make heat?' (No, it traps air, which stops our own body heat escaping.)

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 (stretch) sections A and B now and section C tomorrow after the house lesson. These ask your child to use the ideas on new cases, such as what to wear in Leh or Kerala and why a quilt (razai) is warm. Let them answer the write items aloud while you scribe if writing slows them down.

need: 3 identical bottles and a jug of warm water
a woollen sweater or shawl, a thin cotton cloth, rubber bands
a kitchen thermometer if you have one
a cotton and a polyester handkerchief

days.title: Shelter: what makes a good house?
days.goal: Learn how houses developed and why they differ from place to place, test sloping and flat roofs with a model, survey our own home, and meet an architect who built for the Indian climate.

steps.title: 7.5 Shelter (pages 96–97)
steps.do: Read section 7.5 'Shelter (house)' aloud, from 'Initially human beings used to live in caves' to 'lanes and streets, etc.', and look at the pictures of a house in a snowy area and different kinds of houses. Ask: 'Where did the first people live?' (In caves, then on machans, platforms built in trees.) 'What do houses protect us from?' (Rain, heat, cold, storms, cyclones, snow and wild animals.) 'Why are houses in snowy places built with low ceilings and small doors?' (To keep out cold winds and keep warmth in.) 'Why are some houses built to be earthquake-proof?' (So they don't fall down when the ground shakes.)

steps.title: Snow on the roof model
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Make two little houses from small boxes. Give one a flat roof (a piece of card laid flat) and one a steep sloping roof (a card folded in half like a tent). Your child guesses first: 'If it snows, which roof will hold more snow?' Then sprinkle 'snow' (a spoonful of salt, sugar or atta) over both from the same height. Most slides off the sloping roof; it piles on the flat one. Ask: 'Snow is heavy. What could happen to a flat roof after many days of snow?' (It could leak or even break.) Then ask: 'What about rain in Kerala or Assam? What roofs do you see there?' (Sloping roofs, so rain runs off.)

steps.title: Laurie Baker's breathing walls
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v3: an architect who came to India in 1945, stayed for life in Kerala, and built cheap, cool houses with local bricks, walls with holes (jaali) for air and light, and walls with a hollow gap inside. If you can, show your child a jaali or a brick wall with gaps nearby. Ask: 'How is a hollow wall like a woollen sweater?' (Both trap air, which slows heat moving through.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Our house survey
steps.do: Using the book's checklist from page 97, your child walks around your home with a clipboard and answers yes, no or partly for each: 1. Is the house airy (do fresh air and light come into most rooms)? 2. Is there a drain that carries used water away? 3. Does the kitchen have a window, chimney or exhaust fan so smoke escapes? 4. Is the house clean? 5. Is garbage kept in a covered bin and given to the garbage collector, not thrown into the lane or a neighbour's courtyard? Ask: 'Why is kitchen smoke harmful?' (It hurts the eyes and the lungs.) Then answer 'Let's see, what you have learnt 7.2' aloud: main functions of clothes, benefits of polyester, features of a good house.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 (challenge), and finish section C of ws2 if you did not do it yesterday. Section C of ws3 asks your child to compare scientists' ideas; there is no single right answer, so praise reasons that use evidence ('because in our bottle test...'). Your child can answer aloud while you write.

need: 2 small boxes and 2 pieces of card
a spoonful of salt, sugar or atta

prep.task: Find two small boxes of similar size (toothpaste or tea boxes) and some card

days.title: Let's revise, check and teach it back
days.goal: Review the lesson with the book's revision list and exercises, think about whether needs come in a fixed order, check understanding, and have your child teach the lesson back.

steps.title: Let's Revise (pages 97–98)
steps.do: Read the 'Let's Revise' list on pages 97–98 aloud, one line at a time. After each line, your child holds up something from the week that shows it: the lime-water glass or the breathing count for oxygen and carbon dioxide, the two-thirds bottle for water, the energy-day page for food, the wrapped bottles for clothing, the roof models for shelter. If they cannot find something, ask them to explain the line in their own words instead.

steps.title: Exercise questions (pages 98–99)
steps.do: Do the Exercise on pages 98–99 aloud. Question 1: 'What do you understand by basic needs?' (The things we need to live and stay well: air, water, food, clothing and shelter.) 'Why is air necessary?' (It has oxygen, which our body needs to get energy from food; without breathing we cannot live.) 'How do warm clothes protect us from cold?' (Air is trapped between the fibres and stops body heat escaping.) Then the fill-in-the-blanks (carbon dioxide; pran vayu; two-thirds; air; nutritious components; urine) and the right or wrong items (right, wrong, wrong, right). Your child can check answers against the answer key on page 99.

steps.title: Do needs come in a fixed order?
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v4: Abraham Maslow's idea that people first need air, food and water, then safety, then love and friends, then respect, and only then can they grow into their best selves. Draw it as a ladder with your child. Then ask: 'Can a hungry child still love their family and make friends?' (Yes.) 'Then must the bottom step always come first?' Ask the voice question and let them argue both sides.

steps.title: Lesson check
steps.do: Ask the 7 check questions aloud, one at a time, without the book. Tick the ones answered well. For any miss, open the section of the book (7.1 to 7.5) and read the line together, then ask again in different words. Most children get 5 or more right; fewer than 4 means repeat the Day 2 air lesson and the Day 5 bottle test next week.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the teacher and you (or a grandparent or sibling) are the student. In 5 minutes they teach the five basic needs, using real things: a glass of lime water, a water bottle, a snack, a sweater and the roof models. For each need they must say why we need it and one way to keep it clean or safe (open windows, cover drinking water, wash vegetables, wear clean clothes, put garbage in the bin). Ask two 'student' questions: 'Why does my breath turn lime water milky?' and 'Does a sweater make heat?' End by putting the family's two water-saving promises from the diary on the fridge.

need: things from the week: lime-water glass, two-thirds bottle, wrapped bottles, roof models, energy-day page

worksheets.title: Our five basic needs

sections.p: Our five basic needs are air, water, food, clothing and ____.
Which three things can we NOT survive without at all?
Sort these into needs and wants.

sections: B. Air and water in the body

sections.p: The gas in air that we need to live is ____, also called 'pran vayu'.
When we breathe out, our body gets rid of ____ ____.
About how much of our body is water?
Match each thing to its job.
pairs: Fill with air when we breathe in
Carries oxygen and food to every part of the body
Carry waste out of the body

sections: C. Keeping needs clean and safe

sections.p: Why should we not leave water standing in an old tyre or cooler?
opts: Mosquitoes breed in it and spread disease

sections.p: Write two things the book says we should do while cooking and eating to stay healthy.
Match each place and season to the best clothes.
pairs: A long train trip where clothes get crushed

sections.p: A thick razai (quilt) stuffed with cotton keeps you warm at night. How?
opts: Lots of air is trapped in the fluffy cotton and stops your body heat escaping

sections.p: Two shirts look the same, but one feels cool and one feels sweaty on a hot day. What could the difference be? How could you find out from the shirt itself?
Your cousin sleeps in a small room with every window and the door shut, and a coal angithi (stove) burning for warmth. Why is this dangerous, and what should they do?
Your family water diary: fill in the three biggest water uses.
After running, you breathe faster because:
opts: Your muscles need more oxygen to get energy from food

sections.p: Match the house to the reason it is built that way.
pairs: Sloping roof in a snowy place
So snow slides off and does not pile up
Small doors and low ceiling in the hills
So it does not fall when the ground shakes
Kitchen with a chimney or exhaust fan
So smoke does not stay in the kitchen

sections.p: A family throws its garbage into the lane behind the house. Write two problems this causes and what they should do instead.
In our bottle test, the bare bottle cooled fastest and the wool-wrapped bottle stayed warmest. What would happen to a bottle of ice-cold water wrapped in wool?
opts: It would stay cold longer, because the trapped air slows heat moving in too
Nothing; wool only works on warm things

sections.p: Our breath turned lime water milky but room air did not. What does that tell you about the air coming out of our lungs compared with the air going in?
A candle in a closed jar goes out. A mouse in a closed jar would also be in danger. Both use up the ____ in the air.
What if a city had plenty of food but its only well became dirty? Use John Snow's story to say what might happen and how you would find which water source was the problem.
What if you had to build a house in a very hot desert like the Thar? Think about walls, windows, roof and colour. Draw or write your plan.

Maslow said people need food and safety before they can care about friends and learning. Think of a story or a person you know who cared for others even when they were hungry or poor. Does it support Maslow or not?
Priestley thought his new gas was 'air with the phlogiston taken out'. Lavoisier said it was a new element, oxygen. Which evidence helped Lavoisier most?
opts: Careful weighing showed things that burn gain weight by taking something from the air
The gas had a nice smell

experiments.title: Count your breaths
experiments.question: Does our body need more air when it works harder?
need: space to jump or a staircase
steps: Your child sits still for 2 minutes to rest.
Count their breaths for one minute by watching the chest or tummy rise and fall (one rise and fall is one breath). Write the number.
They do 30 jumping jacks or run up and down the stairs twice.
Straight away, count their breaths for one minute again. Write the number.
Count again after 3 minutes of rest to see how fast breathing comes back to normal.
Make a small bar chart: resting, after exercise, after rest.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: after jumping, will you breathe faster, slower or the same? By how much?
experiments.observe: Record the three counts. Most children of 8 breathe about 18–25 times a minute at rest, much faster just after exercise, and come back close to normal within a few minutes. The heart also beats faster; feel it on the chest.
experiments.why: Every part of the body gets its energy by using oxygen to 'burn' food slowly inside its tiny cells; this makes carbon dioxide as a waste. When muscles work hard they use oxygen faster and make more carbon dioxide. The brain senses the extra carbon dioxide in the blood and makes us breathe faster and deeper, and the heart pumps faster, so that more oxygen reaches the muscles and the carbon dioxide is breathed out.
experiments.safety: Exercise on a non-slippery floor. A child with asthma should not do hard exercise for this test; a short brisk walk is enough.

experiments.title: Lime water: carbon dioxide in our breath
experiments.question: Is there more carbon dioxide in the air we breathe out than in the air around us?
need: half a teaspoon of edible chuna (slaked lime paste for paan)
a bicycle pump or an empty plastic bottle
steps: Night before (adult only): stir half a teaspoon of chuna into a glass or jar of water, cover it and leave it to settle overnight.
Next day, carefully pour only the clear liquid from the top into two clean glasses, about a quarter full each. This is lime water.
Glass 1: your child blows gently out through a straw into the lime water for about one minute. Blow out only; never suck.
Glass 2: push room air into the lime water for the same time, using a bicycle pump or by squeezing an empty plastic bottle again and again with the straw fitted into its mouth.
Hold both glasses against a dark cloth and compare.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which glass will change, the one with your breath, the one with room air, both or neither?
experiments.observe: The breath glass turns cloudy or milky white within a minute. The room-air glass stays clear, or turns only very slightly cloudy after much longer.
experiments.why: Lime water is calcium hydroxide dissolved in water. Carbon dioxide reacts with it to make tiny specks of chalk (calcium carbonate), which do not dissolve, so the water looks milky. Room air has only a very small amount of carbon dioxide (about 0.04 parts in 100), but the air we breathe out has about 4 parts in 100, roughly a hundred times more, because our body makes carbon dioxide when it uses oxygen to get energy from food. Our breath is still mostly nitrogen and some oxygen; it has simply had some of its oxygen swapped for carbon dioxide.
experiments.safety: Chuna is strongly alkaline and can burn the skin and eyes: only the adult handles it, wash hands after, and keep it away from the eyes (rinse with plenty of water if any splashes). Never drink lime water. Use the straw only for blowing out.

experiments.title: Does wool keep things warm?
experiments.question: Which keeps a warm bottle warm longest: wool, cotton or nothing?
need: a thin cotton dupatta or handkerchief
a kitchen thermometer if you have one
steps: Fill all three bottles with warm water from the same jug, to the same level. Close the lids.
Wrap bottle 1 in the woollen sweater, bottle 2 in the thin cotton cloth, and leave bottle 3 bare. Tie with rubber bands.
Stand them side by side, away from the sun and the fan.
After 30 minutes, unwrap them one at a time.
Touch each with the inside of your wrist, or put a thermometer in each, and put them in order from warmest to coolest.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which bottle will be warmest after 30 minutes, and which coolest? Why?
experiments.observe: Record the order (and temperatures, if you have a thermometer). Usually the wool bottle is warmest, the cotton one next, and the bare bottle coolest.
experiments.why: Heat always moves from warm things to cooler surroundings. Still air is very bad at carrying heat. Woollen fibres are crinkly and fluffy, so a sweater holds lots of tiny pockets of still air, which slow down the heat escaping from the bottle, just as the book says it slows heat escaping from our body. A thin cotton cloth traps only a little air. Wool does not make heat; the warmth was already in the water (or, for us, made by our own body).
experiments.safety: Use warm, not boiling, water. An adult should pour it.
experiments.time: 7 min to set up + 30 min wait + 8 min to check

activities.title: Family water diary
need: a notebook page stuck on the fridge
a bucket and a 1-litre bottle to measure it
steps: Find out how many litres your bucket holds (read the number on it, or fill it with a 1-litre bottle and count).
Draw a table: Use, How many buckets or mugs, Who.
Write your guess for the whole family's daily water use at the top.
For one full day, record every use: drinking, cooking, bathing, flushing, washing clothes and dishes, mopping, watering plants.
Add up the total and change it into litres.
Compare with your guess, find the biggest use, and choose two ways to save water this week.
activities.outcome: A real measurement of how much water your family uses in a day, and two family water-saving promises on the fridge.

activities.title: Snow on the roof: flat or sloping?
need: a spoonful of salt, sugar or atta
steps: Tape a flat piece of card on top of one box for a flat roof.
Fold the other card in half and tape it on the second box like a tent, for a sloping roof.
Guess which roof will hold more snow.
Sprinkle the same amount of 'snow' over both from the same height.
Compare how much stays on each roof; tip the extra into a bowl to compare amounts.
Try a gentle slope and a steep slope and see which sheds more.
activities.outcome: Two model houses that show why houses in snowy and very rainy places have sloping roofs.

activities.title: Needs or wants sort
steps: Write one thing on each slip: air, drinking water, roti or rice, TV, shirt, sweater in winter, roof, bicycle, chocolate, bath, mobile phone, blanket, fan, toys, fruit.
Make two piles: Need and Want.
For each slip, say a reason.
Talk about the slips you disagree on and why.
Keep the slips; on the last day, sort the 'Need' pile into the five basic needs.
activities.outcome: A child who can tell a need from a want and give a reason, and a set of slips to reuse on the last day.

voices.who: Joseph Priestley (1733–1804), England, and Antoine Lavoisier (1743–1794), France
voices.idea: In August 1774 Priestley heated a red powder (mercury oxide) and collected a gas in which a candle burned very brightly and a mouse lived longer than in ordinary air. He believed burning released a substance called 'phlogiston', so he named his gas 'dephlogisticated air'. Earlier, in 1771, he had found that a sprig of mint could make air in which a candle had burned out good again. Lavoisier repeated the work with careful weighing, showed that things that burn take something out of the air and get heavier, and named that part of the air oxygen. (The Swedish chemist Carl Scheele had also made the gas, a little earlier, but published later.)
voices.then: Most chemists of the time believed in phlogiston. Lavoisier's new explanation won over most chemists within about twenty years, but Priestley himself never accepted it and defended phlogiston until he died.
voices.now: The phlogiston idea is rejected: the evidence went against it. Burning and breathing both use oxygen from the air and make carbon dioxide, as Lavoisier's work began to show. Priestley is still honoured for discovering the gas and for his finding that plants restore air, which helped later scientists discover that plants give out oxygen.
voices.ask: Priestley and Lavoisier saw the same experiments but explained them differently. What kind of measurement helped decide who was right? Can a famous scientist be wrong about his own discovery?

voices.who: John Snow (1813–1858), England
voices.idea: Snow, a London doctor, argued that cholera spreads through dirty water, not through 'bad air' (miasma) as most doctors believed. In the 1854 outbreak in the Soho area of London, he marked deaths on a map and showed that they clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. On his advice the local officials removed the pump's handle in September 1854. He also compared households supplied by two water companies and found many more cholera deaths among those whose water came from a dirtier part of the river Thames.
voices.then: Many doctors and officials did not accept his idea in his lifetime and kept blaming bad air. Even after the pump handle was removed, an official report still doubted his water explanation.
voices.now: Snow was right. The cholera germ (a bacterium) was described by Filippo Pacini in 1854 and identified more fully by Robert Koch in 1883, and cholera is now known to spread through water or food contaminated with sewage. Snow's map is famous as a founding moment of epidemiology, the science of tracking how diseases spread.
voices.ask: Snow could not see the cholera germ. What evidence did he use instead? Would a map alone convince you, or would you want something more?

voices.who: Laurie Baker (1917–2007), architect, born in England, lived and worked in India
voices.idea: Baker came to India in 1945 and spent the rest of his life here, mostly in Kerala, becoming an Indian citizen. He argued that houses should be built from cheap local materials (brick, lime, mud, laterite stone) and suit the local climate, instead of costly concrete. He used brick jaali walls that let in air and light while keeping out the harsh sun, and the 'rat-trap bond', a way of laying bricks on edge that leaves a hollow gap inside the wall, uses fewer bricks and keeps rooms cooler.
voices.then: Many builders and officials preferred modern concrete buildings, and his unplastered brick walls and odd shapes looked strange or 'poor' to some people. But many families, institutions and later the Kerala government took up his low-cost methods.
voices.now: His ideas are widely accepted and taught in Indian architecture. He received the Padma Shri in 1990. Today, with hotter summers and costly cooling, architects again study his climate-friendly, low-cost buildings.
voices.ask: Baker said a wall with a hollow gap keeps a room cooler. How could you test that idea with two cardboard boxes and a sunny window?

voices.who: Abraham Maslow (1908–1970), USA
voices.idea: In a 1943 paper, the psychologist Maslow suggested that human needs come in levels: first body needs (air, water, food, sleep, warmth), then safety, then love and belonging, then respect, and finally 'self-actualisation', becoming the best version of yourself. He said that, in general, lower needs must be mostly met before people focus on higher ones. Others later drew this as the famous pyramid; Maslow himself did not draw it.
voices.then: The idea became very popular in schools, businesses and books. But researchers soon pointed out that Maslow had little hard evidence, and that the order of needs may differ between people and cultures.
voices.now: A large study by Louis Tay and Ed Diener in 2011, using surveys from 123 countries, found that people everywhere do share these kinds of needs, but that people could feel good from friendship and respect even when their basic needs were not fully met; the strict order did not hold. So the list of needs is useful, but the fixed ladder is debated.
voices.ask: Can a hungry person still be a good friend or love learning? What would you need to find out about many people to decide whether needs really come in a fixed order?

check.q: What are our five basic needs? Which three can we not live without at all?
check.a: Air, water, food, clothing and shelter. We cannot survive without air, water and food.

check.q: Why do we need air? What do we breathe out?
check.a: Air contains oxygen (pran vayu). Blood carries oxygen and food to every part of the body, where they give us energy. We breathe out carbon dioxide.

check.q: About how much of our body is water, and name two jobs water does in our body.
check.a: About two-thirds. Most of our blood is water so it flows easily, and water carries wastes out as urine and sweat.

check.q: Name three ways to keep water clean and safe at home.
check.a: Keep drinking water in covered pots, keep filth away from water sources, do not let water stand near the house (mosquitoes breed in it), and do not waste water.

check.q: Why do cotton clothes feel cool and woollen clothes keep us warm?
check.a: Air passes easily through cotton, so we feel cooler. Wool traps air between its fibres, which stops the body's heat escaping.

check.q: What makes a good house?
check.a: It is airy and lets in light, has proper drainage, a well-ventilated kitchen so smoke does not stay inside, is kept clean, and its garbage is put in the proper place.

check.q: Why do houses in snowy places have sloping roofs?
check.a: So snow slides off instead of piling up and becoming heavy; they also have low ceilings and small doors to keep out cold winds.

c.covers: Why we eat; parts of food and their jobs; balanced food; food safety

p.title: Food
p.source: NIOS Open Basic Education, Environmental Studies Level A (A 102), Lesson 8 (pages 100–112), 2016
p.summary: Food gives us energy, builds and repairs the body, and protects us from disease. Your child learns the five components of food (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, minerals, vitamins) and where each comes from in an Indian kitchen, tests foods for starch and fat, plans a balanced thali, finds out which diseases come from missing nutrients, and learns why water matters, how to make dirty water safe and how to keep food clean.
goals: By the end your child can give the three reasons we need food (energy, growth and repair, protection from disease) and explain that food is 'burnt' with oxygen in the body to give energy.
By the end your child can name the five components of food, say what each does, and sort common Indian foods by their main component.
By the end your child can test a food for starch (iodine turns it blue-black) and for fat (it leaves a see-through grease spot on paper).

By the end your child can plan a balanced meal and link missing nutrients to diseases: anaemia (iron), goitre (iodine), scurvy and bleeding gums (vitamin C), weak bones (calcium and vitamin D), marasmus (not enough food).
By the end your child can explain why we drink more fluids during diarrhoea, help make ORS, and describe four ways to make dirty water safe (alum, filter, chlorine, boiling).
By the end your child can list the clean-food rules and explain how scientists found out about vitamins through careful tests.
words: a useful substance in food that the body needs to work, grow and stay healthy
the energy food found in grains, potato, sugar, gur and honey; starch and sugar are carbohydrates
an energy-rich food in ghee, butter, oil, nuts and oilseeds; extra fat is stored under the skin and keeps us warm
the body-building food in dal, milk, paneer, soybean, eggs, fish and meat, needed for growth and repair
a nutrient like iron, calcium or iodine, needed in small amounts to keep the body working
a nutrient needed in tiny amounts for the body to work properly, such as vitamin C in amla and vitamin A in carrots
a diet with all five components in the right amounts, such as a thali of roti or rice, dal, sabzi, curd and a seasonal fruit
a simple sugar that carbohydrates are broken down into; the body uses it for energy
a condition where the blood is weak and a person feels tired and looks pale, usually from too little iron
a swelling in the neck caused by too little iodine; iodised salt prevents it
oral rehydration solution: clean water with the right amounts of salt and sugar, drunk during diarrhoea to replace lost water
phitkari, a crystal that makes fine mud in water clump together and sink

days.title: Why do we eat?
days.goal: Discover from our own body why food matters (energy, growth and repair, fighting disease) and start the book's one-week food diary.

steps.title: The scooter and the petrol
steps.do: Ask: 'What happens to a scooter or a car when the petrol runs out?' (It stops.) 'Is there anything that is the petrol for your body?' (Food.) Then ask: 'When you are fast asleep, does your body still need energy?' Let them guess, then say: 'Yes! Your heart beats and your lungs breathe all night, so even sleeping uses energy.' Ask your child to put a hand on their chest and feel their heart working right now.

steps.title: 8.1 Why is food necessary? (pages 100–102)
steps.do: Read the lesson opening on page 100 and section 8.1 aloud, the three reasons we need food. After '1. Food gives us energy' ask: 'How does food give energy?' (It is burnt in the body with the help of oxygen we breathe in, a bit like petrol burning in an engine; remind them of the lime-water test in Lesson 7.) After '2. Growth and repair' ask: 'Why do children need more nutritious food than grown-ups?' (They are growing fast.) 'When you scrape your knee, what does food do?' (It helps make new skin to repair it.) After '3. Prevention of diseases' read the four disease names and say you will find out about each on Day 4.

steps.title: Growth mark and repair hunt
steps.do: Stand your child against a door frame with heels, back and head touching it, put a ruler flat on their head and mark the height with today's date. Measure it in centimetres. Say: 'Food built every centimetre of you.' If you have an older photo or a baby outfit, compare. Then hunt for 'repair' on the body: a healed scratch, a scab, short new nails after cutting, or a lost milk tooth with a new one coming. Ask: 'What did your body use to make the new skin, nail or tooth?' (Food: mostly protein and minerals.)

steps.title: Start the one-week food diary
steps.do: Start Activity a1, which is the book's 'Let's do and learn' task on page 111. Rule a notebook page into a table with columns: Day, Breakfast, Lunch, Snack, Dinner. Your child fills in everything they ate today so far, including small things like a biscuit, chai or a handful of peanuts. Explain the rule: write it down soon after eating, every day for a week; on the last day we will check whether the week was balanced. Stick the page on the fridge or keep it near the dining table.

steps.title: Food from plants and animals
steps.do: Look at today's food diary entries. For each item ask: 'Did this come from a plant or an animal?' (Roti: wheat plant; dal: pulse plant; milk: cow or buffalo; egg: hen; sugar: sugarcane.) Read the book line on page 100: air, water and food are needs of all living beings. Ask: 'What does a cow eat? What does a plant use as its food?' (Grass; plants make their own food in their leaves using sunlight, air and water.)

need: a ruler, a pencil and a door frame
a notebook for the food diary

days.title: Energy foods: carbohydrates and fats
days.goal: Learn the five components of food, then test real foods for starch and for fat.

steps.title: 8.2 Components of food and Let's see 8.1 (pages 102–103)
steps.do: Read section 8.2 aloud and help your child learn the five components with a hand trick: one finger each for carbohydrates, fats, proteins, minerals, vitamins. Then do 'Let's see, what we have learnt 8.1' on page 103 aloud. Question 1: why do we need food? (Energy, growth and repair, protection from disease.) Question 2: the five components. Question 3, the matching: carbohydrates and fats give energy; proteins help growth and repair; minerals and vitamins protect from disease and make the body strong. Check with the answers on page 111.

steps.title: Carbohydrates and fats in the table (pages 103–104)
steps.do: Read rows 1 and 2 of the table in section 8.3 aloud. Ask: 'Which foods give carbohydrates?' (Wheat, rice, maize, oats, barley, potato, sweet potato, sugar, gur, honey.) 'What do carbohydrates turn into in the body?' (Glucose, which is used for energy.) 'Which foods give fats?' (Milk, butter, ghee, oils, groundnut, mustard, sunflower, coconut.) 'What else does fat do besides give energy?' (Extra fat is stored under the skin and helps keep us warm.) Tell them starch is the main carbohydrate in grains and potato; sugar is another.

steps.title: The starch test
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Put small pieces of cooked rice, raw potato, bread or roti, banana, cucumber, a little dal, paneer or boiled egg white, and a pinch of sugar on a steel plate, well apart. Ask your child to guess for each: 'Will it turn blue-black (lots of starch) or stay brown?' and write the guesses. You (the adult) put one drop of tincture of iodine or Betadine on each. Your child records the result in a table. Rice, potato, bread and roti go blue-black; cucumber stays brown; sugar stays brown (sugar is a carbohydrate but not starch).

steps.title: The grease-spot test
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Cut a brown paper bag or plain paper into squares and label them: ghee, groundnut (crushed), coconut (a small piece), a biscuit, a slice of apple, boiled potato, water. Your child rubs each food firmly on its own square and guesses which will leave a see-through spot. Wait 10 minutes for water to dry, then hold each square up to a window. A spot that stays see-through after drying shows fat. Ask: 'Which surprised you?' (Many children are surprised by the biscuit and the groundnut.) Read the 'why' of e2.

need: small pieces of rice, raw potato, bread or roti, banana, cucumber, dal, paneer or egg white, and sugar
tincture of iodine or Betadine (adult use)
a brown paper bag or plain paper
ghee, groundnuts, a piece of coconut, a biscuit, an apple slice

prep.task: Buy a small bottle of tincture of iodine or povidone-iodine (Betadine) from a chemist; boil one small potato

days.title: Body-builders and protectors, and the balanced thali
days.goal: Learn the sources and jobs of proteins, minerals and vitamins, sort the kitchen into the five components, plan a balanced thali, and hear how polished rice led to the discovery of vitamins.

steps.title: Proteins, minerals and vitamins (page 104)
steps.do: Read rows 3, 4 and 5 of the table in section 8.3 aloud. Ask: 'Which foods give proteins, and what do proteins do?' (Milk, cheese or paneer, pulses, soybean, green peas, eggs, chicken, fish, meat; they help the body grow and repair.) 'Do we need minerals in big amounts or small?' (Small, but they are essential.) 'Which foods give vitamins?' (Milk, curd, ghee, fish oil, lemon, orange, papaya, mango, tomato, beetroot, green leafy vegetables.) Point out the surprising one: sunlight. Our skin makes vitamin D when sunlight falls on it. Tell them one thing the book leaves out: grains, fruit and vegetables also give fibre (roughage), which keeps our gut working, though it is not on the list of five.

steps.title: Kitchen sort into five groups
steps.do: Make five labelled sheets on the floor: Carbohydrates, Fats, Proteins, Minerals, Vitamins. Your child collects 12–15 items from the kitchen (atta, rice, poha, gur, oil, ghee, groundnuts, moong dal, rajma, a milk packet, eggs, iodised salt packet, a lemon, a carrot, palak, a banana) and puts each on the group it gives most of. Ask the reason each time. When they say 'milk could go in three places!', praise it: most foods have several components, so we put each where it gives the most. Good placements: atta and rice under carbohydrates, dal under proteins, oil under fats, salt under minerals, lemon and carrot under vitamins.

steps.title: Balanced food (page 104)
steps.do: Read the paragraph on page 104 starting 'For a healthy body it is necessary' up to 'it lacks iron and vitamin C'. Ask: 'What is a balanced food?' (Food with all five components in the right amounts: grains, pulses, vegetables, seasonal fruits and ghee or oil.) 'The book says milk is close to a balanced food for children. What two things does it lack?' (Iron and vitamin C.) 'So what could you add to a glass of milk to fill the gap?' (A guava or an orange for vitamin C, and green vegetables or gur for iron.)

steps.title: Design a balanced thali
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Your child draws a big circle as a thali with five small katoris. They plan one balanced lunch from foods your family really eats, for example rice and roti (carbohydrates), dal or rajma (proteins), palak sabzi (minerals and vitamins), curd (proteins, minerals), a little ghee (fat) and a slice of papaya (vitamins). Each katori gets a label naming the component it gives. Check together: are all five there? Is there too much of anything, like three fried items? Choose one day this week to cook this thali together.

steps.title: Eijkman's chickens and the polished rice
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v1: a Dutch doctor in Java in the 1890s noticed that chickens fed polished white rice became ill, and recovered when fed brown rice with its outer layer. Show your child a grain of white rice and, if you have it, brown or hand-pounded rice (or the bran, 'bhusi'), and point out the book's line about 'chaff of the grains' in the minerals row. Tell them honestly: the book also says the chaff has plenty of vitamin A; that is not right, but the bran does have B vitamins, minerals and fibre, which is exactly what Eijkman's story is about. Ask the voice question.

need: white rice and brown or hand-pounded rice if you have it

days.title: When nutrients are missing
days.goal: Learn what happens when the body lacks enough food, iron, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin A, vitamin C or iodine, and hear how a ship's doctor tested a cure for scurvy.

steps.title: Deficiency diseases (pages 104–105)
steps.do: Read from 'When small children do not get sufficient food' on page 104 to the end of the goitre paragraph on page 105. For each, ask the question and listen for the answer. 'What is marasmus?' (When small children do not get enough food, they become very thin and weak and their muscles do not grow; it comes from too little food overall, both energy and protein.) 'Why should we avoid fast food like noodles and burgers?' (They lack nutrients.) 'What causes anaemia, and what can we eat?' (Too little iron; green vegetables, gur, black chana, eggs.) 'For strong bones?' (Calcium and vitamin D: milk, curd, eggs, fish, sunlight.) 'For healthy eyes?' (Vitamin A: carrot, mango, papaya.) 'Bleeding gums?' (Vitamin C: amla, lemon, orange, guava.) 'Goitre?' (Too little iodine; use iodised salt.)

steps.title: Salt packet and nutrient labels
steps.do: Bring out your salt packet. Your child finds the word 'iodised' on it (many packets also show a small rising-sun symbol). Ask: 'Why did the government want all our cooking salt to have iodine?' (So everyone gets a little iodine every day and does not get goitre; salt is something every family buys.) Then look at a milk packet or a biscuit packet's 'Nutrition information' box and find the words protein, carbohydrate, fat, and any vitamin or mineral named. Tell them a national survey (NFHS-5, 2019–21) found more than half of Indian women and most young children had anaemia, which is why iron-rich food matters in every home.

steps.title: James Lind's lemons
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v2: in 1747 a Scottish ship's doctor, James Lind, took 12 sailors sick with scurvy (bleeding gums, weak and tired) and gave six pairs of them six different treatments; the pair given oranges and lemons got better fastest. Act it out: line up 6 pairs of toys or spoons, give each pair a 'treatment' slip (cider, vinegar, sea water, a spice paste, dilute acid, oranges and lemons). Ask: 'Why did Lind give all the sailors the same food otherwise?' (So that only the treatment was different: a fair test.) Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Let's see 8.2 and the core worksheet
steps.do: First do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 8.2' on page 106 aloud: balanced diet, marasmus, anaemia (iron), bleeding gums (vitamin C foods), and the matching (grains: carbohydrates; pulses, cheese, eggs: proteins; butter, ghee, oil: fats; iodised salt, spinach, turnip: minerals; carrot, mango, amla: vitamins). Check with the answers on page 112. Then do Worksheet ws1 (core). For each wrong answer, go back to the table on pages 103–104.

need: a salt packet and a milk or biscuit packet
12 toys or spoons and 6 slips of paper

days.title: Water: safe to drink
days.goal: Learn why water is part of our food, make ORS for diarrhoea, and test two of the book's ways to clean dirty water: alum and a home-made filter.

steps.title: 8.4 and 8.5 Drinking water (page 107)
steps.do: Read sections 8.4 and 8.5 aloud up to 'How to clean water'. Ask: 'Why does the body need water to move food around?' (Everything moves from one organ to another dissolved in water, and food is digested in dissolved form.) Show this: stir a spoon of sugar into a glass of water; ask where it went (it dissolved, and is now spread all through the water). 'What happens in vomiting and diarrhoea?' (The body loses a lot of water, which can be dangerous.) 'Where do we get water from?' (River, pond, well, hand pump, tap.) 'Which diseases come from dirty water?' (Jaundice, typhoid, cholera, diarrhoea.)

steps.title: Make ORS
steps.do: Do Activity a3. With clean hands, your child measures 1 litre of clean, boiled and cooled water into a jug, then adds 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt (level the spoon with a knife), and stirs until dissolved. Your child tastes one sip: it should taste no saltier than tears. Ask: 'Why exactly measured, not a fistful?' (Too much salt can harm a sick child; the right mix helps the gut take in water fastest.) Tell them packets of ORS from the chemist are even better, and a child with diarrhoea should still see a doctor.

steps.title: Alum (phitkari) test
steps.do: Do Experiment e3, following the book's method on page 107. Stir a spoon of fine soil into two glasses of water until both are equally muddy. Your child guesses: 'Will alum make any difference?' Tie a piece of phitkari to a thread and swirl it in glass 1 for about a minute; leave glass 2 alone. Watch both for 10 minutes while you read on. The fine mud in glass 1 clumps into bigger flakes and sinks faster; glass 2 stays cloudy much longer. Then filter glass 1 through a clean cloth. Ask: 'Is this water now safe to drink?' (No! It looks clear, but germs can still be in it; it must also be boiled or treated.)

steps.title: Build a bottle filter
steps.do: Do Activity a4, a small version of the three-pot home-made filter on page 107. Cut a plastic bottle in half (adult). Turn the top half upside down into the bottom half like a funnel. Put a piece of cloth in the neck, then layers from bottom to top: crushed charcoal, then sand, then small gravel, just like the book's three pots but in one. Pour muddy water in and watch it drip out. Ask: 'Which layer catches the big bits? Which the small?' (Gravel catches big bits, sand catches finer ones, charcoal takes away some colour and smell.) Again ask: 'Does this kill germs?' (No; that needs boiling, chlorine or a proper purifier.)

steps.title: Chlorine, boiling and modern filters (page 108)
steps.do: Read methods 3, 4 and 5 on page 108 aloud. Ask: 'Which methods kill germs?' (Chlorine tablets, a pinch of potassium permanganate, boiling, and modern filters.) 'Which only remove mud?' (Alum and cloth or sand filters.) Look at your own water purifier or filter if you have one and find the ISI mark. Note: the book says boil for ten minutes; health agencies say even one minute at a full rolling boil kills the germs, so boiling well is what matters.

need: a jug, 1 litre boiled and cooled water, sugar, salt, a teaspoon
2 glasses, a spoon of soil, a piece of phitkari (alum) and thread
a plastic bottle, scissors (adult), cloth, crushed charcoal, sand, small gravel

prep.task: Buy a small piece of phitkari; collect sand, small gravel and a few pieces of charcoal (from a barbecue bag or a tandoor shop); boil and cool 1 litre of water

days.title: Clean food, healthy body
days.goal: Learn the book's clean-food rules, practise proper handwashing, read a sugary-drink label, and weigh up a live argument among scientists about fat and sugar.

steps.title: 8.6 Clean food (pages 108–109)
steps.do: Read section 8.6 and 'Knowing this is also necessary' aloud. After the seven cleanliness rules, ask your child to say them back in their own words on their fingers: clean kitchen, wash and soak dal and rice, wash vegetables before cutting, keep food covered from dust and flies, avoid stale food, wash hands before cooking and serving, wash hands before eating. After the three extra points, ask: 'Why is it better to eat smaller meals through the day than one huge one?' (A huge meal at once is hard to digest.) 'Why should we not talk with food in our mouth?' (Food could go down the windpipe and make us choke.)

steps.title: Glitter germs handwash
steps.do: Rub a little oil on your child's hands and sprinkle a pinch of glitter, turmeric or atta over them: these are pretend germs. First they rinse with plain water for 5 seconds. Ask: 'Are the germs gone?' (No, most stay.) Then wash with soap for 20 seconds: palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs, fingertips and nails, and wrists. Check again. Ask: 'Why does soap work better than water alone?' (Soap grabs on to oil and dirt and lets water wash them away.) Read the book's rhyme: 'Washing hands prevents disease and puts everyone at ease.'

steps.title: Fat or sugar: Keys and Yudkin
steps.do: Read the fast-food line on page 105 again.
