items.title: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage: Its Conservation and Honour

c.covers: Culture and heritage and why to conserve them; India's natural heritage: forests, wildlife, water and minerals

p.title: India's Cultural and Natural Heritage: Its Conservation and Honour
p.source: NIOS Open Basic Education, Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 1 (lesson pages 1–19)
p.summary: Your child learns what culture is (the seen and unseen ways of living we inherit), how it is learnt, added to, changed and varied across India, and how heritage is the part we receive and must protect, from the Qutub Minar and Sanchi Stupa to the Golden Temple and the work of Aryabhata. The second half turns to natural heritage: India's forests, wildlife, rivers, coasts and minerals, why they matter and how both kinds of heritage are being damaged and can be saved.
goals: By the end your child can explain culture as a way of living we inherit, and sort examples into its physical (seen) and non-physical (unseen) parts.
By the end your child can give the four general characteristics of culture from the book (learnt, accumulated, changing, diverse) with an example of each from their own family.
By the end your child can name at least ten heritage monuments, say which city and state each is in, who built several of them, and find them on a map of India.
By the end your child can explain how monuments get damaged (weather, pollution, careless visitors) and who protects them, and can show with a simple test why acid in polluted air harms marble.

By the end your child can describe India's natural heritage: which trees grow in which regions, where key animals live, which rivers start in the Himalaya, and where coal, iron and petroleum come from.
By the end your child can say why both cultural and natural heritage must be conserved, and what an ordinary citizen can do.
words: the way of living a group of people share and pass on: food, clothes, language, festivals, beliefs, art and knowledge
the parts of culture you can see and touch, such as clothes, food, pots and buildings
the parts of culture you cannot see, such as ideas, ideals, feelings and beliefs
what we have received from our forefathers and want to keep for those who come after us; also called legacy
something handed down from earlier generations
an old building or structure kept because it is important to history or culture
the study of the past through the things people left behind, such as buildings, tools and pots; the Archaeological Survey of India looks after many monuments
a place chosen by UNESCO, a United Nations body, as so important that it belongs to the whole world's heritage
the gifts of nature in a country: forests, animals, rivers, mountains, seas, deserts and minerals
a protected area where wild animals and plants live safely and hunting and tree-cutting are not allowed
a useful substance dug out of the earth, such as iron ore, coal or bauxite
to protect something and use it carefully so that it is not damaged or used up

days.title: What is culture? Look around your home
days.goal: Discover that culture is all around us at home, and learn its two aspects: physical and non-physical.

steps.title: Culture hunt in the kitchen
steps.do: Before opening the book, walk with your child into the kitchen and the room where you keep clothes. Ask them to find five things that would tell a visitor from another country something about your family: for example the tawa or the idli steamer, a jar of achaar, a steel tiffin, a sari or kurta, a rangoli stencil, a puja thali or a calendar with festival dates. For each, ask: 'Did we invent this, or did we get it from someone older?' Good answer: 'We learnt it from Nani or Dadi, and they learnt it from their parents.' Tell them: 'All of these are part of our culture.'

steps.title: What is culture? (lesson pages 1–2)
steps.do: Read section 1.1 'What is Culture?' aloud together (the start of the lesson, with the picture of a woman making rangoli). Stop after 'Culture is a way of living our life, which we have got as a legacy from our forefathers.' Ask: 'What does legacy mean?' (Something handed down to us.) Read the list: art, music, literature, architecture, crafts, philosophy, religion, science, customs, traditions, festivals. Ask your child to give one example of each from India, for example music: a Carnatic song or a bhajan; architecture: a temple, mosque or the Red Fort; science: the zero, or Ayurveda; crafts: a Madhubani painting. If stuck on 'philosophy', say: 'big ideas about how to live, like ahimsa, non-violence.'

steps.title: Seen and unseen: sort the cards
steps.do: Read the paragraph on the two aspects of culture (page 2). Then do Activity a1: write 16 slips (listed in the activity) and ask your child to sort them into two piles, 'Physical: I can see or touch it' and 'Non-physical: I cannot see it'. Discuss the tricky ones. A festival has both: the diyas and sweets are physical, but the joy and the story behind it are non-physical. A language is non-physical, though a written book is physical. Ask: 'Which pile would disappear if nobody remembered it?' Good answer: 'The non-physical pile, because ideas and beliefs live in people's minds.'

steps.title: Your family's culture card
steps.do: Give your child an A4 sheet folded in half. On the left, under 'Physical', they draw three things from your home (a dish, a piece of clothing, an object used in worship or a festival). On the right, under 'Non-physical', they write three things your family believes or values, with your help: for example 'We touch elders' feet to show respect', 'We do not waste food', 'Guests are like God (atithi devo bhava)'. Ask them to explain each one in their own words. Keep the card; you will add to it on Day 2.

steps.title: Three-sentence summary
steps.do: Ask your child to finish these sentences aloud: 'Culture is…' (a way of living we got from our forefathers). 'The physical part of culture includes…' (clothes, food, household things). 'The non-physical part includes…' (ideas, ideals, feelings and beliefs). If they mix up physical and non-physical, hold up a spoon (physical) and then ask them to 'hold up' respect for elders (they can't: non-physical).

prep.task: Write the 16 slips for Activity a1

days.title: How culture is learnt, grows and changes
days.goal: Learn the four general characteristics of culture and the significance of culture, using your own family's story.

steps.title: Four characteristics (lesson pages 2–3)
steps.do: Read section 1.1.1 aloud, one point at a time, and after each one ask for a family example. A. Culture is learnt and acquired: 'Who taught you how we celebrate Diwali, Eid, Christmas, Pongal or Lohri?' B. Culture is accumulated, it grows: the book says joint families have become nuclear families, and women's clothes have changed from lehenga and odhni to salwar suits and trousers. Ask: 'Do we live as a joint family or a nuclear family? What about Dadaji when he was small?' C. Culture keeps changing: the book's example is that wedding guests once stayed for many days. D. Diversity: people in Kashmir wear the pheran and carry a kangri (a small clay pot of hot coals kept under the pheran) against the cold, while in Kerala women often wear saris and men wear a lungi or mundu. Ask: 'Why would a kangri be useless in Kerala?' (It is hot and humid there.)

steps.title: Three-generation interview
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Call or sit with a grandparent or older relative. Your child asks the six questions in the activity (what they ate for breakfast as a child, what they wore to school, how a wedding was done, how they talked to elders, what games they played, how news came to them) and writes short answers in a table with columns 'Grandparent's time', 'Parent's time', 'My time'. You fill in the middle column. Afterwards ask: 'Which things stayed the same in all three columns? Which changed?' This shows culture being learnt, added to and changed, all at once.

steps.title: Why culture matters (lesson page 3)
steps.do: Read section 1.1.2 'Significance of Culture'. Explain the key line: 'Human beings are the creators of culture and it is culture which makes a human, a human being.' Ask: 'If a baby grew up all alone with nobody to teach it, would it know any language, food habits or festivals?' (No. It would have to learn everything from others.) The book also says many Indians have strong faith and believe wrongdoing, lying or stealing will be punished. Ask: 'Apart from fear of punishment, what other reasons are there not to lie or steal?' Good answers: it hurts other people; people stop trusting you; it is unfair.

steps.title: Book check 1.1 (lesson page 4)
steps.do: Do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 1.1' aloud. Fill in the blanks: legacy from our forefathers; traditions; non-physical; transferred; human. Then ask for any two general characteristics of culture, each with an example from the interview. If they can only remember one, give the hint word 'L-A-C-D' (learnt, accumulated, changing, diverse).

steps.title: Add to the culture card
steps.do: On yesterday's culture card, your child adds one sentence at the bottom: 'One thing that has changed in my family's culture is… One thing that has stayed the same is…' Read it aloud together.

need: a grandparent or older relative (in person or by phone)

prep.task: Ask a grandparent or older relative to keep 15 minutes free for a phone or video call

days.title: Our heritage: monuments, books and ideas
days.goal: Learn the difference between culture and heritage, place famous heritage sites on a map, and meet Aryabhata, an underdog who was right.

steps.title: Culture and heritage (lesson pages 4–5)
steps.do: Read section 1.2 'Culture and Heritage'. Point out the sentence: 'Any culture which we have inherited from our forefathers is called cultural heritage.' Read the long list of places together: Taj Mahal, Swaminarayan (Akshardham) temple in Gandhinagar, Qutub Minar, the Dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya, Red Fort, Mysore Palace, the Jain temples at Dilwara in Rajasthan, the Golden Temple, Gurdwara Sis Ganj, Sanchi Stupa, the church of St Francis Xavier in Goa, India Gate, Rameshwaram, Puri Rath Yatra, Dwarka, Badrinath, the Ashoka Pillar, Fatehpur Sikri, Rashtrapati Bhavan. Ask: 'Which of these are places of worship, and of which faiths?' Help them see Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Jain, Buddhist and Christian places all on one list: all are India's heritage. Note the book's last line: 'In culture changes keep happening but not in our heritage.' Ask: 'Why can't heritage change?' (It is what was already handed to us; we can only protect it or lose it.)

steps.title: Heritage map of India
steps.do: Do Activity a3. On an outline map of India, your child marks 12 heritage sites with a dot and a small drawing: Taj Mahal (Agra, Uttar Pradesh), Qutub Minar and Red Fort (Delhi), Golden Temple (Amritsar, Punjab), Dilwara temples (Mount Abu, Rajasthan), Hawa Mahal (Jaipur, Rajasthan), Sanchi Stupa (near Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh), Ajanta caves (Maharashtra), Gateway of India (Mumbai), St Francis Xavier church (Old Goa), Mysore Palace (Karnataka), Charminar (Hyderabad, Telangana), Mahabalipuram (Tamil Nadu), Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu), Puri (Odisha). Use a school atlas or a phone map to check each place. Ask: 'Which part of India has the most dots on your map? Is that because there is more heritage there, or because the book picked more from there?'

steps.title: Heritage in ideas: Aryabhata
steps.do: Read the book's line (page 5): 'Aryabhatta, Varahamihira and Bhaskaracharya have contributed to India's mathematics, astronomy and astrology.' Explain: astronomy is the science of the sun, moon, stars and planets, tested by measuring; astrology is a belief that planets shape our lives, which has not held up when tested, so scientists do not count it as science. Then tell the story of Voice v1, Aryabhata. Do a quick demonstration: your child sits on a swivel chair (or turns slowly on the spot) while looking at the room. Ask: 'Does the room seem to move the other way?' (Yes.) Aryabhata said the stars seem to move across the sky each night because the Earth is spinning, just like this. Discuss the 'ask' question.

steps.title: Book check 1.2 (lesson page 6)
steps.do: Do the matching task 'Let's see, what you have learnt 1.2' aloud. Answers: Agra – Taj Mahal; Mysore – Royal Palace; Delhi – Qutub Minar; Dilwara (the book misprints it as 'Bhilwara') – Jain Temple; Amritsar – Golden Temple; Sanchi – Sanchi Stupa; Goa – St Francis Church. Ask your child to point to each on their map as they answer.

steps.title: Culture or heritage?
steps.do: Ask quickly: 'The film songs you like this year: culture or heritage?' (Culture now; it might become heritage if people keep it for generations.) 'The Ramayana?' (Heritage.) 'The zero and decimal place value used all over the world?' (Heritage of Indian mathematics.) 'The way your family makes dal?' (Both: a living culture handed down to you.)

need: an outline map of India (printed or traced)
a school atlas or phone map
a swivel chair if you have one

prep.task: Print or trace an outline map of India

days.title: Famous monuments and why they need protecting
days.goal: Learn about the book's famous monuments, find out how monuments are damaged, test why polluted air harms marble, and learn who protects heritage.

steps.title: Start the marble and acid test
steps.do: Set up Experiment e1 first, so it can work while you read. Two glasses: one with plain water, one with white vinegar. Drop a piece of white chalk (or a small marble chip) into each. Ask your child to predict before dropping: 'Will anything happen? In which glass?' Write the guesses down. Leave both glasses on the table.

steps.title: Monuments tour (lesson pages 6–9)
steps.do: Read section 1.3 aloud, one monument at a time, finding each on the Day 3 map. Add these accurate details as you go. Indus Valley: cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro about 4,500 years old. Ajanta (Maharashtra): the paintings were painted on the cave walls, not carved, and many are about 1,500 years old. Mahabalipuram: about 1,300 years ago Pallava kings cut whole chariot-shaped temples (rathas) out of single rocks. Qutub Minar: about 73 metres tall, begun by Qutubuddin Aibak around 1199 and finished by later rulers; it is often called the tallest brick minaret in the world. Taj Mahal: built by Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal; the traditional account says it took about 22 years and 20,000 workers. Bada Imambara in Lucknow, on the Gomti, built by Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula, has a huge hall with no pillars and a maze (bhool-bhulaiya). Golden Temple: the holiest place of the Sikhs, with a holy pool. Jantar Mantar in Delhi: stone instruments for measuring the sky built by Raja Jai Singh II of Jaipur. After each, ask: 'Who built it, and in which city is it?' The book says UNESCO had 20 Indian sites; tell your child the list has grown, and India now has more than 40 World Heritage Sites.

steps.title: Check the chalk
steps.do: Look at the two glasses from Experiment e1. The chalk in vinegar should be fizzing with tiny bubbles and getting smaller and softer; the water glass shows little or no change. Ask: 'What is happening?' Then explain the 'why' from the experiment: marble and chalk are both made of calcium carbonate, and acids eat them away. Smoke from factories and vehicles makes the rain a little acidic.

steps.title: Saving the Taj: M.C. Mehta
steps.do: Read the last part of section 1.3 (page 9): monuments are damaged by weather, pollution, people writing names on walls, breaking things and living in them; the Department of Archaeology (the Archaeological Survey of India) looks after them, but every citizen must help. Then tell the story of Voice v2, the lawyer M.C. Mehta and the Taj Mahal case. Ask: 'Is it fair to close a factory that gives people jobs, to protect a monument? What else could be done?' Good answers include moving the factory, making it use cleaner fuel (as the court ordered), or giving workers new jobs.

steps.title: Book check 1.3 (lesson pages 9–10)
steps.do: Do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 1.3' aloud. Matching: Mumbai – Gateway of India; Hyderabad – Charminar; Fatehpur Sikri – Buland Darwaza; Lucknow – Imambara; Amritsar – Golden Temple. Questions: Qutub Minar is in Mehrauli, Delhi; the Taj Mahal took about 22 years; Bada Imambara is on the Gomti; Buland Darwaza is at Fatehpur Sikri; the holy pool is at the Golden Temple, Amritsar; Sanchi Stupa is in Madhya Pradesh; Charminar is in Hyderabad. Then do core worksheet ws1, sections A and B, in writing.

need: 2 pieces of white chalk (or marble chips)

prep.task: Buy a small bottle of white vinegar if you do not have one

days.title: Natural heritage: forests and wildlife
days.goal: Learn why forests matter, which trees grow in which part of India, and where India's animals live, and test how plant cover protects soil.

steps.title: Natural heritage and forests (lesson pages 10–11)
steps.do: Read section 1.4 and 1.4.1 aloud. List what we get from forests (the book names wood, herbs, rubber, lac and silk) and what forests do: help bring rain, stop soil being washed away, enrich the soil and give animals homes. The book says 23% of India is forest; tell your child that the latest government surveys put forest cover at about 21–22%, and about 25% if trees outside forests are counted. Then read the trees of each region and make a quick table aloud: Himalaya – cone-shaped trees like deodar (cedar) and pine; Terai (the land at the foot of the Himalaya) – sal, teak, bamboo; plains – banyan, peepal, neem, sheesham (rosewood), sandalwood, bael; desert – date palm, babool and keekar (acacias), cactus (nagphani), with thick rough bark; coasts – coconut, palm and areca (betel nut). Ask: 'Why do desert trees have thick bark and small or spiny leaves?' (To lose less water in the heat.)

steps.title: Do roots hold the soil?
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Fill two trays or cut-open milk cartons with soil: one bare, one covered with a thick layer of grass clumps with roots (from a garden or a patch of weeds) or a lawn sod. Tilt both on a brick with a bowl at the lower end. Ask your child to predict which bowl will get muddier water. Pour the same mug of water slowly over each, like rain. Compare the two bowls side by side. Link it to the book's line that forests 'help in checking land erosion'.

steps.title: Wildlife of India (lesson pages 11–13)
steps.do: Read section 1.4.2. Mark on the Day 3 map: elephants (Assam, Kerala, Karnataka), Asiatic lions (only in and around the Gir forest, Gujarat), one-horned rhinoceros (Assam and West Bengal), and Himalayan animals (snow leopard, musk deer, yak). Add the hangul, Kashmir's red deer. The book's numbers are older: India's Zoological Survey now records more than one lakh animal species, including over 1,300 kinds of birds, and India has more than 100 national parks, not 55. Ask: 'Why are lions found in only one forest in all of India? What could go wrong if all of them live in one place?' (A disease or fire could harm all of them at once; that is why scientists want a second home for them.)

steps.title: Salim Ali, the birdman of India
steps.do: Read Voice v3 aloud. Then stand at a window or balcony for 3 minutes and count and name every bird you can see or hear (crow, myna, pigeon, sparrow, koel, bulbul, parrot, kite). Ask the 'ask' question from v3.

steps.title: Quick quiz
steps.do: Ask: 'Where would you go to see a lion in the wild?' (Gir, Gujarat.) 'Which animal has one horn and lives in Assam's swamps?' (Rhinoceros.) 'Name a tree of the desert and one of the Himalaya.' (Babool or date palm; deodar or pine.) 'Name two national parks from the book.' (Corbett, Kaziranga, Dudhwa, Kanha.) 'What is our national bird?' (Peacock.)

need: a clump of grass with roots or a piece of lawn

prep.task: Dig up a clump of grass with its roots and soil (from a weedy patch, not a park lawn)

days.title: Rivers, seas and minerals
days.goal: Learn India's river systems and coasts, measure the coastline yourself, and find out where coal, petroleum and iron come from and how we use them at home.

steps.title: Water resources (lesson page 13)
steps.do: Read section 1.4.3. On the map, your child traces the Himalaya from Jammu and Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh in brown, then draws in blue the rivers that start there (Ganga, Yamuna, Sutlej, Ravi, Chenab, Beas, Brahmaputra) and the southern rivers (Narmada, Tapti, Krishna, Kaveri). Label the Bay of Bengal (east), the Arabian Sea (west) and the Indian Ocean (south). Ask: 'Why are Himalayan rivers full of water even in summer when there is no rain?' (Snow and glaciers melt and feed them.)

steps.title: How long is India's coast?
steps.do: Do Activity a4. Your child measures the coastline on an atlas map twice, first with a few straight ruler lines from Gujarat to West Bengal, then by laying a thread carefully along every bend, and converts both with the map's scale. The book says about 7,000 km. Then tell them: an official remeasurement completed in 2024 that followed the coast in much finer detail, including islands, gave about 11,000 km. Ask: 'Did the coast grow? Why did the number change?' (No; a more detailed measurement follows more bends, so it gets longer.)

steps.title: Minerals: coal, petroleum, iron (lesson pages 13–14)
steps.do: Read section 1.4.4. Explain 'mineral' and 'mine or quarry', and that ores come out impure and must be refined in factories. Coal: made from forests buried and pressed under the earth for millions of years; used for electricity, melting iron ore and in industry; mined in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and other states. Petroleum: from deep underground, with natural gas; gives petrol, diesel and kerosene; found off Mumbai (Bombay High), in Assam and Gujarat; India imports most of what it uses. Iron: the most-used metal, for machines, buildings and bridges. Ask: 'If coal is made from ancient forests, why can't we just make more?' (It takes millions of years; we use it far faster than it forms.)

steps.title: Mineral hunt at home
steps.do: Your child walks round the house and lists ten things made from minerals or fuels from the earth, and what each comes from: iron or steel (kadhai, almirah, gate, nails), aluminium from bauxite (pressure cooker, foil), copper (wires, a lota), glass from sand, the LPG cylinder (gas from petroleum), plastic buckets (made from petroleum), electricity (much of India's still comes from coal), cement walls (from limestone), mica (in some paints and electrical parts). Ask: 'Which of these could we use less of, or reuse, to conserve minerals?'

steps.title: Book check 1.4 (lesson pages 14–15)
steps.do: Do the fill-ins from 'Let's see, what you have learnt 1.4' aloud: silk; thick and rough; musk; Arunachal Pradesh; kerosene. Then ask the short questions: two desert trees (date palm, babool); cedar and pine (Himalaya); three grassland animals (deer, tiger, lion); where coal is found (Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh); where petroleum is found (Mumbai offshore, Assam, Gujarat). Also discuss the book's two questions on Ganga and Yamuna pollution (sewage and factory waste) and forest cutting (more people need land, wood and homes).

need: a school atlas with a map scale

days.title: Revise, check and teach it back
days.goal: Review the whole lesson, do the book's exercise and the stretch and challenge worksheets, check understanding and teach the lesson back.

steps.title: Let's Revise (lesson pages 15–16)
steps.do: Read the 'Let's Revise' points aloud, but pause before the end of each and let your child finish it from memory, for example 'Culture has two aspects…' (physical and non-physical). 'Culture is learnt and obtained. It is…' (changing). Correct the book's one slip: '55 National Parks' is now more than 100. Then do the true/false part of the book's Exercise IV aloud. Answers: true, false (culture changes), true, false (Pongal is mainly a Tamil Nadu festival), true, false (the Golden Temple is in Amritsar), true, true, false (the government has made national parks and wildlife laws), true.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child does stretch worksheet ws2 alone. Then check it together. For the open questions, look for reasons, not just names: for example, 'The kangri suits Kashmir because winters there are freezing.'

steps.title: Indus mystery and the challenge sheet
steps.do: Tell the story of Voice v4, the undeciphered Indus script. Show a picture of an Indus seal if you can find one in a book or online. Ask the 'ask' question. Then your child tries challenge worksheet ws3. Do the puzzle items together if needed; praise good reasons even when the answer differs from yours.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Before closing, glance at ws3's last section with your child and agree on one real promise to protect heritage (for example 'I will never write on a monument wall' or 'I will carry my own water bottle on trips so I don't leave plastic behind'). Write it on the culture card.

steps.title: Lesson check
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud, one at a time, without the book. Tick the good answers. For any missed answer, open the right lesson page, read it together for one minute and ask again in different words. Six or more right is good; fewer than five, repeat the Day 3 map and the Day 5 forest reading next week.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the teacher and you are the student. Using the heritage map, the culture card and the chalk from the vinegar test, they teach you in five minutes: what culture is and its two aspects; three monuments, where they are and why they are damaged; and three parts of natural heritage. Ask two 'student' questions: 'Why does the Taj turn yellow?' and 'Why should I care about a forest I will never visit?'

need: the heritage map and culture card
a picture of an Indus seal (optional)

sections.p: Culture is a way of living which we got as a legacy from our ____.

Sort these into the two aspects of culture.

Who built the Sanchi Stupa?
The stone rathas (chariot temples) at Mahabalipuram were made by the ____ kings.

A family moves from Srinagar to Kochi. Which two things in their way of living might change, and why?
Your cousin learns to make Dadi's rasam, then adds a little extra tamarind of her own. Which characteristic of culture does this show best?

sections.p: Name one thing in your home that is heritage (handed down) and one that is new culture from your own time.
Match each region to a tree that grows there.
Sort these animals by where they are mainly found in India.
cats: Forests of Kerala, Karnataka and Assam

sections.p: Fill the table for three minerals or fuels.
cols: One state where it is found

sections.p: Your soil-tray test: why did the bare tray send muddier water into the bowl? What does this tell us about cutting forests on hills?
Why does the marble of the Taj Mahal need protection from smoke and polluted air?
opts: Acids and soot in polluted air eat away and stain marble

sections.p: The book says India's coast is about 7,000 km long, but a newer survey says about 11,000 km. Both teams measured the same coast. Explain how both can be honest.
The lions of India all live in and around one forest in Gujarat. Give one reason this is risky and one reason moving some lions elsewhere could be hard.
What if nobody wrote down or taught Aryabhata's ideas? What would we have lost, and how do ideas survive for 1,500 years?

opts: Finding a long inscription with the same text written in a language we can read
Painting the seals in bright colours
Counting how many seals are in museums
Guessing what each sign looks like

sections.p: A factory near a monument gives jobs to 500 people but its smoke damages the monument. Write what the factory owner, a worker, and a heritage lover might each say. Then write what you would decide and why.
My promise to protect our cultural or natural heritage is:

experiments.title: Why does polluted air harm marble?
experiments.question: What happens to chalk (which is made of the same stuff as marble) when it sits in an acid, compared with plain water?
need: 2 equal pieces of white chalk, or 2 small marble chips from a stone or tile shop
steps: Label one glass 'Water' and one 'Vinegar (acid)'. Fill each half full.
Look closely at the two pieces of chalk and draw them. If you have a kitchen scale, weigh them.
Drop one piece into each glass at the same moment.
Watch for 2 minutes and note what you see.
Leave both glasses for 30 minutes to an hour, then take the chalk out with a spoon, compare and draw again.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: will anything happen in either glass? Which piece will change more? Write both guesses down.
experiments.observe: In vinegar, tiny bubbles stream off the chalk at once and it slowly crumbles and gets smaller and softer at the edges. In water, the chalk may give off a few air bubbles and soften a little but does not fizz steadily or shrink in the same way.
experiments.why: Chalk, limestone and marble are all made mostly of calcium carbonate. An acid reacts with calcium carbonate: it breaks it apart, making carbon dioxide gas (the bubbles) and a substance that dissolves in water, so the stone is slowly eaten away. Vinegar is a weak acid. When coal, petrol and diesel are burnt in factories, power stations and vehicles, they give off gases such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides that mix with rain and moisture to make weak acids. Over many years this 'acid rain' and soot can roughen, pit and stain marble buildings and statues like the Taj Mahal. Real acid rain is much weaker than vinegar, so the damage takes years, not minutes.
experiments.safety: Vinegar is safe, but do not let it get into eyes. Do not use stronger acids such as toilet cleaner.
experiments.time: 5 min to set up + 5 min check after 30–60 min

experiments.title: Do plants and roots stop soil washing away?
experiments.question: When rain falls on a slope, does soil covered with plants lose less soil than bare soil?
need: 2 trays or milk cartons cut open lengthwise (same size)
a clump of grass or weeds with roots and soil, enough to cover one tray
a brick or thick book to tilt the trays
steps: Fill one tray with loose bare soil, pressed down lightly.
Fill the second tray with soil and press the grass clumps firmly on top so the roots are in the soil and the top is covered.
Rest one end of each tray on a brick so they slope the same amount, with a bowl under the lower end of each. Cut a small V at the low end of a carton so water can run out.
Pour one mug of water slowly over the high end of the bare tray, like steady rain. Repeat exactly the same for the grassy tray.
Put the two bowls side by side on white paper and compare the colour and the amount of mud. Let them settle for 10 minutes and look at the mud at the bottom.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which bowl will have more mud? Will the grassy tray let any water through at all?
experiments.observe: Look at how brown the water is, how much mud settles at the bottom of each bowl, and whether gullies (little channels) formed in the trays. Usually the bare tray's water is thick brown with a layer of mud, and grooves appear in the soil; the grassy tray's water is clearer and its soil stays in place.
experiments.why: Falling water hits bare soil hard and knocks particles loose; then the water running downhill carries them away. This washing away of the top soil is called soil erosion. Plants protect soil in three ways: leaves break the force of the falling drops, roots hold soil particles together like a net, and fallen leaves and plant matter help water soak in slowly instead of rushing over the top. That is why the book says forests check land erosion. When forests on hills are cut, the rich top layer of soil, which took hundreds of years to form, can wash into rivers in a few monsoons, making rivers muddy and floods worse.
experiments.safety: Wash hands after handling soil. Do this outside or on newspaper.

activities.title: Seen and unseen culture sort
steps: Write one item on each slip: sari, dhoti, idli, roti, steel tiffin, diya, temple or mosque or church building, tabla, respect for elders, belief in God, the idea of non-violence (ahimsa), joy of a festival, our language, a lullaby Nani sang, honesty, a wedding.
Make two headings on the floor: 'Physical (seen)' and 'Non-physical (unseen)'.
Your child places each slip and says why.
Put the hard ones (language, lullaby, wedding, festival) in the middle and talk about how they have both a seen and an unseen part.
Ask your child to add two slips of their own to each pile.
activities.outcome: Two piles that show culture is not only things we can see but also ideas, values and feelings, and that most real customs have both parts.

activities.title: Three-generation interview
need: a notebook with a 4-column table drawn: Question, Grandparent's time, Parent's time, My time
steps: Your child asks: What did you eat for breakfast as a child?
What did you wear to school, and how did you get there?
How long did a wedding last, and how long did guests stay?
How did children greet and speak to elders?
What games did you play?
How did news from far away reach your family (letter, radio, telegram, phone)?
Your child writes short answers; the parent fills in the 'Parent's time' column; the child fills in 'My time'.
Circle in green what stayed the same and in red what changed.
activities.outcome: A family table showing culture being passed on (learnt), added to (accumulated) and changing, with the child's own family as the evidence.

activities.title: Heritage map of India
need: a school atlas or phone map
steps: Mark and label 12–14 heritage sites from the book with a dot and a tiny drawing: Taj Mahal, Qutub Minar, Red Fort, Golden Temple, Dilwara temples, Hawa Mahal, Sanchi Stupa, Ajanta caves, Gateway of India, St Francis Xavier church, Mysore Palace, Charminar, Mahabalipuram, Kanyakumari, Puri.
Colour the dot by type: places of worship in orange, palaces and forts in red, others in green.
Write the state name next to each.
Keep the map: on Day 5 add animals and national parks, and on Day 6 add rivers and seas.
activities.outcome: One map of India that grows through the week to show both cultural and natural heritage.

activities.title: Measure India's coastline
need: a school atlas map of India with a scale bar
steps: Find the scale bar on the map (for example 1 cm = 200 km) and write it down.
Measure 1: draw 5–6 straight ruler lines along the coast from the Gujarat–Pakistan border round Kanyakumari to the Bangladesh border. Add up the centimetres and change to km using the scale.
Measure 2: lay the thread along the coast following every bend you can, from the same start to the same end. Mark the thread, straighten it on the ruler and convert to km.
Compare the two answers with the book's 7,000 km and the 2024 figure of about 11,000 km (which also counts island coasts).
Write a sentence: 'The more carefully we follow the bends, the ____ the coastline gets.'
activities.outcome: Two measurements of India's coastline and an understanding that a coastline's length depends on how finely you measure it, so careful measuring, and saying how you measured, matter in science.

voices.who: Aryabhata (476 CE–about 550 CE), Kusumapura near Pataliputra (today's Patna), India
voices.idea: In his book the Aryabhatiya, which he wrote at the age of 23 in 499 CE, Aryabhata said that the Earth spins on its axis, and that the stars only seem to move across the sky each night because of this, just as a person on a moving boat sees the trees on the bank moving backwards. He also explained that eclipses happen because of the shadows of the Earth and the Moon, not because of a demon (Rahu) swallowing the Sun or Moon, and he gave a very good value for pi.
voices.then: Many later Indian astronomers did not accept that the Earth spins. The famous astronomer Brahmagupta, about a century later, criticised the idea, and for a long time most astronomers in India and elsewhere believed the Earth stood still while the sky turned around it.
voices.now: We now know for certain that the Earth spins once a day; satellites and pendulum experiments show it directly. Aryabhata's explanation of eclipses is also correct. India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named Aryabhata in his honour. He was right on these points, though like everyone in his time he also held some ideas that later turned out wrong.
voices.ask: When you turned on the chair, the room seemed to move. Standing on the ground, how could you tell whether the sky is turning or the Earth is spinning? What evidence would change your mind?

voices.who: M.C. Mehta (born 1946), environmental lawyer, and the Supreme Court of India's Taj Mahal case (judgement 1996)
voices.idea: In 1984 Mehta asked the Supreme Court to protect the Taj Mahal, arguing that smoke from foundries, factories and a nearby oil refinery was yellowing and damaging its marble. In 1996 the court agreed and ordered factories in a large protected zone around the Taj (the Taj Trapezium Zone) to switch to cleaner natural gas or move away.
voices.then: Many factory owners and workers protested, because their jobs and businesses were at stake. Some people argued that the damage was mainly from age and weather, not industry.
voices.now: Scientists accept that air pollution discolours and harms marble. A 2015 study by researchers from IIT Kanpur and universities in the USA found that tiny particles of soot, smoke from burning rubbish and dung, and dust settling on the marble cause its brownish colour. The Archaeological Survey of India now cleans the Taj with a special clay pack, and the fight against pollution around Agra continues.
voices.ask: Some people said the Taj was going yellow just from old age. What test or measurement would show whether pollution or age is to blame?

voices.who: Salim Ali (1896–1987), ornithologist (bird scientist), Mumbai, India
voices.idea: Salim Ali spent his life travelling across India studying birds carefully: where they live, what they eat and how they nest. His 'The Book of Indian Birds' (1941) helped ordinary people identify birds, and with S. Dillon Ripley he wrote a ten-volume handbook of the birds of India and Pakistan. He argued that wild places must be protected for birds to survive.
voices.then: In his early years there were few jobs for a bird scientist in India, and he did not complete a formal degree in zoology, so he had to make his own way. Much bird study then meant shooting birds to collect them; he used collecting too, as scientists of his time did, but gradually moved more towards watching living birds in the wild.
voices.now: He is called the 'Birdman of India'. His work helped protect the Bharatpur bird sanctuary (now Keoladeo National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site), and he spoke up for saving Silent Valley in Kerala from being flooded by a dam. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 1976.
voices.ask: You counted birds from your window for 3 minutes. If you did this every day for a year, what could you find out that one day could not tell you?

voices.who: The Indus script debate: Iravatham Mahadevan (1930–2018) and Asko Parpola (born 1941), and their critics Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat and Michael Witzel (2004)
voices.idea: The Indus Valley people left thousands of small seals and objects with rows of signs, about 4,500 years old. Most scholars, including Mahadevan in India and Parpola in Finland, who each spent decades listing and studying the signs, think the signs are writing of a real language.
voices.then: In 2004 Farmer, Sproat and Witzel argued that the inscriptions are too short (usually about five signs) and that the signs may be symbols like those on flags or road signs, not full writing. Many experts strongly disagreed.
voices.now: In 2009 a team led by Rajesh Rao published a statistical study suggesting the signs follow patterns like those of languages, but the critics said the test could not prove it. Nobody has yet deciphered the script, mainly because no long text has been found written both in Indus signs and in a known language. This is a live debate.
voices.ask: If someone found only very short labels in our house, like 'salt', 'sugar' and 'Om', could they work out our whole language? What would they need to find?

check.q: What is culture? Give one physical and one non-physical example.
check.a: Culture is a way of living we have received from our forefathers. Physical: clothes, food, pots, buildings. Non-physical: ideas, ideals, feelings and beliefs, such as respect for elders.

check.q: Name the four general characteristics of culture in the book.
check.a: It is learnt and acquired; it is accumulated (it grows from generation to generation); it keeps changing; it is diverse.

check.q: What is the difference between culture and heritage?
check.a: Culture is our whole way of living and keeps changing; heritage is what we have received from our forefathers, such as monuments, scriptures and knowledge, which we must protect and pass on.

check.q: Where are the Taj Mahal, Charminar, Sanchi Stupa and the Golden Temple, and who built the Taj?
check.a: Taj Mahal: Agra, built by Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal. Charminar: Hyderabad. Sanchi Stupa: near Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. Golden Temple: Amritsar, Punjab.

check.q: Give three ways monuments get damaged and say who looks after them.
check.a: Weather and age, air pollution (acids and soot), and careless people writing on walls, breaking things or living in them. The Archaeological Survey of India (department of archaeology) looks after them, but every citizen must help.

check.q: Why did the chalk fizz in vinegar, and what does it teach us about the Taj Mahal?
check.a: Chalk and marble are calcium carbonate, which acids eat away, giving off carbon dioxide bubbles. Polluted air makes rain slightly acidic and leaves soot, so it slowly harms and stains marble.

check.q: Name three things forests give us and two things they do for the land.
check.a: Wood, herbs, rubber, lac, silk, food and homes for animals. They help bring rainfall, stop soil erosion and make the soil richer.

check.q: Where in India are coal and petroleum found, and why should we use them carefully?
check.a: Coal: Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and other states. Petroleum: off Mumbai, Assam, Gujarat. They took millions of years to form and will run out, and India has to import most of its petroleum.

items.title: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society

c.covers: People and customs of India; unity in diversity; peace and harmony; Ashoka and Akbar

p.title: Peace, Unity and Harmony in Indian Society
p.source: NIOS Open Basic Education, Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 2 (lesson pages 21–32)
p.summary: India is home to people of many religions, communities, tribes and more than twenty officially recognised languages, yet they share one national identity. Your child learns where this diversity comes from (geography, climate and peoples who came and mingled over thousands of years), how it shows in festivals, crafts and words, what holds the country together (the freedom struggle, the Constitution, the flag, sport, the armed forces), what peace and harmony mean at home and between nations, and how Emperor Ashoka and Emperor Akbar tried to build respect between faiths.
goals: By the end your child can describe India's diversity of religions, communities, tribes and languages using real facts, and explain the idea of 'unity in diversity'.
By the end your child can give reasons why India's culture is mixed: its size and climate, and peoples who came from outside and mingled, and show it in words we use every day.
By the end your child can name things that unite Indians: the freedom struggle, the Constitution, the national flag and anthem, sport and the armed forces.
By the end your child can explain peace and harmony at home, in the village and between countries, and say what the Constitution says about equality.
By the end your child can tell how Ashoka and Akbar tried to spread peace and respect for all faiths, and how historians know about them from evidence such as Ashoka's rock edicts.
By the end your child can say one way they themselves can help keep harmony with people who are different from them.
words: many different kinds together, such as many languages, religions and foods in one country
being joined together as one, even when we are different
living together peacefully, with respect, as if all are part of one tune; no one high or low
a group of people who share things such as a place, language, religion or way of life
a smaller group within a religion that follows some different practices, such as Shia and Sunni in Islam
a community descended from India's early inhabitants, with its own customs, language and beliefs, such as the Gond, Bhil and Santhal
communities listed in a schedule of the Constitution so that they get special protection and support because they were treated unfairly in the past
the list in the Constitution of 22 officially recognised Indian languages
the feeling and effort that keeps all Indians together as one nation
an official message from a ruler; Ashoka had his edicts carved on rocks and pillars
Ashoka's word (from Prakrit) for right conduct: kindness, honesty, respect and tolerance
Akbar's policy of 'peace with all', treating people of every faith fairly

days.title: Many Indias in one India
days.goal: Notice how much diversity there is in your own building or street, and read the book's opening on unity in diversity.

steps.title: How many languages do we know?
steps.do: Ask your child to list every language they have heard spoken by family, neighbours, the vegetable seller, the watchman, school friends and on TV. Count them together. Most Indian children can name five or more. Then ask: 'How do you say water in each?' (for example paani, neer/thanni, jal, jol, vellam, nīru). Ask: 'If people say water in so many ways, are they still talking about the same thing?' (Yes. The words differ but the thing and the need are the same: that is the heart of unity in diversity.)

steps.title: Opening of the lesson (lesson pages 21–22)
steps.do: Read the lesson opening aloud. Stop at the lines on identity: people may have a religious identity (Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Sikh, Buddhist, Parsi), a regional identity (Punjabi, Tamil, Bengali, Manipuri), but 'their national identity is paramount'. Ask: 'What are your identities?' Help them make a short list, for example 'I am Ananya; I am a girl; I am Marathi; I am from Pune; I am Indian.' Explain that a person has many identities at once and none cancels the others. Correct two old facts: the book says India is the second most populated country; since 2023 India has been estimated to have the largest population in the world. The book says 'more than 850 languages and dialects': the exact count depends on how you count dialects, but it is in the hundreds.

steps.title: Neighbourhood diversity survey
steps.do: Start Activity a1. Make the survey sheet together and fill in your own family's row now. Your child then calls or visits three or four families you know well (neighbours, relatives in another city, a family friend) and asks the five survey questions politely: home language, state their family is from, one festival they celebrate, one special dish, and one word in their language for 'thank you'. Finish the rest over the next two days. Before they start, tell them: 'We ask these questions because we are curious and want to learn, never to judge or tease.'

steps.title: A note on respectful words
steps.do: Parent note: this lesson touches religion, caste and tribe, which can be sensitive. Keep the tone curious and respectful. Tell your child: 'Every family's faith and customs matter to them as much as ours matter to us. We never make fun of how someone prays, dresses or eats.' Ask: 'Has anyone ever teased you or a friend for being different? How did it feel? What would have been a kind thing to say instead?' Listen fully before you answer.

steps.title: Say it in one line
steps.do: Ask your child to explain 'unity in diversity' in one sentence using an example from today. A good answer: 'People in India speak many languages and follow many religions but we are all Indians together, like the different words for water all mean water.'

need: a notebook for the survey sheet

prep.task: Message three or four families to ask if your child can ask them five short questions this week

days.title: People of India: religions, tribes and languages
days.goal: Learn the main religions and their sects, India's tribal communities, and the 22 languages of the Constitution.

steps.title: Religions and communities (lesson pages 22–23)
steps.do: Read section 2.1 'People of India' up to the Jews of Maharashtra and Kerala. The book's figure of about 4,635 communities comes from the 'People of India' survey by the Anthropological Survey of India. Update one number: the 2011 Census counted about 80% of Indians as Hindus, about 14% Muslims, about 2% Christians, about 2% Sikhs, and smaller numbers of Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, Jews and followers of tribal faiths. Make a table of the sects the book names: Islam – Shia and Sunni; Christianity – Catholic and Protestant (there are also Orthodox churches, such as the old Syrian churches of Kerala); Buddhism – Mahayana and the older school the book calls Hinayana, which its followers call Theravada; Jainism – Digambara and Shvetambara. The '33 crore gods' is a traditional saying; many Hindus understand all gods as forms of one divine. Ask: 'Why might one religion split into groups?' (People came to understand teachings or practices differently over time.)

steps.title: Tribes of India (lesson pages 22–23)
steps.do: Read the part on tribes. Explain: Adivasi means 'original inhabitants'. The Gond, Bhil and Santhal are among the largest tribes; the Meena, Munda and Oraon are also large. Many tribal people have been pushed off their forest land and did not get fair chances, which is why the Constitution gives them reserved seats and protections. Tell them about Gond art: today artists such as Jangarh Singh Shyam (1962–2001) made Gond painting famous across the world. Show a Gond or Warli painting online if you can and let your child copy one small part (Warli uses circles, triangles and lines). Ask: 'Why would a community that lived in forests for thousands of years know things that city people don't?' (They know the plants, animals, seasons and medicines of the forest.)

steps.title: One name, many scripts
steps.do: Read the list of 22 languages on page 23 (the Eighth Schedule) aloud together. Then your child writes their own first name in three or four scripts, using a phone keyboard or an online transliteration tool to see how: Devanagari (Hindi, Marathi, Sanskrit, Nepali), Bengali-Assamese, Gurmukhi (Punjabi), Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, Gujarati, and Urdu (written right to left). Ask: 'Which scripts look similar to each other?' (Many Indian scripts come from the ancient Brahmi script, the one Ashoka used: you'll meet it on Day 6.) Note: the book says many languages have no script; they are spoken, and can be written in another script.

steps.title: Book check 2.1 (lesson pages 23–24)
steps.do: Do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 2.1' aloud. Fill in the blanks: all (people of all religions of the world live in India); gods and goddesses (tribes have their own); Mahayana. Questions: the two sects of Islam are Shia and Sunni; two tribes, for example Gond and Bhil (also Santhal, Munda, Oraon, Meena). Then add two more rows to the Activity a1 survey with your child.

steps.title: Count the twenty-two
steps.do: Without looking, how many of the 22 languages can your child name? Give a clue for the hard ones: 'It is spoken in Goa' (Konkani); 'in Manipur' (Manipuri, also called Meitei); 'by the Santhal people' (Santali); 'in Jammu' (Dogri); 'in Assam's Bodoland' (Bodo); 'in Mithila, north Bihar' (Maithili). Note: the book lists English among the 22, but English is not in the Eighth Schedule; it is an official language of the Union alongside Hindi.

need: a phone or computer to see different scripts

days.title: Our mixed culture
days.goal: Find out why India's culture is mixed, and discover the mixing hiding in the words, crafts and festivals of our daily life.

steps.title: Why our culture is mixed (lesson pages 24–25)
steps.do: Read section 2.2 'Our Mixed Culture: Unity in Diversity' up to the crafts. The book gives two reasons for diversity: the vastness and different climates of India, and peoples who came from outside over thousands of years (Iranians, Greeks, Kushanas, Shakas, Huns, Arabs, Turks, Mughals and Europeans) and settled and mingled. Ask: 'How would a cold climate change what people wear and eat?' (Woollens, pherans, more wheat and meat, hot drinks like kahwa.) Then read the crafts: chikankari embroidery of Lucknow, phulkari of Punjab, kantha embroidery of Bengal. One correction: patola silk sarees come mainly from Patan in Gujarat; Odisha is famous for its own ikat weaving, such as Sambalpuri sarees. Look at any embroidered or printed cloth in your home and ask: 'Where was this made?'

steps.title: Word detectives
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Your child predicts which of 12 everyday words are 'pure Indian' and which came from another country, then checks with you using the answer list. Discuss the surprise: chabi (key), balti (bucket), almari (cupboard) and pav (bread roll) came from Portuguese; kitab (book) and kursi (chair) from Arabic; bazaar, darwaza (door) and sabzi from Persian. Ask: 'Did these words replace our language, or make it richer?'

steps.title: Festivals and folk dances (lesson pages 25–26)
steps.do: Read about festivals and folk music. Draw a map of India and mark the January harvest festival when the sun moves into Makara (Capricorn): Khichdi in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, Lohri in Punjab, Haryana and Himachal (the night before), Magh Bihu or Bhogali Bihu in Assam, Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Makar Sankranti in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat (Uttarayan, the kite festival) and many other states. Correct one slip in the book: Onam is Kerala's harvest festival but it comes in August–September, not in January. Read the question 'What is common between the Bhangra of Punjab and Bihu of Assam?' (Both celebrate the harvest.) Play a short clip of each if you can and let your child try two steps.

steps.title: Festival calendar
steps.do: Using the survey answers from Activity a1 and a calendar, your child marks every festival they now know of, from different faiths and regions: for example Eid-ul-Fitr, Diwali, Christmas, Guru Nanak Jayanti, Mahavir Jayanti, Buddha Purnima, Navroz (the Parsi new year), Onam, Durga Puja, Ganesh Chaturthi, Bihu, Pongal. Ask: 'Which festival from another community would you most like to see? Who could you ask to take you?'

steps.title: Two reasons
steps.do: Ask: 'Give the book's two reasons why India's culture is so varied.' (Different geography and climate; people from outside came and mingled.) 'Give one word, one dish and one festival that show mixing.' (For example pav; samosa, which came from Central Asia; Christmas celebrated by people of all faiths.)

need: an embroidered or printed cloth from home

prep.task: Write the 12 word slips for Experiment e1 and keep the answer list hidden

days.title: What binds us together
days.goal: Learn how the freedom struggle, the Constitution, national symbols, sport and the armed forces unite India, and test why a bundle is stronger than one stick.

steps.title: From princely states to one nation (lesson pages 25–26)
steps.do: Read the part beginning 'Earlier our country was divided into many princely states'. Explain: before 1947 India was a patchwork of British-ruled provinces and over 500 princely states ruled by kings and nawabs. The Indian National Congress, formed in 1885, brought people from every region and religion together against British rule, and after Independence most princely states joined India, with Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon leading that work. The Constitution makes unity and integrity a goal and a duty of every citizen. Ask: 'Why would people who speak different languages feel like one nation during the freedom struggle?' (They faced the same rulers, shared the same goal, worked and went to jail together.)

steps.title: The bundle of sticks
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. First tell the old story (found in many cultures, including Aesop and Indian folk tales) of a father who shows his quarrelling sons that one stick breaks easily but a bundle cannot be broken. Then test it for real with ice-cream sticks or thin bamboo skewers. Your child predicts, then tries to snap one stick, then two, then a bundle of ten tied with a rubber band. Ask: 'Why is the bundle stronger? Is it just a story, or is there real science in it?' Explain using the 'why' of the experiment.

steps.title: Sport, soldiers and the flag (lesson pages 26–27)
steps.do: Read about cricket, hockey, football and the armed forces. Ask your child to name sports stars they know and which state or community they come from, for example cricketers from Mumbai, Ranchi, Punjab, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, hockey players from Odisha's tribal districts and Punjab, boxer Mary Kom from Manipur, chess's D. Gukesh from Chennai. Ask: 'When India wins, do we ask which religion the player follows?' Then read about the national flag and anthem. Ask what the three colours and the Ashoka Chakra on the flag stand for. (Saffron is often explained as courage and sacrifice, white as truth and peace, green as faith, growth and the land; the 24-spoke wheel is from Ashoka's lion capital at Sarnath, which you will read about on Day 6.)

steps.title: Does meeting people change minds?
steps.do: Read Voice v4, Gordon Allport's contact idea. Ask: 'Why might soldiers from different states who eat, train and celebrate festivals together end up as friends, as the book describes on page 27?' Then ask the 'ask' question. Finally do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 2.2': unity; together; religions.

steps.title: Things that unite us
steps.do: Your child draws a big circle labelled 'India' with spokes like the Ashoka Chakra, and writes one uniting thing on each spoke: the Constitution, the flag, the national anthem, the freedom struggle, cricket, the army, Indian Railways, festivals shared across faiths, shared foods, Hindi films and songs, and anything else they think of.

need: 15 ice-cream sticks or thin bamboo skewers
a picture of the Indian flag

days.title: Peace and harmony: at home, in the country, in the world
days.goal: Understand peace and harmony from the family up to the world, and learn what the Constitution says about equality and the person who fought for it.

steps.title: Peace begins at home (lesson pages 27–28)
steps.do: Read section 2.3 'Peace and Harmony' aloud. Pause at the book's questions and answer them honestly together: 'Do all the members of the family honour each other's views? Do they give each other enough importance?' Ask your child: 'When was the last time someone in our family did not feel listened to?' Accept their answer without arguing. Then read how peaceful families and countries prosper, while countries at war spend their strength and money on fighting. Ask: 'Where would a country rather spend money: on schools and hospitals, or on soldiers and weapons? Why does it sometimes have to spend on soldiers?'

steps.title: Family harmony agreement
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Hold a short family meeting. Each person, including the youngest, says one thing that helps them feel respected at home and one thing that upsets them. Your child writes the agreements on a chart, such as 'We let each person finish speaking' or 'We sort out fights by talking, not shouting'. Everyone signs it, and it goes up on the fridge.

steps.title: Peace with neighbours and equality (lesson page 28)
steps.do: Read the rest of 2.3: India's policy of peace with all countries, solving disputes by talking; harmony means 'to become soaked in one flavour', where nobody is high or low, rich or poor; and 'All people are equal in our Constitution.' Explain: Article 14 of the Constitution promises everyone equality before the law; Article 15 says the state cannot discriminate because of religion, caste, sex or place of birth; Article 17 ended 'untouchability'. Ask: 'If everyone is equal by law, why does the book still need to remind us?' (Laws are a start; people's behaviour must change too.)

steps.title: Dr B.R. Ambedkar
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v3, Dr B.R. Ambedkar. Then ask the 'ask' question. Parent note: if your child asks about caste, say simply and honestly: 'Long ago, society was divided into groups by birth, and some groups were treated as lower and kept away from water, schools and temples. That was wrong and unfair, and the Constitution has made such treatment illegal. Some people still behave unfairly, and we must not.'

steps.title: Book check 2.3 and core worksheet
steps.do: Do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 2.3' aloud: respect; attack; relations; soaked; equal. Then your child does core worksheet ws1 in writing. Check it together and look back at the page for any wrong answer.

need: chart paper and sketch pens for the family agreement

prep.task: Ask everyone at home to be free for a 10-minute family meeting

days.title: Ashoka and Akbar: rulers who spread peace
days.goal: Learn how Ashoka and Akbar tried to bring peace and respect between faiths, and how historians know about them from evidence.

steps.title: Ashoka after Kalinga (lesson pages 28–29)
steps.do: Read section 2.4 about Ashoka. Correct the date: the book says 'nearly 3400 years ago', but the Kalinga war was fought around 261 BCE, about 2,280 years ago. Kalinga is the old name for coastal Odisha. Ashoka himself, in his Rock Edict 13, says about 1,50,000 people were taken captive, 1,00,000 were killed and many more died, and that he felt deep regret. Read his problems (quarrels between religions, animal sacrifice, cruel treatment of servants) and his solution: Dhamma-Mahamattas, officers who travelled to teach right conduct, and messages carved on rocks and pillars and read aloud to people who could not read. Ask: 'Why carve messages on rocks instead of writing on paper?' (Rock lasts thousands of years and stands where people pass by.)

steps.title: How do we know? Reading the rocks
steps.do: Read Voice v1, about James Prinsep and the decoding of Ashoka's Brahmi script. Show your child a picture of a Brahmi inscription and the Ashoka lion capital at Sarnath (on every Indian banknote and coin). Point out that many Indian scripts, including Devanagari, Tamil and Bengali, grew from Brahmi. Ask the 'ask' question.

steps.title: Ashoka's message and Akbar (lesson page 29)
steps.do: Read Ashoka's message: good behaviour to servants, respect for elders, compassion for all creatures, gifts to Brahmins and monks, and the famous line that praising only your own religion and criticising others harms your own religion. Then read about Akbar: he gave high posts to Hindu nobles and scholars such as Raja Todar Mal and Raja Man Singh, married a Rajput princess of Amber who kept her own faith, celebrated festivals of both faiths, and began 'Sulh-i-kul' (peace with all). Add two facts: in 1564 he abolished the jizya, a tax that non-Muslims had to pay, and he held debates between Hindu, Jain, Muslim, Zoroastrian and Christian scholars in his Ibadat Khana (house of worship) at Fatehpur Sikri. Note honestly that the name 'Jodhabai' for his wife became popular later; records of his time call her by other titles, such as Mariam-uz-Zamani.

steps.title: What was Din-i-Ilahi?
steps.do: Read Voice v2 about the historians' debate over Akbar's Din-i-Ilahi. Ask the 'ask' question. Point out that two people of the same time, Abul Fazl and Badauni, wrote very different accounts, so historians must compare sources, just as a scientist compares measurements.

steps.title: Carve your own edict
steps.do: Do Activity a3. Your child writes their own three-line 'edict' of good conduct for your home or building, starting like Ashoka's, 'Thus speaks…', and 'carves' it into a slab of clay or atta dough with a toothpick, or writes it on a flat stone with a marker. Then do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 2.4' aloud: Dhamma; rocks; respect; roti and beti; Sulh-i-kul.

need: a picture of an Ashokan inscription and the Sarnath lion capital (online or on a coin or note)
clay or a ball of atta dough, or a flat stone and marker

days.title: Revise, check and teach it back
days.goal: Review the lesson with the book's exercise and the stretch and challenge worksheets, check understanding and teach the lesson back.

steps.title: Let's Revise and Exercise (lesson pages 30–31)
steps.do: Read 'Let's Revise' together, letting your child finish each point. Then do the Exercise aloud. Fill-ins: second (but say India is now first); ancient; society or culture; gods and goddesses; 22; Indians. Questions: major religions are Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi (Zoroastrian) and Jewish; Islam, Christianity, Zoroastrianism and Judaism began outside India and arrived many centuries ago, and Indians have followed them for hundreds of years; two of Ashoka's teachings: respect elders, be kind to all living creatures, respect other religions. True/false: false (food and living habits differ); true (the Buddha and Mahavira taught that birth does not make a person high or low); true.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child does stretch worksheet ws2 alone. Check together, asking for the reason behind each answer.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do challenge worksheet ws3 together, talking through the 'different views' questions. Praise answers that see more than one side. Finish the survey poster from Activity a1: a chart showing all the languages, states, festivals and 'thank you' words collected.

steps.title: Lesson check
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud, one at a time, without the book. Tick good answers. For any miss, open the page and read the part together, then ask again in other words. Six or more right is good; fewer than five, repeat Day 3 and Day 6 next week.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the teacher. Using the survey poster, the festival calendar, the bundle of sticks and their edict, they teach you for five minutes: what unity in diversity means; why India's culture is mixed; what unites us; and what Ashoka and Akbar did. Ask two 'student' questions: 'If everyone is different, how can we be one country?' and 'How do we know what Ashoka said 2,000 years ago?'

need: the survey sheet, festival calendar, sticks and edict

sections.p: Match each religion to its two sects named in the book.
The Constitution of India recognises ____ languages in its Eighth Schedule.
Name three tribes of India.
Which of these is a reason the book gives for India's diverse culture?
opts: Everyone in India eats the same food
People from outside came, settled and mingled with local people
India has only one kind of climate

sections.p: Match the January harvest festival to the state.
Bhangra and Bihu are both danced to celebrate a good ____.
It is the duty of every citizen to work towards the ____ and integrity of the nation.
In the Constitution of India, all people are:
Ashoka's officers who spread his message were called Dhamma-____.
Akbar's policy of 'peace with all' was called Sulh-i-____.
Write five identities of yourself (for example name, language, state, religion or none, school, Indian). Which of these do you share with your best friend?
Ravi is Tamil, Christian and a cricket fan. Which is true?
opts: He cannot be Indian because he is Christian
He has many identities and all of them can be true together
He must choose only one identity
Being Tamil means he cannot like cricket

sections.p: Sort these words by the language they came into Hindi from.
Climate shapes culture. Give one example of how the clothes or food of a cold place in India differ from a hot, wet place, and why.
Two neighbours fight over where to park their scooters. Using the book's idea for countries ('sort it through dialogue'), write what each could say to solve it peacefully.
The bundle of ten sticks did not break. Explain why using the word 'share'.
Why did Ashoka have his messages read aloud by officers?
opts: Because most people could not read
Because the rocks were too high

sections.p: Ashoka's own edict says he regretted the Kalinga war. Why might a historian want other evidence too, not only what a king says about himself?
Abul Fazl praised Akbar's Din-i-Ilahi; Badauni criticised it. Both lived at Akbar's court. How would you decide what really happened?
The book says India had 'more than 850 languages and dialects', and elsewhere '544 languages'. What is the best explanation for the two numbers?
opts: Counts differ because experts disagree on what is a separate language and what is a dialect
Languages disappear every year by hundreds
Only one of them counts Hindi

sections.p: Allport said contact between groups reduces prejudice best when they are equals working on a shared goal. Design one activity for your building that would bring families of different backgrounds together in this way.
Some people say a strong country needs everyone to be the same. The book says India is strong because of unity in diversity. Which do you agree with? Give two reasons.
Write one thing you will do this month to keep harmony with someone who is different from you.

experiments.title: Word detectives: where do our words come from?
experiments.question: Are the everyday words we use all from Indian languages, or did some come from people who travelled to India from other lands?
need: 12 slips with these words: paani, chabi, balti, almari, pav, kitab, kursi, bazaar, darwaza, sabzi, ghar, aankh
a sheet with three columns: 'My guess', 'Real origin', 'Surprised? yes/no'
steps: Read each word aloud and say what it means.
Your child sorts the slips into two piles: 'Always Indian' and 'Came from outside', and writes each guess in the first column.

Reveal the answers one by one: chabi (key), balti (bucket), almari (cupboard) and pav (bread roll) came from Portuguese; kitab (book) and kursi (chair) from Arabic; bazaar (market), darwaza (door) and sabzi (vegetables) from Persian; paani, ghar (house) and aankh (eye) grew from old Indian languages related to Sanskrit.
Count how many guesses were right.
Ask your child to find two more 'traveller words' at home, and check them in a dictionary or with an elder.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: how many of the 12 words came from outside India? Write the number down.
experiments.observe: Record the number of correct guesses and which words surprised them most. Most children are surprised by chabi, balti and pav, because these feel completely Indian.
experiments.why: When people meet and trade, live side by side or rule over each other, they borrow words for new things and ideas. Persian was the language of courts and government in India for about 600 years under the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals, so many words for government, buildings and daily life came from it (darwaza, bazaar). Persian itself had borrowed many words from Arabic (kitab, kursi). The Portuguese arrived by sea in 1498 and traded and ruled in Goa and other coastal places, bringing things like bread made with yeast (pão, which became pav) and words like chave (key) and balde (bucket). Linguists trace a word's origin by comparing old texts and the sounds and meanings of words in related languages. The result shows the book's point: culture mixes, and the mixed language becomes richer, not poorer.

experiments.title: Is a bundle really stronger than one stick?
experiments.question: How much harder is it to snap a bundle of sticks than a single stick, and why?
need: 15 wooden ice-cream sticks or thin bamboo skewers, all the same
steps: Hold one stick at both ends and bend it until it snaps. Note how easy it was on a scale of 1 (very easy) to 5 (impossible).
Try two sticks held together. Score it.
Tie five sticks tightly into a bundle. Try to bend and snap it. Score it.
Tie ten sticks into a bundle. Try again. Score it.
Make a simple table: number of sticks, score, did it break?
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: if one stick needs a little push to break, will ten sticks need ten times the push, or more, or less?
experiments.observe: One stick snaps easily. Two need more effort. A tight bundle of ten is very hard or impossible for a child (and often an adult) to break by hand.
experiments.why: When you bend a stick, its outer side stretches and its inner side is squashed; it snaps when the wood on the stretched side can no longer hold together. In a tight bundle, the force from your hands is shared among all the sticks, so each one carries only a small part of the load. A bundle is also thicker, and a thicker beam resists bending much more strongly than its thickness alone suggests: doubling the thickness of a beam makes it several times stiffer. That is why bridges and buildings use thick beams and bundled steel cables. The old story uses this real fact as a picture of unity: people who stand together share the strain and are hard to break. Like all comparisons, it is not perfect: real people, unlike sticks, can also disagree and still stand together.
experiments.safety: Snapped sticks can have sharp splinters; hold them away from faces and do not use skewers with sharp points towards anyone.

activities.title: Neighbourhood diversity survey
need: chart paper for the final poster
steps: Draw a table with columns: Family, Home language, State family is from, One festival, One special dish, 'Thank you' in their language.
Fill in your own family's row first.
Ask three or four other families, politely, and thank them.
Add rows over Days 1–3.
On Day 7, make a poster showing the languages, states, festivals and thank-you words, with a heading 'Unity in diversity on our street'.
activities.outcome: A real survey of diversity in your own neighbourhood and a poster that shows how many cultures live side by side.

activities.title: Family harmony agreement
steps: Each person says one thing that makes them feel respected at home.
Each person says one thing that upsets them.
Together, agree on four or five rules, such as 'We let each person finish speaking.'
Your child writes them neatly on the chart.
Everyone signs, and the chart goes on the fridge. Look at it again after one week: which rule was hardest to keep?
activities.outcome: A signed family agreement that shows peace and harmony starting at home, as the book says.

activities.title: Carve your own edict
need: clay or a ball of stiff atta dough rolled flat (or a smooth flat stone and a permanent marker)
steps: Write three rules of good conduct for your home or building, in Ashoka's style: 'Thus speaks Meera, friend of all…'
Include one rule about kindness to animals, one about respect for elders or helpers, and one about respecting other faiths or views.
Flatten the clay or dough into a slab and scratch the words in with the toothpick.
Let clay dry; take a photo of the dough version.
Read the edict aloud to the family, as Ashoka's officers did.
activities.outcome: A home-made 'rock edict' and a feel for why Ashoka chose stone to make his message last.

voices.who: James Prinsep (1799–1840), who decoded Ashoka's script, and Emperor Ashoka (ruled about 268–232 BCE)
voices.idea: For centuries nobody in India could read the old letters on Ashoka's pillars. Prinsep, an Englishman working at the Calcutta mint, compared hundreds of short inscriptions, including gifts recorded at Sanchi, and in 1837–38 worked out the Brahmi script. The edicts spoke of a king called 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' (beloved of the gods, of gracious looks). In 1915 an edict found at Maski in Karnataka used the name 'Asoka' together with this title, confirming that Piyadasi was Ashoka.
voices.then: Scholars were thrilled: suddenly a great Indian emperor could speak in his own words. Prinsep built on the work of others, including Indian pandits and earlier scholars, and the work was checked by many people afterwards.
voices.now: The decipherment of Brahmi is fully accepted, and more than 30 Ashokan inscriptions are now known across India, Nepal, Pakistan and Afghanistan, some in Greek and Aramaic too. Historians accept that Ashoka promoted Dhamma, but they also note that his own Rock Edict 13 warns forest peoples that he still has the power to punish, so he did not give up force completely.
voices.ask: Prinsep cracked the code by comparing many short inscriptions. Why does having lots of examples help you decode a script? What single discovery proved that Piyadasi was Ashoka?

voices.who: The Din-i-Ilahi debate: Abul Fazl (1551–1602) and Abd al-Qadir Badauni (about 1540–1615), courtiers of Akbar, and later historians
voices.idea: Around 1582 Akbar started a circle of followers sometimes called Din-i-Ilahi ('faith of God') or Tauhid-i-Ilahi. Abul Fazl, his friend and official historian, described Akbar as a wise ruler bringing together the best of all faiths under 'Sulh-i-kul', peace with all.
voices.then: Badauni, another scholar at the court, wrote in secret that Akbar was abandoning Islam and inventing a new religion. Later writers often repeated one side or the other.
voices.now: Many modern historians argue that Din-i-Ilahi was not a full religion at all but a small circle of loyal nobles (only around 18–20 are known by name) who pledged devotion to the emperor, while Sulh-i-kul was a wider policy of fairness in government. Others still describe it as an attempt at a new faith. Historians agree that Sulh-i-kul was real and important; what Din-i-Ilahi was is still debated.
voices.ask: Two people who knew Akbar wrote opposite things about him. What questions would you ask about each writer to decide whom to trust more?

voices.who: Dr Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar (1891–1956), Mhow (now in Madhya Pradesh), India
voices.idea: Born into the Mahar community, which was treated as 'untouchable', Ambedkar was made to sit apart at school and was refused water from the common tap. He went on to earn doctorates from Columbia University in New York and the London School of Economics. He argued that every person has equal dignity and that caste discrimination must end by law and in society. As Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution, he helped write the promises of equality (Article 14), no discrimination (Article 15) and the ending of untouchability (Article 17).
voices.then: Many people of his time opposed him, and his public campaigns were attacked. In 1927 he led the Mahad Satyagraha, where people of 'untouchable' castes drank water from a public tank they had been kept away from. He and Mahatma Gandhi disagreed strongly on how to end untouchability, especially in 1932 over separate electorates.
voices.now: His idea that the Constitution must guarantee equal rights to all is the law of India today. He was given the Bharat Ratna in 1990. Discrimination by caste is illegal, but surveys and news show it still happens, so the work he began is not finished.
voices.ask: Ambedkar was refused water as a boy. Why did he think a law was needed, and not just asking people to be kind? Can a law change how people think?
