voices.who: Gordon Allport (1897–1967), psychologist, USA, 'The Nature of Prejudice' (1954); tested by Thomas Pettigrew and Linda Tropp (2006)
voices.idea: Allport proposed the 'contact hypothesis': when people of different groups spend time together as equals, working towards a shared goal, with support from those in charge, their unfair dislike or fear of each other (prejudice) usually goes down.
voices.then: Many people thought prejudice was fixed and could not be changed, and some worried that bringing groups together would only cause more fights. Allport warned that contact helps only under the right conditions.
voices.now: In 2006 Pettigrew and Tropp combined the results of 515 studies from many countries and found that contact between groups generally reduces prejudice, and works best under Allport's conditions. Scientists also find that bad, forced or unequal contact can sometimes make things worse.
voices.ask: Soldiers from many states train and celebrate festivals together. By Allport's idea, why would that build friendship? What kind of meeting might NOT reduce prejudice?

check.q: What does 'unity in diversity' mean? Give one example.
check.a: People with many different languages, religions, foods and customs living together as one nation. For example, Lohri, Pongal and Bihu are different names for harvest festivals, but all celebrate the same season.

check.q: Name four religions followed in India and the two sects of Islam.
check.a: Any four of Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism (Parsi) and Judaism, and tribal faiths. Islam: Shia and Sunni.

check.q: How many languages does the Constitution recognise, and name four.
check.a: 22, for example Hindi, Tamil, Bangla, Marathi, Telugu, Urdu, Santali, Konkani.

check.q: Give two reasons why India's culture is mixed.
check.a: India's large size and different climates and land; and peoples from outside (Greeks, Kushanas, Shakas, Huns, Arabs, Turks, Mughals, Europeans) came, settled and mingled with local people.

check.q: Name three things that unite all Indians.
check.a: Any three: the Constitution, the national flag, the national anthem, the shared freedom struggle, sport such as cricket and hockey, the armed forces, shared festivals.

check.q: What is harmony, and what does the Constitution say about equality?
check.a: Harmony is living together peacefully with no one treated as high or low, rich or poor. The Constitution says everyone is equal before the law and no one may be discriminated against because of religion, caste, sex or place of birth.

check.q: Why did Ashoka change after the Kalinga war, and what did he do to spread peace?
check.a: He was horrified by the killing and suffering and was inspired by the Buddha's teachings. He appointed Dhamma-Mahamattas, had messages carved on rocks and pillars and read aloud, and taught respect for all religions and kindness to all creatures.

check.q: What did Akbar do to build harmony between Hindus and Muslims?
check.a: He gave high posts to Hindu nobles and scholars, married a Rajput princess who kept her own faith, celebrated festivals of both, abolished the jizya tax, held debates between faiths and followed Sulh-i-kul, peace with all.

c.covers: Small families; education and girls' literacy; equality of men and women; dowry and the law; female foeticide

p.title: Our Social Issues
p.source: NIOS Open Basic Education, Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 3 (lesson pages 33–54)
p.summary: Every society has strengths and problems, and this lesson looks honestly at some of India's: the strain of very large families on food, health and schooling; why education matters for everyone, especially girls; why women have not had equal respect and chances, and how laws, schooling and politics are changing that; and the unfair practice of dowry and the laws against it. Your child works with real numbers (literacy rates, sex ratios, sharing a family budget) and real people who fought for fairness, and learns that girls and boys have exactly equal rights.
goals: By the end your child can explain, with a simple sharing test, how the number of people in a family affects each person's share of food, money and attention, and why the book calls a small family a happy household.
By the end your child can give at least five reasons why education matters, and explain that education is more than reading and writing.
By the end your child can read a simple graph of male and female literacy in India from 1961 to 2011 and say what changed and why.

By the end your child can name reasons why women have been treated unequally (social customs, money, men making decisions, illiteracy, poverty, old ways of thinking) and spot unfairness in everyday life, such as who does the housework.

By the end your child can name laws and steps that protect girls' and women's rights, including the Right to Education Act, one-third seats for women in panchayats, and the ban on finding out a baby's sex before birth.
By the end your child can explain what dowry is, why it is unfair and illegal, how it differs from stri-dhan (gifts that belong only to the woman), and what young people can do to end it.
words: a problem that affects many people in a society and needs everyone's effort to solve
the number of people living in a place
poor health caused by not getting enough of the right kinds of food
the percentage of people (aged 7 and above in India's census) who can read and write with understanding
treating someone unfairly because of who they are, such as being a girl
everyone having the same rights, respect and chances
keeping a share of seats or posts for a group that was kept out unfairly, such as one-third of panchayat seats for women
the number of girls or women for every 1,000 boys or men
money or goods demanded from a bride's family by the groom's family as a condition of marriage; illegal in India since 1961
gifts given freely to a woman before, at or after her marriage, which belong to her alone
hurting or bullying a family member at home; a crime under Indian law
having the knowledge, money, confidence and rights to make your own choices

days.title: Social issues, and the sharing problem
days.goal: Learn what a social issue is, test how family size changes each person's share, and read about big and small families.

steps.title: A note for you before you begin
steps.do: Parent note: this lesson covers big families, unfair treatment of girls, dowry and harm to women. Your child is about 10. Keep the substance honest but frame everything around fairness, equal rights for girls and boys, and the law. Avoid graphic details. If your child asks a hard question you don't know how to answer, it is fine to say, 'That's an important question. Let me think and we will talk about it tonight.' Never let the lesson suggest that any child in a big family, or any poor family, is to blame. Start by telling your child: 'This week we are going to be fairness detectives.'

steps.title: Start the chores audit
steps.do: Start Activity a1. Draw a chart with a row for each household job (cooking, washing dishes, sweeping, washing clothes, buying vegetables, paying bills, helping with homework, fixing things, driving, looking after elders) and a column for each family member. For the next three days, your child puts a tick each time they see someone do a job. Do not discuss it yet; on Day 4 you will look at the results together.

steps.title: What are social issues? (lesson page 33)
steps.do: Read the opening of the lesson aloud: every society has good qualities and shortcomings. The book names some: girls getting less education, women not cared for properly, women considered less than men, dowry, and the killing of girls before birth, plus a growing population. Ask: 'Why does the book say these problems stop the whole society from moving forward, not just the people they hurt?' (Because if half the people, the girls and women, can't study, work or decide, the country loses half its talent.)

steps.title: The sharing test
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Your child shares the same 'family income' (24 biscuits or 24 coins) between a family of 3 and a family of 8, and works out each person's share, then does the same for 'attention' (60 minutes of a parent's evening). Ask for a prediction first. Discuss what the numbers mean for food, school fees and a parent's time.

steps.title: Big family and small family (lesson pages 34–35)
steps.do: Read 3.1 'Small family – Happy Household', 3.1.1 'Problems of a big family' and 3.1.2 'Benefit of a small family'. After each bullet, ask: 'Did our sharing test show this?' Link: limited income not enough for all; children not getting a balanced diet; mothers' health suffering when babies come one after another; farms split into tiny plots between many sons; country-wide shortages of water, housing and jobs. Then look at 'We have to think' on page 35: compare the two family pictures. Gentle balance: say 'Many big families are loving and happy too. The book's point is that when money and food are limited, fewer people means each child gets more.'

steps.title: Was Malthus right?
steps.do: Read Voice v1 about Thomas Malthus and what actually happened in India. Tell your child that India's average number of children per woman has fallen from about six in 1950 to about two today. Ask the 'ask' question. Then do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 3.1' aloud: happy; love and affection; nurturing (care); balanced; poverty.

steps.title: One-line summary
steps.do: Ask your child: 'In one sentence, why does the book think a small family is a happy household?' A good answer: 'When the same income is shared by fewer people, each child gets enough food, care and schooling.'

need: chart paper for the chores audit

prep.task: Draw the chores-audit chart with jobs down the side and family members across the top

days.title: Education is a must for all
days.goal: Understand what education really means, why it matters, and what families can do to make sure every child learns.

steps.title: Baiju and Sudhakar (lesson pages 36–37)
steps.do: Read section 3.2 aloud: Baiju's family, where nobody went to school, and Sudhakar's, where everyone did. Then read: 'Education is not only reading and writing. Education means gaining knowledge, learning and knowing,' and that a child's first teachers are the parents. Add a gentle balance: 'Baiju's family is poor because they never got a chance to study, not because they are bad people. Many families who never went to school are clean, wise and hard-working.' Ask: 'What could Baiju's children do to change things?' (Go to school; free schooling is a right up to class 8; adults can join literacy classes and then study through NIOS, as the book says.)

steps.title: Ways we learn
steps.do: Ask your child to list ten things they know, and how they learned each one: by seeing, hearing, reading or practising (the book's four ways). For example: tying shoelaces (practising), a bhajan or a song (hearing), how to make chai (seeing and practising), the names of planets (reading). Then ask: 'Which of these could you not have learnt without being able to read?' This shows why the book calls books a 'store-house of knowledge'.

steps.title: Why education is important (lesson page 37)
steps.do: Read 3.2.1 'Why is education important?' aloud. Your child picks the three points they think matter most and explains each with an example: for instance, 'Education makes us aware of our rights and duties: a person who can read can check their bank passbook, a ration card or a medicine label.' 'It helps remove superstition: if you know germs cause illness, you wash your hands instead of blaming bad luck.' Then read the paragraph about boys going to school while girls do housework all day. Ask the book's question: 'Why is she not given the right to study?' Listen to your child's answer.

steps.title: What can we do? (lesson page 39)
steps.do: Read 3.2.4 'What can we do?' Make a list together of the ones a child can help with: telling a friend's parents gently that school is free and important; sharing books; teaching a younger child or a household helper's child to read letters. Tell your child about India's Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, which made free schooling a right for every child aged 6 to 14. Ask: 'If a child aged 9 is working in a tea stall instead of going to school, is that allowed?' (No. Children under 14 must not be employed in such work, and every child has a right to free school.)

steps.title: Book check 3.2 (lesson pages 39–40)
steps.do: Do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 3.2' aloud, choosing from the given words: mother-father (first teachers); store-house; way (education opens the way, the door, to employment); life; helpful.

steps.title: Education poster line
steps.do: Your child makes up a short slogan for a poster about education for all, for example 'Padhega India, tabhi badhega India' ('When India learns, India grows') or one of their own, and draws a small picture to go with it. Stick it near their study table.

days.title: Girls' education: then and now
days.goal: Learn the history of girls' education in India, meet Savitribai Phule, and draw a graph of how female literacy has grown.

steps.title: Status of girl education (lesson page 38)
steps.do: Read 3.2.2 'Status of Girl Education'. The book says that in Vedic times girls studied mostly at home and were not sent to gurukuls, and that in the Buddhist period few women studied. Add a balanced fact: there were exceptions, such as Gargi and Maitreyi, women thinkers who appear in the Upanishads, and Buddhist nuns whose poems were collected in the Therigatha. But most girls did not get the same chances as boys. The book says at Independence only about 9% of Indian women could read (the 1951 census figure). Ask: 'Out of 100 women, how many could read?' (About 9.) 'What would that mean for a mother trying to read her child's medicine label?'

steps.title: Savitribai Phule
steps.do: Tell your child the story of Voice v2, Savitribai Phule, who started teaching girls in Pune in 1848. Act out the part where she carried a second sari to school, because people threw mud and dung at her on the way, and changed when she reached the school. Ask: 'Why did people get so angry at the idea of girls learning?' (They were afraid of change and thought girls belonged only at home.) Then ask the 'ask' question.

steps.title: Draw the literacy graph
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Using the census numbers given in the activity, your child draws a bar graph with two bars for each census year, one for men and one for women. Ask: 'In which year was the gap between men and women biggest? Is the gap getting smaller?' (The gap was about 27 points in 1961 and 1971 and narrowed to about 17 points by 2011; women's literacy more than quadrupled from 15% to 65%.)

steps.title: Why educate women? (lesson pages 38–39)
steps.do: Read 3.2.3 'Women's Education and its objective'. Discuss two points: 'Educate women and make them self-reliant and empowered' (they can earn, decide and stand up for themselves) and 'Make them aware of their rights' (a woman who can read the law knows dowry is illegal). Ask: 'The book says if a mother is educated, the whole family becomes educated. Why?' (She teaches the children, helps with homework, and understands health and money matters.)

steps.title: Then and now
steps.do: Ask your child to say one sentence about girls' education 'then' (1848 or 1951) and one about 'now' (2011), using numbers from the graph.

days.title: Men and women are equal
days.goal: Understand the reasons women have been treated unequally and find out what the chores audit shows about our own home.

steps.title: Men–women equality (lesson pages 40–41)
steps.do: Read section 3.3 aloud up to 'Women have not got an equal honor.' Point out the book's list of brave and learned women in Indian history: Rani Durgavati (who defended Gondwana against the Mughals), Mirabai (poet-saint), Rani Padmini (known mainly from legend and a poem by Malik Muhammad Jayasi, so historians are unsure of her story), Jijabai (mother and guide of Shivaji), Ahilyabai Holkar (ruler of Indore who built ghats and temples across India) and Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi. Ask: 'The book says some women reach the top while others, in many villages, cannot even speak in front of men. How can both be true in one country?'

steps.title: Why women are left behind (lesson pages 40–42)
steps.do: Read the seven reasons the book gives: social system (girls 'married off', a boy's birth celebrated more), economic freedom (women working all day but not earning or controlling money), a male-dominated society (men making decisions), illiteracy, poverty, population (the wish for a son leading to many children), and social thinking (women seen as weak). After each, ask your child for an example or a fix. Parent note: the book mentions very serious harms like violence; you can say simply, 'Sometimes women are hurt or bullied at home, and that is a crime.' Do not go into details.

steps.title: Chores audit results
steps.do: Bring out the Activity a1 chart. Count the ticks for each person. Ask: 'Who does the most jobs? Are some jobs done only by women or only by men? Is any job a girl's job or a boy's job by nature?' (No. Anyone can learn to cook, fix a tap, pay a bill or sweep.) Then make a fairer plan with your child: one new job each family member, including boys and men, will take on this week. Write it at the bottom of the chart. Be honest if the audit shows your own home is unequal; children learn most from seeing adults change.

steps.title: Book check 3.3 and core worksheet
steps.do: Do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 3.3' aloud: backbone; teacher; weak; stories; girl. Then your child does core worksheet ws1 in writing. Check it together.

days.title: Special attention to girls: progress and laws
days.goal: Learn how education, politics, work, social change and the law are improving the status of girls and women, and use numbers to see why girls must be protected before birth.

steps.title: Progress in education and politics (lesson pages 42–43)
steps.do: Read section 3.4, parts 1 and 2. Point back to the Day 3 graph for the literacy numbers. Name the help girls get: free books and uniforms, scholarships, mid-day meals, hostels. Then politics: the 73rd and 74th Amendments to the Constitution (1992) reserve at least one-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities for women, and many states, such as Bihar, now reserve half. Add: in 2023 Parliament passed a law (the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) to reserve one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women; it will come into force after the next census and redrawing of constituencies. Ask: 'Why does it matter that women sit in the panchayat?' (They raise problems men may ignore, like water, toilets and girls' schooling.)

steps.title: Work, social change and legal rights (lesson pages 43–44)
steps.do: Read parts 3, 4 and 5. Pick five rights to explain simply: a woman can choose whom to marry after 18; she can keep her own name after marriage; her stri-dhan belongs to her alone; she has a right to a share of family property (since 2005, daughters have the same right as sons in Hindu family property); she can go to court if she is treated cruelly. Correct the book's law names: the law against domestic violence is the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. Ask: 'Why do girls need a law to say they can keep their own name?' (Because custom often took away a woman's choices.)

steps.title: Count the missing girls
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. First toss a coin 100 times with your child and count heads and tails, after asking them to predict. Then compare with India's real numbers: naturally about 950 girls are born for every 1,000 boys, but the 2011 Census counted only 918 girls for every 1,000 boys aged 0–6. Parent note: explain simply and calmly: 'Some families wanted only sons. They used machines to find out before birth whether the baby was a girl, and then stopped the girl being born. This is completely wrong and against the law. Every girl has exactly the same right to be born and to live as every boy.' Read the book's paragraph on the 1994 law that makes finding out a baby's sex before birth illegal.

steps.title: Amartya Sen's 'missing women'
steps.do: Read Voice v3. Ask the 'ask' question. Point out how a scientist or economist uses numbers to uncover an unfairness that is hidden in everyday life.

steps.title: Book check 3.4 (lesson page 45)
steps.do: Answer 'Let's see, what you have learnt 3.4' aloud. 1: the Right to Education Act (2009), free and compulsory school for ages 6–14. 2: one-third of seats (half in many states). 3: schools, colleges, hospitals, offices, industries, shops, farms, the police and the army. 4: maintenance (money to live on) and custody of children. 5: the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

days.title: Dowry: an unfair custom and the law
days.goal: Understand what dowry is, why it spread, why it is unfair and illegal, how it differs from stri-dhan, and how a brave girl like Phulwa can stop it.

steps.title: Phulwa's story (lesson pages 45–46)
steps.do: Read the story of Phulwa's wedding aloud: the happy preparations, the groom's father suddenly demanding ₹50,000 in cash, Bodhlal and Kaushalya pleading, and the police arriving because Phulwa had sent her uncle to report the demand. Ask: 'How did Phulwa feel when the demand came? What did she do that took courage?' (She used the law instead of accepting injustice.) 'Was the groom's father being fair? Why not?' (Marriage is between two people and families; it is not a sale.)

steps.title: What is dowry and why it spread (lesson pages 46–47)
steps.do: Read 3.5.1 and 3.5.2. Explain the change the book describes: long ago parents gave their daughter household things willingly, by their own choice, to help her start a new home. Over time, the groom's side began to treat it as their right and to demand it. List the book's reasons it spread: love of money and showing off (TV, car, fridge as 'prestige'), a narrow choice of partners because of caste rules, false pride, and families wanting to 'recover' what they spent on a son's education. Ask: 'What is the difference between a gift and a demand?' (A gift is freely chosen; a demand is forced.)

steps.title: Harms, solutions and the law (lesson pages 48–50)
steps.do: Read 3.5.3 to 3.5.7, choosing age-appropriate parts. Harms: debt for the girl's family for life, girls married to unsuitable grooms, girls being harassed by in-laws. Parent note: the book mentions suicide and deaths; you can say simply, 'Some women were badly harmed because of dowry, and that is why the law punishes it very strictly.' Then the law: the Dowry Prohibition Act was passed by Parliament on 9 May 1961; both giving and taking dowry are crimes, with at least 5 years' jail and a fine of ₹15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is more; demanding dowry and advertising for it are also punished. Read 3.5.6: gifts given freely to the bride are her stri-dhan and belong only to her, and a signed list should be made. Mention that the old Indian Penal Code was replaced in 2024 by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which still punishes dowry death very severely.

steps.title: Phulwa's wedding: act it out
steps.do: Do Activity a3. Act out the scene with family members: the groom's father makes the demand; Phulwa, her parents, the groom and a neighbour each respond. Then act it a second time with a different ending: the groom himself refuses the dowry and tells his father it is wrong and illegal. Ask afterwards: 'Which ending was better? Who has the most power to stop dowry?' The book's answer: young people must take the initiative.

steps.title: Book check 3.5 (lesson page 51)
steps.do: Do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 3.5'. True/false: false (dowry is harmful); true; true; false (only the woman has a right to her stri-dhan); true; false (a dowry death is one within seven years of marriage). Fill-ins: prestige; money (wealth); expense (the money spent); life; youth. Then your child begins stretch worksheet ws2, Section A.

days.title: Revise, check and teach it back
days.goal: Review the lesson, finish the worksheets, check understanding, and teach back what you learned as a fairness detective.

steps.title: Let's Revise and Exercise (lesson pages 51–53)
steps.do: Read 'Let's Revise' together. Then do the Exercise aloud. Fill-ins: discord (tension) in a large family; self-reliant; problems; responsibility of two families (the book's key says 'commitment'); thinking. Short answers: two benefits of a small family (better education, better health and food); two benefits of education (jobs and earning, knowing about the country and world, knowing your rights); a solution to dowry (educate girls and make them self-reliant, young people refusing dowry, using the law). True/false: false, true, true, false, true. Tick the right answer: d, a, a, d.

steps.title: Finish the stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child finishes stretch worksheet ws2, Sections B and C. Check together, asking 'Why?' for each answer.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do challenge worksheet ws3 together. These questions have no single right answer; praise reasons that use evidence (numbers, the law, the book) and that consider other people's views.

steps.title: Lesson check
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud, one at a time, without the book. Tick good answers; for any miss, read the right page together and ask again. Six or more right is good.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the teacher. Using the sharing-test plates, the literacy graph, the coin-toss tally and the chores chart, they teach you: why small families can give each child more; why education matters, especially for girls; three laws that protect girls and women; and why dowry is wrong. Ask two 'student' questions: 'Isn't housework a woman's job?' and 'If the bride's parents want to give a gift, is that dowry?' (No, if it is freely given with no demand; then it is her stri-dhan.)

need: the sharing plates, literacy graph, coin tally and chores chart

sections.p: In the book, a small family is called a ____ household.
Sort these into what the book says about a big family with limited income and a small family.
items: Children may not get a balanced diet
Mother's health suffers when babies come quickly
Children get full love and attention
School fees are easier to pay
Farms get divided into tiny pieces
Basic needs are met more easily

sections.p: A child's first teachers are the ____.
Books are a ____ of knowledge and information.
The book says education is:
opts: gaining knowledge by seeing, hearing, reading and practising

sections.p: Write three reasons why education is important.
Match each reason women were left behind to its meaning.
pairs: Women work but don't control the money
Men make all the big decisions
Many women could not read or write

sections.p: Which job is a 'girl's job' by nature?
opts: None: anyone can learn any household job

sections.p: Match the law or step to what it does.
pairs: Free and compulsory school for ages 6–14
One-third of panchayat seats for women
Makes giving and taking dowry a crime
Law of 1994 on tests before birth
Bans finding out a baby's sex before birth
Protects women from harm at home

sections.p: Phulwa's grandmother gives her a gold chain, freely, at the wedding. Whose is it?
opts: Phulwa's alone: it is her stri-dhan

sections.p: Your literacy graph: fill in the gap between men and women in each year.
A family earns ₹12,000 a month for food. How much is that per person for a family of 3? For a family of 8? What does the difference mean for the children?
Your neighbour's 11-year-old daughter has stopped going to school to look after her baby brother. Using the book's 'What can we do?' list, write two kind, practical things your family could do.
A boy in your class says 'Girls can't be engineers.' Write what you could say back, using one fact from this lesson.

If boys and girls are born in nearly equal numbers, why might a district count only 900 girls for every 1,000 boys aged 0–6? Give two possible explanations, and say what extra information would help you find out which is true.

Malthus predicted that population growth would always lead to famine. India's population grew more than four times since 1951, yet famines like those of the past did not return. What best explains this?
opts: The population did not really grow
Farmers grew much more food per field (better seeds, irrigation, fertiliser), and families also chose to have fewer children

sections.p: Dowry has been illegal since 1961, but the book says the laws' 'impact is not visible'. Why might a law not be enough to end a custom? What else is needed?
Savitribai Phule was attacked for teaching girls in 1848. Today almost everyone agrees girls should study. What changed people's minds over time, do you think?
Write a short speech (5 sentences) for your building's Republic Day function titled 'Equal rights for girls and boys begin at home'.

experiments.title: The sharing test: does family size change each person's share?
experiments.question: If two families have the same income, how much does each person get in a family of 3 compared with a family of 8?
steps: Lay out 3 plates for Family A and 8 plates for Family B.
Give Family A 24 biscuits and share them equally. Count how many each person gets.
Collect them and give Family B the same 24 biscuits. Share equally and count.
Now share 'attention': a parent has 60 minutes free each evening. Divide 60 minutes among the children: Family A has 1 child, Family B has 6 children.
Write a table: Family, people, biscuits each, minutes of attention each child.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: will each person in the big family get a little less, half as much, or much less than in the small family?
experiments.observe: Family A: 8 biscuits each. Family B: 3 each. Attention: 60 minutes for the only child in Family A, 10 minutes each for the six children in Family B.
experiments.why: When a fixed amount is shared equally, each share equals the total divided by the number of people, so more people means smaller shares. Going from 3 to 8 people does not take away just a little: each share falls to less than half. This is why the book links very large families with limited income to poor nutrition, less schooling and less time with each child. In real life, income can grow when more grown-up family members earn, so big families are not always poorer; but children do not earn, so a family with many young children has many people to feed from the same income for many years. The same simple rule, total divided by people, also applies to a whole country's water, hospitals and schools.

experiments.title: Coin tosses and the missing girls
experiments.question: If whether a baby is a boy or a girl is left to nature, how close to equal are the numbers? And what do India's census numbers show?
need: a tally sheet with two columns: Heads, Tails
steps: Toss the coin 10 times and tally heads and tails. Is it exactly 5 and 5?
Toss it 90 more times (take turns) to reach 100 tosses. Tally again.
Work out how many heads there would be for every 1,000 tails if your result held (heads ÷ tails × 1,000).

Now look at the real numbers: in nature, roughly 950 girls are born for every 1,000 boys (boys are very slightly more common at birth). India's 2011 Census counted 918 girls for every 1,000 children aged 0–6; in 1961 it was 976.
Work out: if there should be about 950 girls per 1,000 boys and there were 918, how many girls are 'missing' per 1,000 boys? (About 32.)
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: in 100 coin tosses, will heads and tails be exactly equal, nearly equal, or very different?
experiments.observe: In 10 tosses the result can be uneven, like 7 and 3. In 100 tosses it usually comes close to 50–50, such as 47 and 53. The bigger the number of tosses, the closer to even it tends to get.
experiments.why: Chance events even out over large numbers: this is called the law of large numbers. Whether a baby is a boy or girl is a natural chance event, just slightly tilted (about 105 boys born for every 100 girls). So in a country of crores of babies, the numbers of boys and girls should come out very close to this natural ratio. When a large population shows far fewer girls than nature would give, the gap cannot be bad luck; it is a sign that something people did, such as stopping girls from being born or caring for girls less when they are ill, is causing it. This is why the 1994 law bans finding out a baby's sex before birth, and why campaigns like 'Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao' (Save the daughter, educate the daughter), begun in 2015, focus on districts with the fewest girls.

activities.title: Chores audit: who does what at home?
steps: Day 1: draw a chart with household jobs down the side and family members across the top.
Days 1–3: each time your child sees someone do a job, they make a tick in the right box.
Day 4: count the ticks for each person and each job.
Discuss: who does most? Are some jobs only done by one gender? Why?
Make a fairer plan: each person takes one new job for a week. Write it on the chart.
After a week, check: did the plan work?
activities.outcome: Real evidence from your own home about how work is shared, and a family plan to make it fairer, so equality becomes something your child sees, not just reads about.

activities.title: Graph of literacy in India, 1961–2011
need: two colour pencils (one for men, one for women)
steps: Draw the axes: census years along the bottom (1961, 1971, 1981, 1991, 2001, 2011), and percentage up the side from 0 to 100, with one square for every 5%.
Plot the census figures (rounded): 1961 men 40%, women 15%; 1971 men 46%, women 22%; 1981 men 56%, women 30%; 1991 men 64%, women 39%; 2001 men 75%, women 54%; 2011 men 82%, women 65%.
Draw two bars for each year, side by side, in the two colours.
Write the gap between men and women above each pair.
Write two sentences: one about how women's literacy has changed, one about the gap.
activities.outcome: A bar graph showing that women's literacy has risen more than four times since 1961 and the gap between men and women is closing but not yet gone.

activities.title: Phulwa's wedding role-play
need: simple props (a dupatta, a toy phone)
steps: Give roles: Phulwa, her father Bodhlal, the groom's father, the groom, a neighbour.
Act 1: follow the book's story, with the demand for ₹50,000, the pleading, and Phulwa sending her uncle to the police.
Act 2: replay it, but this time the groom stands up and tells his father, 'Dowry is wrong and against the law. I will not take it.'
After each act, each actor says in one sentence how their character felt.
Discuss: what made the second ending possible? (A young person's courage and knowing the law.)
activities.outcome: Your child understands from the inside why dowry is unfair and that young people, boys as well as girls, can refuse it.

voices.who: Thomas Robert Malthus (1766–1834), England, 'An Essay on the Principle of Population' (1798)
voices.idea: Malthus argued that population tends to grow faster than food supply, so unless people have fewer children, hunger, disease and famine will keep pulling the population back down. In the 1960s and 1970s, some writers predicted mass famines in India for the same reason.
voices.then: Many people in his time and later were persuaded, and his ideas shaped government policies. Others, such as the Danish economist Ester Boserup (1965), argued that a growing population can push farmers to find better ways of growing food.
voices.now: His grim prediction did not come true in the way he said. India's population grew from about 36 crore in 1951 to over 140 crore, yet the Green Revolution of the 1960s–70s (better seeds, irrigation and fertilisers, with scientists such as M.S. Swaminathan) greatly increased food production, and India has had no famine like the Bengal Famine of 1943. Families also chose fewer children: India's average fell from about 6 children per woman in the 1950s to about 2 by the National Family Health Survey of 2019–21, falling fastest where girls were educated. Experts agree that very fast population growth puts pressure on resources, but Malthus's claim that famine is unavoidable is rejected.
voices.ask: Malthus looked at the numbers of his time and made a prediction that turned out wrong. What did he not foresee? What should we be careful about when we predict the future from today's numbers?

voices.who: Savitribai Phule (1831–1897) and Jyotirao Phule (1827–1890), Pune, Maharashtra
voices.idea: Savitribai was married at about nine and was taught to read by her husband Jyotirao. In 1848 the Phules started a school for girls in Bhide Wada, Pune, one of the first schools for girls run by Indians, and Savitribai became its teacher. They went on to open many more schools, including for children of castes that were then treated as 'untouchable'. She believed every girl and every person, whatever their caste, had the right to learn.
voices.then: Many people in Pune were furious. On her way to school, people threw mud, stones and dung at her, so she carried a second sari to change into. Jyotirao's own family was pressured to throw the couple out of the house. She kept going.
voices.now: Her belief that girls have an equal right to education is now part of India's law and is accepted almost everywhere. She is honoured as one of India's first women teachers, and Savitribai Phule Pune University is named after her. Her birthday, 3 January, is marked in Maharashtra as a day honouring girls' education.
voices.ask: People who threw mud at Savitribai thought they were protecting society. What could have changed their minds: an argument, a law, or seeing educated girls succeed? Which do you think works best?

voices.who: Amartya Sen (born 1933), economist, Santiniketan, West Bengal; Nobel Prize in Economics 1998
voices.idea: In 1990 Sen wrote an essay titled 'More Than 100 Million Women Are Missing'. He compared the number of women and men in countries such as India and China with what you would expect if girls and women got the same food, health care and care as boys and men, and calculated that about 10 crore women were 'missing' worldwide, meaning they had died early or never been born because of unequal treatment.
voices.then: The idea shocked many readers. Some experts argued over his exact numbers and how to calculate the 'expected' ratio, and others looked for different explanations, such as diseases that affect men and women differently.
voices.now: Other researchers have refined his numbers, but the main finding is widely accepted: in parts of the world, including many parts of India, girls have been born and survived in smaller numbers than nature would give, because sons were preferred. India's sex ratio at birth has been improving in recent years, especially after laws and campaigns against sex selection.
voices.ask: Sen found an unfairness by comparing real numbers with expected numbers. What expected number did we compare with in our coin-toss test? What other unfairness at home or school could you measure with numbers?

check.q: What is a social issue? Name three from this lesson.
check.a: A problem that affects many people and holds society back. For example: very large families with limited income, lack of education especially for girls, unequal treatment of women, dowry, and girls not being allowed to be born.

check.q: Why can a small family give each child more?
check.a: The same income, food and parents' time are shared among fewer people, so each child gets a bigger share: better food, health, schooling and attention.

check.q: Give four reasons why education is important.
check.a: It increases knowledge; opens the way to jobs and earning; helps us make good decisions; makes us aware of our rights and duties; helps remove superstition; builds self-confidence; helps the country develop.

check.q: How has women's literacy in India changed, and who started a girls' school in Pune in 1848?
check.a: It rose from about 15% in 1961 to about 65% in 2011, and the gap with men is shrinking. Savitribai Phule and Jyotirao Phule started the school; Savitribai was the teacher.

check.q: Give three reasons the book gives for women being treated unequally.
check.a: Any three: social customs that value boys more; women not controlling money; men making all decisions; illiteracy; poverty; the wish for sons leading to big families; the wrong idea that women are weak.

check.q: Name three laws or steps that protect girls and women.
check.a: Any three: Right to Education Act (free school 6–14); one-third (or half) of panchayat seats for women; Dowry Prohibition Act 1961; the 1994 law banning tests to find a baby's sex before birth; the Domestic Violence Act 2005; equal share in family property.

check.q: Why does a census showing far fewer girls than boys tell us something is wrong?
check.a: Nature gives nearly equal numbers of boys and girls (about 950 girls per 1,000 boys at birth). With crores of babies, a big gap cannot be chance; it means girls were stopped from being born or cared for less.

check.q: What is the difference between dowry and stri-dhan, and what does the law say about dowry?
check.a: Dowry is money or goods demanded from the bride's family as a condition of marriage; stri-dhan is gifts freely given to the woman, which belong to her alone. Since 1961, giving, taking, demanding and advertising dowry are all crimes punished with jail and fines.

c.covers: How British rule was established; people from every state in the freedom struggle; Gandhiji and other leaders; safeguarding independence

items.title: The States of India and their Physical Features

c.covers: States and Union Territories on the map; India on the world map; physical features, resources, climate, crops and vegetation
Democracy; the right to vote; how government works; rural and urban administration
How plants and animals depend on each other; food chains and food webs; natural balance; protecting forests and animals
Types of soil and crops; preparing the field, sowing, manure and fertiliser; protecting crops; irrigation, weeding, harvesting; crops by season
Soil erosion, its harm and prevention; soil pollution; why forests must be protected

p.title: Conservation of Soil and Forests
p.source: NIOS Open Basic Education, Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 9 (lesson pages 136–146)
p.summary: The fertile top layer of soil is a farmer's wealth, and rain and wind can carry it away. Your child sees soil erosion happen in trays at home, learns how farmers stop it with field boundaries (dolbandi), embankments, terraces, check dams, drainage and, above all, trees and grass whose roots hold the soil. They then find out how polythene, glass, pesticides, too much chemical fertiliser and factory waste pollute soil, and how compost and other organic manures keep it healthy, including where scientists still argue.
goals: By the end your child can explain what soil erosion is and show, with a home model, how fast-flowing water and strong wind carry away loose topsoil.
By the end your child can list at least five harmful effects of soil erosion, from lower crop yield to blocked canals and floods.
By the end your child can describe six ways of preventing erosion (boundary or dolbandi, embankment, terrace farming, forests and grass, check dams, drainage) and say why each works.
By the end your child can explain why forests matter for soil, water and living things, and tell the story of the Chipko movement.
By the end your child can name the main causes of soil pollution and ways to prevent it, including segregating waste and using compost and other organic manure.
By the end your child can weigh the debate about organic and chemical farming, and say what evidence would help decide it.
words: the dark, crumbly top layer of soil, usually only a hand's depth or so, which holds most of the humus and food for plants; it is the most fertile layer
the wearing away and carrying off of soil from its place by fast-flowing water or strong wind; the book also calls it de-layering or degradation of soil
a narrow channel cut into the ground by rainwater rushing along the same path again and again; big gullies can grow into ravines
a deep, narrow valley with steep sides cut by water over many years, like the Chambal ravines
a raised earth boundary (bund) built around all four sides of a field so the topsoil and manure are not washed away
a raised bank of earth across a sloping field that slows down water, with an outlet so extra water can flow out
cutting a steep hillside into a series of flat steps, each higher than the one before, so water cannot rush down and carry the soil away
a small low wall built across a stream or drain to slow the water; the soil settles behind it and water seeps into the ground
salty; land where water stands for too long can become saline as water evaporates and leaves salt behind, and few crops grow in it
damage to the soil when poisonous or harmful things such as plastic, glass, pesticides or factory waste mix into it
a chemical used to kill insects and other pests that eat crops; used carelessly, it also harms soil life, water, animals and people
plant food made from once-living things, such as compost, cow-dung manure, vermicompost (made by earthworms), khali (oilseed cake such as neem cake) and green manure

days.title: Why is soil a farmer's wealth?
days.goal: Start from the mud and dust in our own lives, find out what topsoil is and why it is precious, and set up a long test of what rots in soil and what does not.

steps.title: Where does the mud go?
steps.do: Ask your child: 'After heavy rain, what colour is the water running down the road or in the drain? Why is it brown?' Good answer: 'Because it is carrying soil.' Then ask: 'In summer, when the loo (hot wind) blows or a dust storm comes, what settles on the windowsill?' (Fine dust, which is soil carried by wind.) Ask: 'Where did that soil come from, and where is it going?' Let them guess freely. Tell them: 'Today we start finding out why losing this soil is a big problem for farmers, and for all of us who eat.'

steps.title: Opening of Lesson 9 (lesson pages 136–137)
steps.do: Read aloud the opening paragraph of Lesson 9: 'Soil is called a farmer's wealth...' and the start of section 9.1 about the top layer of soil. Stop and ask: 'Why does the book call soil a farmer's wealth?' (Crops grow in it; without good soil there is no harvest and no income.) 'Which layer is most valuable?' (The top layer.) 'What happens to crops if it is destroyed?' (The yield falls sharply.) Read the definition: soil wearing away from its place is called soil erosion, degradation of soil or de-layering, and its two causes are rainwater and wind. Ask your child to say the two causes back to you.

steps.title: Dig and look: topsoil and the soil below
steps.do: Take a spoon or small trowel to a flower bed, a park corner or a large plant pot. Dig a small hole about a hand deep and look at the side of the hole together. Ask: 'Is the top the same colour as the bottom?' Usually the top is darker and crumbly, with bits of leaves and roots, and lower down it is lighter and harder. Tell them: 'The dark top part is topsoil. The dark colour comes from humus, rotted leaves and roots that feed plants. Nature takes hundreds of years to make just a few centimetres of it.' Put one spoonful of topsoil and one of the lower soil on a white paper and let your child compare with a magnifying glass if you have one: colour, smell, roots, tiny creatures. Fill the hole back in.

steps.title: Set up the buried-objects test
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. In a pot or a bucket of damp garden soil, bury side by side (5 cm deep, a hand apart): a piece of banana peel, a scrap of newspaper, a piece of polythene bag, a cotton thread and a small piece of broken glass bangle wrapped safely in paper by you (you handle the glass, not your child). Push an ice-cream stick next to each one with its name. Ask your child to predict which will rot away and which will stay the same in two weeks, and write the guesses in the notebook. Ask: 'Why do we bury them all in the same soil at the same depth?' (So that only the material is different, which makes it a fair test.) Keep the soil damp.

steps.title: Soil in our plate
steps.do: Ask: 'Name everything on today's lunch plate. Which of these grew in soil?' Go through it: rice or wheat roti (grass grown in soil), dal (seed of a soil-grown plant), sabzi, even milk and paneer (the cow ate grass grown in soil). Ask: 'So if the topsoil of India's farms washed away, what would happen to our plates?' Write your child's answer in the notebook under the heading 'Why soil matters'.

need: NIOS Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 9 (lesson pages 136–137)
a pot or bucket of damp garden soil
banana peel, newspaper scrap, polythene piece, cotton thread, a small piece of broken glass bangle

prep.task: Find a pot or bucket and fill it with garden soil; collect the five test items

days.title: Rain and wind carry soil away
days.goal: See erosion by water and by wind happen in our own trays, and understand gullies, ravines and why bare soil suffers most.

steps.title: Erosion by rainfall and wind (lesson page 137)
steps.do: Read aloud 'Erosion due to rainfall' and 'Wind Erosion' on lesson page 137, and look at the two pictures. Ask: 'What is gully erosion?' Good answer: 'When water rushes again and again down narrow channels, it cuts small gullies; over a long time they become big streams and ravines.' Ask: 'Where is wind erosion more common?' (In dry, arid areas, like the Thar desert in Rajasthan.) Tell them about the Chambal ravines in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh: a huge area of deep gullies cut by water over many years, where farmland has been lost.

steps.title: Rain on three trays
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Fill three trays or cut-open milk or juice cartons with soil, all the same amount. Leave tray 1 bare. Cover tray 2 with a layer of dry leaves. In tray 3, use a patch of grass with its roots dug from the garden, or sprouted methi or moong you grew a week earlier. Prop each tray at the same slope on a book, with a cup at the low end. Ask your child to predict which cup will have the muddiest water. Then pour one full mug of water slowly through a watering can or a bottle with holes in the cap over each tray, from the same height. Line up the three cups and compare. Ask: 'Which tray lost the most soil? Why?'

steps.title: Wind on dry and damp soil
steps.do: Do Experiment e2 on newspaper outdoors or on the balcony. Make three small heaps of fine soil or sand on plates: one dry, one sprayed until damp, one dry but covered with a few small stones and dry grass. Stand a sheet of paper behind them as a 'wall'. Ask your child to predict which heap will blow away most. Fan each heap with a hand fan, or a hairdryer on cool (you hold it), for 10 seconds from the same distance. Ask: 'Which heap lost most soil? Why are deserts and dry, bare fields worst hit by wind?' (Dry, loose particles with nothing on top are easy for wind to lift.) Wear old clothes and keep eyes away from the blowing dust.

steps.title: Bare soil is weak soil
steps.do: Ask your child to write two sentences in the notebook beginning 'Water carries soil away when...' and 'Wind carries soil away when...'. Good answers: '...it flows fast down a slope over bare soil' and '...the soil is dry, loose and has no plants or cover.' Ask: 'What did the leaves and grass do in both tests?' (They covered and held the soil.)

steps.title: Check the buried pot
steps.do: Check the pot from Experiment e3: just feel that the soil is still damp and add a little water if it is dry. Do not dig yet. Ask: 'Which item do you think is changing the fastest under there?' Note the guess with today's date.

need: 3 trays or cut milk or juice cartons
a small patch of grass with roots, or seedlings
a watering can or bottle with holes in the cap
fine soil or sand, 3 plates, a spray bottle, small stones, a hand fan or hairdryer

prep.task: If you have no grass patch, sow a thick layer of moong or methi in a tray of soil so it has sprouted by today

days.title: Harm from erosion and how farmers stop it
days.goal: Understand the harmful effects of soil erosion and the six ways of preventing it, and build a hillside model with terraces and a check dam.

steps.title: Harmful effects of soil erosion (lesson page 137)
steps.do: Read the list 'Harmful effects of soil erosion' on lesson page 137 aloud, one point at a time. After each, ask your child to explain it in their own words. Key points to listen for: the top layer is most fertile, so crops grow poorly when it goes; a field that has lost its topsoil soaks less water, so the water in wells and under the ground goes down; soil deposited in canals and drains blocks them; soil deposited in rivers makes them shallower and floods more likely; small rivers can dry up; pastures lose grass so animals go hungry; and farmers lose income. Ask: 'Which of these could reach us in the city?' (Floods, costlier vegetables, blocked drains.)

steps.title: How to prevent soil erosion (lesson pages 138–139)
steps.do: Read 'How to prevent soil erosion' on lesson pages 138–139: making a boundary (dolbandi), making an embankment with an outlet, terrace farming, conservation of forests, check dams, and drainage. Look at each picture. For each method ask: 'How does it stop the soil going?' Good answers: boundary and embankment hold back the water and soil; terraces turn a steep slope into flat steps so water cannot rush; roots hold the soil; check dams slow the water so the soil settles; drains take extra water away so the land does not turn saline (salty). Tell them that terraced fields are a common sight in the hills of Uttarakhand, Himachal, Sikkim, the North-East and the Nilgiris tea gardens.

steps.title: Build a hill with terraces and a check dam
steps.do: Do Activity a1. In a large tray or a basin, heap damp soil into a steep hill. On one side, press the slope into 4–5 flat steps with your fingers (terraces), each with a tiny raised edge. Leave the other side as a smooth slope. At the bottom, make a little stream channel and place a row of pebbles across it as a check dam. Your child pours a mug of water slowly from a bottle with holes over the top of the hill. Watch together: on the smooth side, water rushes and cuts a gully; on the terraced side, water pools on each step and trickles down slowly. Ask: 'Where did soil collect at the check dam?' (Behind the pebbles.) Take a photo or draw the model.

steps.title: Hugh Bennett, the man who warned about the dust
steps.do: Tell your child the story in Voice v1 in your own words: an American soil scientist warned in 1928 that soil erosion was a national danger, many thought he was exaggerating, and then the Dust Bowl storms of the 1930s blew away the soil of whole farm regions. Tell them that in 1935 a huge dust storm reached Washington while he was speaking to lawmakers, and soon after the US government set up its Soil Conservation Service. Then ask the voice question and let your child answer fully before you share your view.

steps.title: Core worksheet: erosion and its prevention
steps.do: Give your child Worksheet ws1 (core), sections A and B, to do on their own. Then go over the answers together, and ask them to explain one wrong answer using the model hill. Also ask the four questions in 'Let's see, what you have learnt 9.1' on lesson page 139 aloud; the book's answers are on lesson page 145.

need: a bottle with holes in the cap

prep.task: Keep a bucket of soil slightly damp so it holds a hill shape

days.title: Forests: roots that hold the earth
days.goal: Understand why forests must be protected, see the effect of plant cover on soil after rain, and meet the people of the Chipko movement and the Forest Man of Majuli.

steps.title: Conservation of forests (lesson pages 136 and 138)
steps.do: Re-read the opening lines on lesson page 136: 'Forests are our natural inheritance. Destruction of forest means our own ruin.' Then re-read point 4, 'Conservation of forests', on lesson page 138. Ask: 'What two things happen when trees are cut and uprooted?' (Soil erosion increases, and plants and animals lose their homes.) 'What does the book tell us to do with vacant land?' (Sow grass, shrubs and trees.) Add what forests also do: they slow rain so it soaks into the ground and fills wells and springs, give shade and cooler air, give fruit, wood, honey, medicines and fodder, and take in carbon dioxide from the air.

steps.title: Come, let's do: after the rain (lesson page 144)
steps.do: Do the first 'Come, let's do' task on lesson page 144. Go to a nearby park, ground or empty plot (best after rain; if it has not rained, pour a bucket of water on a bare patch and a grassy patch on a slope). Look for: places with grass and places without; a slope and a flat surface. Ask at each place: 'Can you see little channels? Is the soil washed off? Is there mud at the bottom of the slope? Has soil splashed up on walls?' Your child draws two quick sketches in the notebook: 'grassy patch' and 'bare patch'. Ask: 'Why is there this difference?' Good answer: 'Grass covers the soil and its roots hold it, so water cannot carry it away; bare soil on a slope washes off.' Also look under a big tree for exposed roots where soil has gone.

steps.title: Gaura Devi and the Chipko movement
steps.do: Tell your child the story in Voice v2: in March 1974 in Reni village in the hills of Uttarakhand, Gaura Devi and the women of the village stood guard over their forest and hugged the trees so that the contractors' men could not cut them. 'Chipko' means 'to stick to' or 'to hug'. Ask: 'Why would village women care so much about a forest?' (It gave them firewood, fodder, water from springs, and held their hill slopes so landslides and floods did not come.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Jadav Payeng grows a forest
steps.do: Tell the story in Voice v3: on a bare sandbar near Majuli island in the Brahmaputra in Assam, a young man started planting bamboo and trees around 1979, and kept planting for decades until a forest grew. Ask: 'What would the river do to a bare sandbar during floods?' (Wash the sand and soil away.) 'What changed when the trees grew?' (Roots held the ground, and animals came to live there.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Root power test
steps.do: Gently pull out one small weed or grass clump with its roots from a pot or the park (with permission) and shake it. Show your child how many fine roots there are and how the soil clings to them. Then hold a spoonful of loose soil with no roots on your palm and blow gently on both. Ask: 'Which soil stays put?' Write in the notebook: 'Roots hold soil like a net.'

need: a park, ground or empty plot with grassy and bare patches
a bucket of water (if it has not rained)
a small weed or grass clump

days.title: Soil pollution and healthy soil
days.goal: Learn the causes of soil pollution and how to prevent it, dig up our buried-objects test, make a small compost pot, and weigh the debate about organic and chemical farming.

steps.title: Soil pollution: causes (lesson pages 139–140)
steps.do: Read section 9.2 'Soil Pollution' and 'Causes of soil pollution' on lesson pages 139–140 aloud. Ask your child to count on their fingers the four causes the book gives: household and street waste with polythene, glass and iron; chemical pesticides used carelessly; too much chemical fertiliser; and poisonous factory waste dumped in rivers and drains that reaches the farms. Ask: 'Why does the book say we are all responsible?' (Because we all throw waste, and we buy the crops grown this way.)

steps.title: Dig up the buried objects
steps.do: Finish Experiment e3. With gloves or a spoon, dig up each object and lay it on newspaper. Your child records in a table: item, what it looked like on Day 1, what it looks like now. Usually the banana peel is dark, soft and partly gone; the newspaper is soft and torn; the cotton thread is weakening; the polythene and the glass look exactly the same. Ask: 'Which did your guess get right? What would happen if a farm got a little polythene and glass every year for twenty years?' (It would build up, block roots and water, and never go away.) You handle the glass and throw it safely in a newspaper wrap. Wash hands.

steps.title: How to prevent soil pollution (lesson pages 140–141)
steps.do: Read 'How to prevent soil pollution' on lesson pages 140–141: segregate polythene, glass and iron; factories must not dump poison; use organic manure such as compost, cow-dung manure, nadep compost, vermicompost, khali (oilseed cake) and green manure; neem-based sprays; and seed treatment with helpful microbes. Explain the garbled names in the book: 'dricoderma' is Trichoderma, a helpful fungus; 'raijobium' is Rhizobium, bacteria that live in the roots of dal plants and add nitrogen to the soil; P.S.B. means phosphate-solubilising bacteria. Be honest with your child: neem cake and neem sprays really do repel many pests; some others in the list, like cow urine sprays, have much weaker scientific evidence; and dhatura and tobacco are poisonous plants that children must never handle.

steps.title: Start a small compost pot
steps.do: Do Activity a2. In a bucket or pot with a few holes in the bottom, your child adds layers: dry leaves, vegetable and fruit peels from today's kitchen (no oil, meat, dairy or cooked food), a handful of garden soil, then dry leaves again. Sprinkle water till it is damp like a squeezed sponge, and cover with a cloth or lid. Ask: 'Who will turn this into manure?' (Tiny bacteria, fungi and small creatures in the soil, which break down once-living things.) Plan to stir it once a week; it should be ready in 6–8 weeks.

steps.title: Organic or chemical? A live debate
steps.do: Tell your child Voice v4 in simple words: the book says organic farming is best. Sikkim made all its farming organic by 2016. But in 2021 Sri Lanka suddenly banned chemical fertiliser, and its rice and tea harvests fell so much that the ban was taken back within months. Explain both sides: organic manure builds humus and soil life, while chemical fertiliser gives a quick, large dose of plant food; too much of it, or careless pesticide use, harms soil and water. Ask the voice question, and help your child see that 'how much, and how carefully' may matter more than 'organic or chemical'.

need: old newspaper, a spoon or gloves
a bucket or pot with holes
dry leaves, fruit and vegetable peels, garden soil, water, a cloth or lid

prep.task: Save the day's fruit and vegetable peels in a bowl

days.title: Let us revise, check and teach it back
days.goal: Review the whole lesson with the book's revision and exercises, try the stretch and challenge worksheets, check understanding and have your child teach the lesson back.

steps.title: Let's Revise and the 9.2 questions (lesson page 142)
steps.do: Read 'Let's Revise' on lesson page 142 together, one point at a time; after each point your child says which day's experiment or model showed it. Then ask the four questions of 'Let's see, what you have learnt 9.2' on lesson page 142 aloud. Good answers: polythene, glass and iron pieces; compost, cow-dung manure, vermicompost, green manure, khali manure; neem-based sprays and other organic treatments; organic farming.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws2 (stretch) on their own. Then go over it together. For the 'which method for which place' items, ask them to explain their reason using the model hill or the rain trays.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 (challenge) together, talking it through. Let your child do the thinking and writing; you only ask 'Why?' and 'How do you know?'. The last section revisits the voices of Hugh Bennett, Chipko and the organic debate.

steps.title: Lesson check
steps.do: Ask the 7 check questions aloud one at a time without the book. Tick the ones answered well. For any missed one, open the matching lesson page (erosion page 137, prevention pages 138–139, pollution pages 139–141), read the part together for one minute and ask again in different words. Five or more right is good; fewer than four means redo the rain trays and the model hill next week.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child becomes the teacher for a family member. In 5 minutes, using the rain trays, the model hill and the dug-up objects, they must teach: what topsoil is and why it is precious; how water and wind cause erosion; three ways to stop it; and two causes of soil pollution. The 'student' asks: 'Why don't farmers on hills just plough the slope?' and 'Why can't we bury polythene to get rid of it?'. End by agreeing one family action: segregate dry waste (plastic, glass, metal) from wet waste at home from today, and stir the compost pot every Sunday.

need: the rain trays, model hill and dug-up objects (or photos of them)

worksheets.title: Soil in new places
sections: A. Which method for which place?

sections.p: Pema's family grows cardamom on a steep hillside in Sikkim. Rain washes the soil down. What should they do first?
opts: Cut the trees for more space

sections.p: Water stands for many weeks in Ramesh's field and a white crust appears on the soil. What is happening and what will help?

The soil is too dry; build a check dam

sections.p: A village in Rajasthan has dry, loose sandy fields and strong summer winds. Which helps most?

Ploughing the fields many times in summer

sections.p: A small stream near Leela's village floods every monsoon and carries mud. Suggest one method and explain how it helps.

The cake left after pressing oil from neem seeds

Design a fair test to find out whether grass or dry leaves protect soil better from rain. Fill in the plan.
prefill: What will I keep the same?

sections.p: Hugh Bennett was called an alarmist before the Dust Bowl. How can we tell the difference between a warning that is true and one that is exaggerated?
Sikkim went fully organic; Sri Lanka's sudden ban on chemical fertiliser cut its harvests. List one reason each experience might have turned out so differently.
Which of these is the strongest kind of evidence that a pest spray works?
opts: Many fields with and without the spray are compared over several seasons

sections.p: The Chipko women had no power or money. Why do you think their protest worked?

experiments.title: Rain on three trays
experiments.question: Does covering soil with leaves or growing plants protect it from being washed away by rain?
need: 3 trays or cut milk or juice cartons
a patch of grass with roots, or sprouted seedlings
a watering can or a bottle with holes in the cap
books to prop the trays at the same slope
steps: Fill all three trays with the same amount of soil and press it down the same way.
Leave tray 1 bare, cover tray 2 with dry leaves, and use grass or seedlings with roots in tray 3.
Prop all three on books at the same slope, with the low end over a clear cup.
Pour one full mug of water slowly over each tray from the same height, using the watering can.
Line up the three cups and compare how muddy the water is. Let them stand for 10 minutes and compare how much soil settles at the bottom.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which cup will have the muddiest water, and which the clearest? Write the order down.
experiments.observe: Record the colour of the water in each cup and the depth of mud that settles. Usually the bare tray gives very muddy water and many little channels in the soil; the leaf tray gives less; the grass tray gives the clearest water and almost no channels.
experiments.why: Raindrops hit bare soil hard and knock loose particles free; then flowing water carries them downhill, faster on a slope. Leaves act like an umbrella that takes the hit of the drops and slows the water. Grass does that too, and its roots also form a net that binds soil particles together, while the water soaks into the soil along the roots instead of running off. This is why forests, grass and crop cover protect fields, and why the book asks us to sow grass, shrubs and trees on empty land.
experiments.safety: Work outdoors or on newspaper. Wash hands after handling soil.

experiments.title: Wind on dry, damp and covered soil
experiments.question: Which soil does wind carry away most easily: dry, damp or covered?
need: a few small stones and some dry grass
a hand fan or a hairdryer on the cool setting
a sheet of paper as a backdrop
steps: Make three equal heaps of fine soil on three plates.
Spray heap 2 until it is damp all through. Cover heap 3 with a few stones and dry grass. Leave heap 1 dry and bare.
Stand the paper behind the plates.
Fan each heap for 10 seconds from the same distance, or the parent holds the hairdryer on cool.
Compare how much each heap shrank and how much dust landed on the paper.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which heap will lose the most soil? Which the least?
experiments.observe: The dry, bare heap usually loses the most and coats the paper with dust. The damp heap hardly moves. The covered heap loses a little from the gaps.
experiments.why: Wind can only lift particles that are loose, light and dry. Water makes soil particles stick to each other, so damp soil holds together. Stones, grass and plant roots shield the surface from the wind. This is why wind erosion is worst in dry, arid areas such as parts of Rajasthan, and why farmers there plant rows of trees as windbreaks and leave crop stubble on fields.
experiments.safety: Do this outdoors. Keep faces away from the blowing dust. Only a parent uses the hairdryer, on cool, away from water.

experiments.title: What rots in soil and what stays?
experiments.question: Which kinds of waste break down in soil, and which stay and pollute it?
need: a pot or bucket of damp garden soil
a small piece of broken glass bangle (parent handles it)
steps: Bury each item about 5 cm deep in the soil, a hand's width apart.
Mark each with a labelled ice-cream stick.
Keep the soil damp, like a squeezed sponge, and keep the pot in shade.
After about two weeks (or at least 4 days if that is all the time you have), dig each item up gently with a spoon or gloves.
Lay them on newspaper and compare with what they were like on Day 1.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which items will have changed, and which will look the same? Write the guesses down with the date.
experiments.observe: Record each item's colour, softness and size. Usually the banana peel has turned dark and soft and part has gone; the newspaper is soft and falling apart; the cotton thread is weaker; the polythene and glass are unchanged.
experiments.why: Soil is full of bacteria, fungi and small creatures such as earthworms that feed on things that were once alive (peel, paper made from wood, cotton from a plant). They break them down into humus and plant food. This is called biodegrading. Polythene is a plastic made from petroleum and glass is melted sand; soil microbes cannot eat them, so they stay for hundreds of years, block water and roots, and break into tiny bits that pollute soil. That is why the book asks us to segregate polythene, glass and iron and send them for recycling, not throw them into fields or manure pits.
experiments.safety: Only the parent handles the glass piece, wrapped in paper, and throws it away safely afterwards. Wear gloves or use a spoon to dig, and wash hands after.
experiments.time: 14 min to set up + 3 min checks + 10 min to dig up after 4–14 days

activities.title: Model hill with terraces and a check dam
need: a bottle with holes punched in the cap
steps: Heap the damp soil into a steep hill in the tray.
On one side, press the slope into 4–5 flat steps with tiny raised edges (terraces). Leave the other side smooth.
Scoop a little stream channel at the foot of the hill and lay a row of pebbles across it as a check dam.
Pour water slowly over the top of the hill from the bottle.
Watch the smooth side and the terraced side, and where the soil settles at the check dam.
Photograph or draw the model before and after.
activities.outcome: A working model that shows how a smooth slope gets cut by gullies while terraces hold water and soil, and how a check dam traps soil behind it. Your child can use it on Day 6 to teach the lesson back.

activities.title: A kitchen compost pot
need: a bucket or large pot with a few holes in the bottom
steps: Put a layer of dry leaves at the bottom.
Add a layer of raw peels (no oil, meat, dairy or cooked food, which smell and attract pests).
Add a handful of garden soil; it brings the microbes that do the work.
Add another layer of dry leaves. Sprinkle water until it is damp like a squeezed sponge.
Cover with a cloth or lid and keep it in the shade. Stir once a week and add peels and leaves in layers.
After 6–8 weeks, when it looks dark and crumbly and smells like earth, use it in a plant pot.
activities.outcome: Home-made compost, one of the organic manures in the book, and a habit of keeping wet waste out of the dustbin. Your child sees that soil life turns waste into food for plants.

voices.who: Hugh Hammond Bennett (1881–1960), USA
voices.idea: Bennett, an American soil scientist, studied farms across the USA and saw that topsoil was being washed and blown away from ploughed, bare fields. In 1928 he co-wrote a government report called 'Soil Erosion: A National Menace', warning that erosion was destroying the country's farmland. He argued for contour ploughing, terraces, cover crops and grass strips.
voices.then: Many people, including some officials, thought erosion was a small local problem and that he was exaggerating. Then in the 1930s, after years of drought on over-ploughed grasslands, huge dust storms (the 'Dust Bowl') blew away the soil of farms across the American plains and drove many families from their land. In 1935 the US Congress set up the Soil Conservation Service, with Bennett as its first chief.
voices.now: Bennett is often called the father of soil conservation in the USA, and the methods he pushed for are standard practice around the world, including in India. Scientists today agree that soil is lost much faster than it forms on poorly managed land.
voices.ask: Bennett's warnings were ignored until disaster struck. What evidence could he have shown that might have convinced people earlier? Think of our rain-tray test.

voices.who: Gaura Devi (about 1925–1991) and the Chipko movement, Uttarakhand, India
voices.idea: In the early 1970s villagers in the Garhwal hills (now in Uttarakhand) protested against forests being given to outside contractors for felling. Leaders included Chandi Prasad Bhatt and later Sunderlal Bahuguna. On 26 March 1974, in Reni village in Chamoli district, while the men were away, Gaura Devi led the village women into the forest and stood guard, refusing to let the loggers cut the trees. 'Chipko' means 'to stick to' or 'to hug'. The villagers knew that the forests held their hill slopes, fed their springs and gave them fodder and firewood.
voices.then: At first the government and timber companies saw the villagers as standing in the way of development. The protests spread and drew attention across India and the world.
voices.now: The Chipko movement is remembered as one of the most important forest movements in the world. In 1980 the central government put a 15-year ban on cutting green trees in the Himalayan forests of Uttar Pradesh (which then included Uttarakhand). Today scientists widely agree that cutting forests on steep slopes increases soil erosion, landslides and floods, as the hill women said.
voices.ask: The Reni women knew from daily life that their forest held the hills together. Scientists know it from measurements. How could a scientist test what the women knew?

voices.who: Jadav 'Molai' Payeng (born 1963), Assam, India
voices.idea: Starting around 1979, as a teenager, Payeng began planting bamboo and then trees on a bare, eroding sandbar of the Brahmaputra river near Majuli, Assam. He kept planting and caring for it, mostly alone, for decades. The forest, often called the Molai forest, is reported to cover several hundred hectares and to be home to birds, deer and visiting wild elephants.
voices.then: For many years few people outside his area knew about his work. It became widely known after reports by journalists around 2007–2012.
voices.now: He was given the Padma Shri in 2015 and is called the 'Forest Man of India'. His forest shows how plant roots can stabilise land that floods and erosion keep eating away, though one forest alone cannot stop a giant river like the Brahmaputra from eroding its islands.
voices.ask: One person planted a forest. But Majuli island is still losing land to the river. What does that tell us about what one person can do and what needs many people or a government?

voices.who: The organic versus chemical farming debate: Sikkim (2016) and Sri Lanka (2021)
voices.idea: The book says organic farming, using compost, cow-dung manure, vermicompost and green manure instead of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, is best for soil, people and animals. Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in 2016, after phasing out chemical fertilisers and pesticides over about a decade.
voices.then: In April 2021 Sri Lanka suddenly banned imports of chemical fertilisers and pesticides to make the whole country organic at once. Farmers had little time or organic manure to switch, and rice and tea harvests fell sharply. The ban was mostly reversed by the end of 2021.
voices.now: Scientists agree that organic manure builds humus and soil life, and that overusing chemical fertilisers and pesticides harms soil, water and health. But many studies find that organic farms usually grow less food per field than farms using some fertiliser, so whether the whole world could be fed by organic farming alone is still debated. Many experts now support a mix: build soil with manure and compost, and use chemicals only in the right amounts, tested by soil tests.
voices.ask: Sikkim switched slowly; Sri Lanka switched overnight. If you were in charge of farming for a country, what would you want to measure before deciding?

check.q: What is soil erosion, and what are its two main causes?
check.a: The wearing away and carrying off of soil from its place. It is caused mainly by fast-flowing rainwater and by strong wind.

check.q: Why is losing the top layer of soil so harmful?
check.a: The top layer is the most fertile; without it crops grow poorly and yields fall, the field soaks less water so wells go down, and the farmer loses income.

check.q: What is gully erosion?
check.a: When rainwater rushes again and again through narrow channels, it cuts small gullies; over time they can become streams and deep ravines.

check.q: How does terrace farming prevent erosion on steep slopes?
check.a: It cuts the slope into flat steps, so water cannot rush downhill; it stays on each step, soaks in and flows slowly, leaving the soil in place.

check.q: Name three other ways of preventing soil erosion.
check.a: Any three: a boundary around the field (dolbandi), embankments with an outlet, planting trees, grass and shrubs, check dams on streams, and proper drainage.

check.q: How do forests help stop soil erosion?
