check.a: Leaves break the force of rain, and roots hold the soil like a net so water and wind cannot carry it away; forests also let rain soak into the ground.

check.q: Give two causes of soil pollution and two ways to prevent it.
check.a: Causes: polythene, glass and iron in waste; careless use of pesticides; too much chemical fertiliser; factory poison in rivers. Prevention: segregate and recycle dry waste, use compost and other organic manure, use pesticides carefully or neem-based ones, stop factories dumping waste.

items.title: Sources of Energy and their Importance

c.covers: Why we need energy; sources and kinds of energy; alternatives; saving energy

p.title: Sources of Energy and their Importance
p.source: NIOS Open Basic Education, Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 10 (lesson pages 149–160)
p.summary: Energy is the power to do work, and we need it for everything, even while asleep. Your child learns the difference between non-renewable sources (coal, kerosene, petrol, diesel, cooking gas) and renewable ones (food, sunlight, wind, flowing water, biogas), meets seven kinds of energy from the book through hands-on tests with sunlight, a pinwheel, a water wheel and magnets, builds the book's solar cooker, and finds practical ways to save energy at home. Along the way they meet a forgotten woman scientist, a solar inventor ahead of his time and a live debate about how long oil will last.
goals: By the end your child can explain what energy is and why we need it, even when we sleep.
By the end your child can sort sources of energy into non-renewable and renewable, give examples of each and explain why non-renewable sources will run out.
By the end your child can name the seven kinds of energy in the book (food, solar, wind, hydro, organic or biogas, electrical, magnetic) and say where each is used.
By the end your child can show with home tests how sunlight heats things, how moving air and moving water can turn a wheel, and how a magnet separates iron.
By the end your child can suggest at least five ways to save energy at home and explain why each one works.
By the end your child can explain why predictions about how long oil will last keep changing, and what kind of evidence they depend on.
words: the power or ability to do work, such as moving, lifting, heating, lighting or growing
a thing from which we get energy, such as food, coal, petrol, the Sun or the wind
a source that gets used up and cannot be made again in our lifetime, like coal, petrol, diesel, kerosene and natural gas; they took millions of years to form underground
a source that keeps coming back and does not run out, like sunlight, wind and flowing water
coal, oil (petrol, diesel, kerosene) and natural gas, formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient plants and tiny sea creatures buried underground
energy from the Sun, which reaches us as light and heat
a flat panel that turns sunlight directly into electricity, like the panels on rooftops and on solar street lights
a machine with large blades turned by the wind; it can pump water, grind flour or, as a wind turbine, make electricity
energy from flowing or falling water; in a hydro power station the water turns machines that make electricity ('hydro' means water)
a gas that burns, made when animal dung, crop waste and dry leaves rot inside a closed tank without air; also called gobar gas
energy carried by electricity through wires to run bulbs, fans, fridges, computers and trains
the book's name for the power of a magnet to pull iron and steel towards it, used in cranes and electric bells

days.title: Why do we need energy?
days.goal: Start from how our own bodies feel when hungry or tired, learn what energy means, and find energy being used everywhere at home.

steps.title: Hungry and tired
steps.do: Ask your child: 'How do you feel when you have skipped breakfast and it's nearly lunch? Can you run as fast?' Good answers: 'weak', 'tired', 'cranky', 'my tummy grumbles'. Then ask: 'What happens to Papa's scooter or the car when the petrol runs out?' (It stops.) Ask: 'What is the same about you without food and the scooter without petrol?' Listen for: 'Both need something to give them power to work.' Tell them: 'Scientists call that power energy. Today we find out where it comes from.'

steps.title: The opening and 10.1 'Why is energy required?' (lesson pages 149–150)
steps.do: Read the opening of Lesson 10 on lesson page 149 and section 10.1 on lesson page 150 aloud, and look at the pictures of lifting weight, washing clothes and cooking food. Ask: 'What does the book call the strength to do work?' (Energy.) 'Do we need energy while sleeping? Why?' (Yes; the heart keeps beating, the lungs keep breathing and the body stays warm.) 'Which work in the book's list do you do every day?' Then read the line that we need energy even for eating and passing stool and urine, and ask: 'Can you think of anything you do that needs no energy at all?' (No; even thinking uses energy, as the brain is working.)

steps.title: Your sleeping heart
steps.do: Show your child how to find the pulse on the inside of the wrist below the thumb, using two fingers (not the thumb). Count the beats for 15 seconds while sitting still and multiply by 4. Then they lie flat with eyes closed for 2 minutes and you count again. Then they do 30 jumping jacks and count again. Write the three numbers. Ask: 'Did your heart stop when you were resting?' (No, it slowed down but kept going.) 'When did it beat fastest? Why?' (After jumping, because the muscles needed more energy, so the heart pumped faster to bring food and oxygen.)

steps.title: Home energy hunt
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Walk through every room with your child and a notebook with three columns: 'Thing or work', 'What energy does it use?', 'Where does that come from?'. Find at least 12 examples, for example: gas stove (cooking gas), ceiling fan (electricity), mixer-grinder (electricity), Dadi's walk to the temple (food energy), clothes drying on the balcony (sunlight and wind), scooter (petrol), torch (battery), mobile phone charger (electricity), plants on the window (sunlight). If your child is stuck, ask: 'What makes this move, heat up or light up?' Leave the third column blank where you are not sure; we will fill it in over the week.

steps.title: What did we find?
steps.do: Look at the list together and ask: 'Which energy did we find most often?' (Usually electricity.) 'Which things need fuel that gets burnt?' (Stove, scooter, perhaps a generator or diya.) Ask your child to write the sentence 'Energy is the power to do work' in the notebook and then add one sentence of their own about why our home needs it.

need: NIOS Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 10 (lesson pages 149–150)

days.title: Sources that run out and sources that don't
days.goal: Learn the two kinds of sources of energy, why fossil fuels are non-renewable, and that all our food energy comes from plants that capture sunlight.

steps.title: 10.1.1 Sources of energy (lesson pages 150–151)
steps.do: Read 10.1.1 on lesson pages 150–151 aloud: non-renewable sources (coal, kerosene oil, cooking gas, petrol, diesel) and renewable sources (wind, water, sunlight, and food, which nature keeps providing). Look at the pictures of coal, kerosene, diesel and cooking gas. Ask the book's question: 'If we keep using them continuously, won't they come to an end?' (Yes.) Explain where they come from: coal formed over millions of years from buried ancient forests, and oil and natural gas from tiny sea creatures buried under the sea floor. 'Once we burn them, can we make more?' (Not in our lifetime; it took millions of years.)

steps.title: Renewable or not? Card sort
steps.do: Write these on small paper slips: coal, petrol, diesel, kerosene, LPG cooking gas, sunlight, wind, river water, food, cow dung, firewood, battery. Your child sorts them into two piles: 'Runs out' and 'Keeps coming back'. Ask the reason for each. Talk about the two tricky ones: firewood and cow dung come back only if we grow trees and keep animals, so they are renewable only if we do not use them faster than they grow back. A battery is not a source itself; it stores energy that came from somewhere else, often from electricity made by burning coal.

steps.title: How long will oil last? (Do you know?, lesson page 151)
steps.do: Read the 'Do you know?' box on lesson page 151: the book estimates oil and gas will finish in 30–35 years and coal will last up to 100 years. Then tell your child Voice v1 in simple words: such predictions have been made again and again, and new oil keeps being found and new ways to dig it out keep being invented, so the dates keep moving. But everyone agrees there is only a fixed amount underground. Ask the voice question and let your child answer fully.

steps.title: 10.2.1 Energy from food (lesson page 152)
steps.do: Read 'Let's see what you have learnt 10.1' questions on lesson pages 151–152 aloud and let your child answer them (answers on lesson page 159). Then read 10.2.1 'Energy received from food' on lesson page 152. Ask: 'Where does the energy in your roti come from?' Trace it with them: roti from wheat; wheat is a plant; the plant made its food from sunlight in its leaves. 'And the energy in milk?' (Cow ate grass; grass used sunlight.) Draw a chain in the notebook: Sun → grass → cow → milk → me.

steps.title: Food energy on the packet
steps.do: Bring three packets from the kitchen, for example biscuits, a breakfast cereal or poha packet, and a packet of namkeen. On the back, find 'Energy' in the nutrition table, written in kcal (kilocalories) per 100 g. Your child writes each number down. Ask: 'Which gives the most energy for the same weight?' (Usually the fried namkeen, because fat stores a lot of energy.) Explain: 'kcal is how scientists measure food energy. A child of 10 needs roughly 1,700–2,000 kcal a day; it depends on how active they are.' Ask: 'Does more energy always mean healthier?' (No; food also needs to give protein, vitamins and fibre. We will learn more in Lesson 12.)

days.title: Solar energy: the Sun's light and heat
days.goal: Learn how we use the Sun's light and heat, test which colour soaks up the most heat, and meet a solar inventor who was ahead of his time.

steps.title: 10.2.2 Solar energy (lesson pages 152–153)
steps.do: Read 10.2.2 on lesson pages 152–153 aloud and look at the pictures of the solar cooker and grains drying. Ask: 'In what two forms does solar energy reach us?' (Light and heat.) 'Name five uses in the book.' (Drying clothes and grains, plants making food, cooking, heating water, lighting bulbs through solar cells, running small vehicles.) Read the line about Vitamin D and explain properly: when sunlight falls on our skin, the skin makes Vitamin D, which helps our bones take in calcium; a little time in morning or late-afternoon sun is enough, and too much midday sun can burn the skin. Tell them the Sun will keep shining for billions of years, which is why we treat it as never-ending.

steps.title: Black bottle, white bottle
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Take two identical plastic bottles or steel tumblers. Wrap one in black paper or cloth and one in white paper. Fill both with the same amount of tap water and check that the water feels the same (or measure with a thermometer). Ask your child to predict which will get warmer. Put both in direct sunshine on a balcony or terrace. Set a timer for 40 minutes; they will check on them during the rest of the session. Meanwhile also put a wet handkerchief in the sun and another in the shade, and note which dries first.

steps.title: Augustin Mouchot's sun engine
steps.do: Tell your child the story in Voice v2: about 150 years ago a French teacher built machines that used curved mirrors to focus sunlight, boil water and run a small steam engine, and he even printed a newspaper with it at a big fair in Paris in 1878. Then coal became cheap and his work was dropped. Ask: 'Why do you think people chose coal then?' (It was cheap and worked at night and on cloudy days.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Solar around us
steps.do: Look out of the window or on a short walk for solar panels: on rooftops, solar street lights, traffic signals, a solar water heater tank on a roof, or a solar calculator at home. Ask: 'Which of these turns sunlight into electricity, and which uses the Sun's heat?' (Panels and cells make electricity; the water heater uses heat.) Tell them that Kochi airport in Kerala became the world's first airport to run fully on solar power in 2015.

steps.title: Read the bottles
steps.do: After 40 minutes bring both bottles in. Your child feels the water in each with a finger, or reads the thermometer, and writes the result. Ask: 'Was your guess right? Why do people in hot places like Rajasthan wear white clothes, and why are solar cooker boxes painted black inside?' (White reflects sunlight and stays cooler; black absorbs it and gets hot.) Also check the two handkerchiefs.

need: black paper or cloth, white paper, rubber bands

prep.task: Check the weather; this day needs at least an hour of sunshine (swap with Day 4 if it is cloudy)

days.title: Wind and water at work
days.goal: Learn how wind energy and hydro energy do work, make the book's pinwheel spin, and build a water wheel.

steps.title: 10.2.3 Wind energy (lesson page 153)
steps.do: Read 10.2.3 'Wind Energy' on lesson page 153 aloud and look at the pinwheel picture. Ask the book's question: 'Why does the pinwheel spin faster when children run with it?' Good answer: 'More air pushes harder on the blades, so more work of spinning gets done.' Ask: 'What three jobs can windmills do?' (Pump water from wells, make electricity, grind flour.) Tell them that India has many big wind farms, especially in Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Karnataka and Rajasthan, where strong winds blow for much of the year.

steps.title: Make a pinwheel and test the wind
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Make the pinwheel from a square of paper: draw both diagonals, cut along each from the corners about two-thirds of the way to the centre, bend every other point into the centre and pin them with a drawing pin through a pencil eraser or a straw (you handle the pin). Then test: hold it still indoors (no spin), blow gently, blow hard, walk with it, run with it, and hold it in front of a table fan on low and on high. Your child counts how many times a coloured dot on one blade goes round in 10 seconds each time. Ask: 'When did it spin fastest? What does that tell you about stronger wind?'

steps.title: 10.2.4 Hydro energy (lesson page 153)
steps.do: Read 10.2.4 on lesson page 153 aloud and look at the hydro power station picture. Ask: 'How does the book show that flowing water has energy?' (Rivers carry heavy wooden logs downstream.) Explain how a hydro station works: a dam stores water high up; the water falls down through pipes and spins big wheels called turbines; the turbines turn a generator that makes electricity. Tell them about the Bhakra dam on the Sutlej in Himachal Pradesh, one of India's biggest dams, whose stored water spins turbines to make electricity.

steps.title: Build a water wheel
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Push 6–8 plastic spoons into the sides of a round cork, a bottle cap glued to cardboard circles, or a small paper cup, all facing the same way, like a wheel with paddles. Push a straight skewer or pencil through the middle as an axle and rest it across the top of a big bowl or bucket so the wheel can turn. Ask your child to predict: 'Will the wheel turn faster with a thin trickle or a fast stream, and from low or high?' Pour water from a jug onto the spoons: first a thin trickle from just above, then a thick stream from higher up. Count the turns in 10 seconds each time.

steps.title: Wind and water compared
steps.do: Ask: 'What was the same about the pinwheel and the water wheel?' (Something moving, air or water, pushed the blades and made them turn.) 'Are wind and flowing water renewable? Why?' (Yes; the Sun heats the air and makes winds, and the Sun evaporates water that falls as rain and flows down rivers, again and again.) Write in the notebook: 'Moving air and moving water have energy that can turn a wheel.'

need: a square of paper, scissors, a drawing pin, a pencil with an eraser or a straw
6–8 plastic spoons, a cork or small paper cup, a skewer or pencil
a big bowl or bucket and a jug of water

prep.task: Collect plastic spoons and a cork or cup for the water wheel

days.title: Biogas, electricity, magnets and alternatives
days.goal: Learn about organic (biogas), electrical and magnetic energy, test what a magnet picks out of a mixed pile, and understand why we need alternative sources.

steps.title: 10.2.5 Organic energy and 10.2.6 Electrical energy (lesson page 154)
steps.do: Read 10.2.5 and 10.2.6 on lesson page 154 aloud and look at the biogas plant picture. Ask: 'What goes into a biogas or gobar gas plant?' (Animal dung, crop waste, dry leaves and branches.) Explain what happens: inside a closed tank with no air, tiny bacteria break down the dung and waste and give off a gas, mostly methane, which burns with a blue flame for cooking and light; what is left is good manure. Ask: 'Why is this better than throwing the dung away?' (We get fuel and manure from waste.) Then ask: 'Name five things in our home that use electrical energy.' Tell them that most of India's electricity is still made by burning coal in power stations, which is why saving electricity also saves coal.

steps.title: Magnet rescue from the scrap pile
steps.do: Read 10.2.7 'Magnetic Energy' on lesson pages 154–155 first and look at the crane and electric bell pictures. Then do Experiment e3. Mix on a tray: iron nails or safety pins, steel paper clips, a steel spoon, an aluminium foil ball, a copper coin or wire, a brass key, plastic buttons, wooden matchsticks and some sand. Ask your child to predict which things the magnet will pull out. Then they sweep a fridge magnet or bar magnet (inside a thin plastic bag, so the bits come off easily) over the pile and sort what it picks up. Ask: 'Why do scrap yards use giant magnets on cranes?' (To quickly separate iron and steel from other scrap.)

steps.title: 10.2.8 Alternative sources and 'Let's see 10.2' (lesson pages 155–156)
steps.do: Read 10.2.8 'Alternative sources of energy' on lesson page 155 aloud. Ask: 'Why do we need alternatives to coal, kerosene and petrol?' (They are running out with heavy use.) 'Which alternatives does the book name?' (Solar, wind, water, organic/biogas.) Then do 'Let's see, what you have learnt 10.2' on lesson pages 155–156 aloud: the seven types of energy and the five fill-in-the-blanks. Answers are on lesson page 159 (solar, water, organic, electrical, iron).

steps.title: Eunice Foote and the warm jar
steps.do: Tell your child Voice v3: in 1856 an American woman scientist put different gases in glass jars in the sunshine and found the jar with carbon dioxide got hottest. Burning coal, petrol and gas gives off carbon dioxide. Her work was mostly forgotten for over 150 years. Ask: 'Why might her finding matter for the choice between coal and solar energy?' (Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide, which traps heat and warms the Earth; sun and wind do not burn anything.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Core worksheet: sources and kinds of energy
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws1 (core) on their own. Then go through the answers together; for each wrong one, ask them to find the right lesson page (sources on pages 150–151, kinds on pages 152–155) and correct it.

need: a fridge magnet or bar magnet and a thin plastic bag
a tray with iron nails or safety pins, steel clips, a steel spoon, aluminium foil, a copper coin or wire, a brass key, plastic buttons, matchsticks, sand

days.title: Saving energy and cooking with the Sun
days.goal: Learn the book's ways to save energy, prove one of them with a covered-pot test, and build the book's solar cooker.

steps.title: 10.3 How can energy be saved? (lesson page 156)
steps.do: Read 10.3 on lesson page 156 aloud, one point at a time. After each, ask your child: 'Why does this save energy?' Listen for: switching off saves electricity (and the coal burnt to make it); water reaches our taps using electric pumps; a lid keeps heat in; extra water needs extra gas to boil; soaked dal and rice cook faster; a bus carries 40 people for the fuel of a few cars; a pressure cooker cooks faster. Tell them that the book mentions CFL bulbs, but today LED bulbs use even less electricity than CFLs, and far less than old yellow bulbs.

steps.title: Lid on or lid off?
steps.do: Do Experiment e4 with you at the stove and your child as timekeeper at a safe distance. Use two identical small steel vessels with 2 cups of tap water each. Heat one with a lid and then the other without a lid, on the same burner at the same flame setting. Your child times how long until each comes to a rolling boil and writes both times. Ask them to predict first. Ask afterwards: 'How much gas did the lid save? If we cook three times a day for a year, how much would that add up to?'

steps.title: Build the book's solar cooker (lesson page 160)
steps.do: Do Activity a3, the 'Come, let's do and observe' task on lesson page 160. Use a shoebox or cardboard carton. Line the inside with black paper. Cover the top of the box opening with a sheet of clear plastic or a glass pane (you handle the glass; clear cling film or a plastic folder is safer). Cover the inside of the lid flap with aluminium foil, smooth side out, as the reflector. Put a small black or steel bowl inside with soaked poha or a few slices of tomato, or a cube of butter or a chocolate to melt. Prop the flap open with a stick so the sunlight bounces off the foil into the box. Place it in strong sun around noon. Ask: 'What is the job of the black paper, the foil and the plastic?' (Black absorbs heat; foil reflects more sunlight in; plastic lets light in and traps the heat.)

steps.title: Check the cooker
steps.do: After about an hour (or at the end of the day), open the cooker. Your child feels around the bowl carefully with the back of a hand (it may be hot) and notes what happened: melted butter or chocolate, softened tomato or warm poha. Ask: 'Why does the book call this the Sun God preparing your food? What fuel did we use?' (None; only sunlight.) 'When would this cooker not work?' (At night, on cloudy days, in the monsoon.)

need: 2 identical small steel vessels, one lid, measuring cup
a shoebox or carton, black paper, aluminium foil, glue or tape, clear plastic sheet or cling film, a stick
a small black or steel bowl, soaked poha or tomato slices or a cube of butter

prep.task: Collect a shoebox, black paper, foil and cling film for the solar cooker; check that tomorrow's forecast is sunny

days.title: Let us revise, check and teach it back
days.goal: Review the lesson with the book's revision and exercises, plan a family energy-saving pledge, check understanding and have your child teach it back.

steps.title: Let's Revise and the home energy hunt (lesson page 157)
steps.do: Read 'Let's Revise' on lesson page 157 together. After each point, your child points to something from the week that showed it (pulse count, card sort, black bottle, pinwheel, water wheel, magnets, solar cooker). Then go back to the Day 1 home energy hunt (Activity a1) and fill in any blanks in the 'Where does that come from?' column, now that they know about coal power stations, LPG and food energy.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet: an energy audit
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws2 (stretch). The table section needs them to go round the house for 5 minutes and list things that were left on when no one was using them. Go over the answers together.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 (challenge) together. Let your child think and write; you only ask 'Why?' and 'How do you know?'. Make sure they bring in the voices of Mouchot, Foote and the oil-forecast debate in the last section.

steps.title: Lesson check
steps.do: Ask the 7 check questions aloud one at a time, without the book. Tick each answer given well. For a missed one, open the matching lesson page (sources pages 150–151, kinds pages 152–155, saving page 156), read the part together, and ask again in other words. Five or more right is good; fewer than four means redo the card sort and magnet tests next week.

steps.title: Teach it back and family pledge
steps.do: Your child is the teacher for the family. In 5 minutes, using the pinwheel, water wheel, magnet and solar cooker, they must explain: what energy is; renewable and non-renewable sources with examples; four kinds of energy; and why we must save energy. The 'student' asks: 'If the Sun gives so much energy, why don't we use only solar?' and 'Is a battery a source of energy?'. End with a family pledge on a paper stuck on the fridge: three energy-saving actions the family will follow, chosen by your child, such as 'lids on every pot', 'last one out switches off the fan', 'soak dal before cooking'.

need: the pinwheel, water wheel, magnet and solar cooker from the week

sections.p: The power or capacity to do work is called ____.
Sort these sources of energy.
Why are coal and petrol called non-renewable?
opts: They finish after use and take millions of years to form
They come from the Sun every day

sections.p: Why do we need energy even when we are asleep?
Match each kind of energy to where it is used.
On earth life is possible because of ____ energy.
Magnetic energy is used to separate ____ from a pile of scrap.
In a biogas plant the gas is made from:
Draw the energy chain for your glass of milk, from the Sun to you.

worksheets.title: Energy in new situations
sections: A. Which source would you choose?

sections.p: A village in Ladakh gets bright sun almost every day but has no electricity line. Which would help most to light homes?
opts: A hydro dam on a dry stream
A windmill in a still valley

sections.p: A dairy farmer in Punjab has 20 buffaloes. Which source can turn his waste into cooking fuel and manure?
Kanyakumari has strong winds for much of the year. What kind of energy could it use and how?
Your black bottle got hotter than the white one. Use this to explain why the inside of a solar cooker is black.
Walk around your home for 5 minutes. List things that were on or wasting energy when no one needed them, and what you would do.
Match the habit to why it saves energy.
pairs: Heat does not escape with the steam
It cooks faster, so less gas
One vehicle's fuel carries many people
Same light for much less electricity

sections.p: Coal, petrol and your roti all got their energy from the Sun long ago or recently. Explain how coal's energy came from the Sun.
A battery runs a torch. Is a battery a source of energy or a store of energy? Explain where its energy came from.
Solar panels do not work at night. Suggest two ways a town using solar power could still have lights at night.
Which makes the water wheel turn fastest?
opts: A thin trickle from low down
A thick stream from high up

sections.p: The book says oil will last 30–35 years. Others said similar things 50 years ago. Why do these forecasts keep changing? Does that mean oil will never run out?
Mouchot's sun engine worked, but people chose coal. What has changed since 1878 that makes solar power popular now?
Eunice Foote's result was ignored for over a century. What can we do to make sure good ideas get noticed, whoever finds them?

experiments.title: Black bottle, white bottle
experiments.question: Does the colour of a container change how much of the Sun's heat it soaks up?
need: 2 identical plastic bottles or steel tumblers
tap water and a measuring cup
steps: Wrap one bottle in black paper and the other in white paper.
Fill both with the same amount of tap water from the same tap. Check that both feel the same, or measure the temperature.
Put both side by side in direct sunshine.
After 40 minutes, feel the water in each with a finger or measure it with the thermometer.
Write down which is warmer and by how much.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which bottle will be warmer after 40 minutes? Or will they be the same?
experiments.observe: Record the starting and ending temperature (or 'cool', 'warm', 'hot') for both. Usually the black bottle is clearly warmer, often by several degrees.
experiments.why: Sunlight carries energy. When it falls on a surface, some is bounced back (reflected) and some is soaked up (absorbed) and turns into heat. White and shiny surfaces reflect most of the light, so they stay cooler. Black surfaces absorb almost all the light, so they heat up more. That is why solar cookers and solar water heater pipes are black, why the solar cooker has a shiny foil reflector to send more light in, and why light-coloured clothes feel cooler in summer.
experiments.safety: Use plastic or steel, not glass, and do not leave bottles in the sun for many hours. Do not look at the Sun directly.
experiments.time: 15 min to set up + 40 min in the sun + 7 min to read

experiments.title: Build a water wheel
experiments.question: Can flowing water do work, and does faster or higher water do more?
need: a cork or a small paper cup
a skewer, straight stick or pencil for the axle
steps: Push the spoons into the sides of the cork or cup, evenly spaced, with all the bowls facing the same way.
Push the skewer through the centre so the wheel can spin on it.
Rest the skewer across the top of the bowl or bucket, holding the ends lightly.
Pour a thin trickle of water from just above the wheel onto the spoons. Count the turns in 10 seconds.
Pour a thick stream from higher up. Count again.
Try pouring onto the middle of the spoons and onto the edge, and see which works better.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: will a thin trickle or a thick stream turn the wheel faster? Does pouring from higher up make a difference?
experiments.observe: Record the number of turns in 10 seconds for each kind of pour. A thick stream from higher up usually spins the wheel fastest.
experiments.why: Moving water has energy of motion. The more water there is and the faster it moves, the harder it pushes on the paddles. Water falling from higher up speeds up as it falls, so it hits harder. A hydro power station works the same way: a dam stores a lot of water high up, it falls through big pipes and spins turbines, and the turbines turn generators that make electricity. Old water mills (gharats) in the Himalayas use streams to turn millstones that grind flour.
experiments.safety: Do it in the bathroom or outside to avoid slippery floors. Wipe up spills.

experiments.title: Magnet rescue from the scrap pile
experiments.question: Which materials does a magnet pull, and how can that help sort scrap?
need: a fridge magnet or bar magnet
steel paper clips and a steel spoon
steps: Mix all the items and the sand on the tray.
Put the magnet inside the plastic bag.
Sweep the bagged magnet slowly over the pile.
Hold the bag over a plate and pull the magnet out of the bag; the stuck items drop off.
Sort the items into 'pulled' and 'not pulled' and write the lists.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: will the magnet pull every metal thing? Which ones will it leave behind?
experiments.observe: Usually the magnet pulls the iron nails, safety pins, steel clips and often the steel spoon, and sometimes tiny black specks from the sand (iron-containing grains). It leaves the aluminium foil, copper, brass, plastic and wood.
experiments.why: Magnets pull strongly only on a few metals, mainly iron and steel (steel is mostly iron), plus nickel and cobalt. They do not pull aluminium, copper, brass, plastic or wood, so 'all metals stick to magnets' is a myth this test breaks. Scrap yards use huge electromagnets on cranes: when electricity flows through the coil it becomes a magnet and lifts the iron; when it is switched off the iron drops. An electric bell also uses an electromagnet that pulls a striker again and again. The book calls this magnetic energy.
experiments.safety: Keep magnets away from phones, cards and small children, who might swallow small magnets. Handle nails and pins carefully.

experiments.title: Lid on or lid off?
experiments.question: Does covering a pot really save cooking gas?
steps: Pour exactly 2 cups of tap water into each vessel.
Parent heats the first vessel with the lid on, on a medium flame. The child times how long until it reaches a rolling boil.
Let the burner cool for a minute. Parent heats the second vessel without a lid, same burner, same flame. The child times it.
Write both times and work out the difference.
Use the boiled water for tea, dal or washing up so nothing is wasted.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: will the covered pot boil faster, slower or at the same time? By how much?
experiments.observe: Record both times. The covered pot usually boils noticeably sooner, often a minute or more quicker for 2 cups.
experiments.why: Heating water takes energy from the gas flame. Without a lid, hot steam and warm air escape from the surface and carry heat away, and water evaporates and takes heat with it. A lid traps that heat and steam so more of the energy stays in the water. Less time on the flame means less LPG burnt. A pressure cooker goes further: it traps the steam so tightly that the water inside gets hotter than 100 °C, so dal and rice cook much faster.
experiments.safety: Only the parent handles the stove and hot vessels. The child stands back and times from a safe distance. Lift lids away from your face.

activities.title: Home energy hunt
need: a notebook with three columns: 'Thing or work', 'What energy does it use?', 'Where does that come from?'
steps: Walk through every room, including the kitchen, bathroom and balcony.
For each thing that moves, heats, cools or lights up, write it in column 1.
In column 2, write the energy it uses: electricity, gas, petrol, food, sunlight, wind or battery.
In column 3, write where that energy comes from, if you know. Leave blanks you are unsure of.
Count how many used electricity, how many burnt a fuel and how many used sunlight or wind.
On Day 7, fill in the blanks with what you have learnt.
activities.outcome: A list of at least 12 uses of energy in your own home, showing your child that energy is behind almost everything a family does, and a starting point for the family's energy-saving pledge.

activities.title: Paper pinwheel wind test
need: a square of stiff paper about 15 cm
a pencil with an eraser or a straw
steps: Draw both diagonals on the square.
Cut along each diagonal from the corner about two-thirds of the way to the centre.
Bend every other point into the centre and hold them there.
The parent pushes the drawing pin through the points and the centre into the eraser or straw, loosely enough to spin.
Mark one blade with a coloured dot.
Count how many times the dot goes round in 10 seconds: still air, gentle blow, hard blow, walking, running, fan on low, fan on high.
activities.outcome: A working pinwheel and a table of results showing that stronger wind does more work, the same idea used by windmills and wind turbines.

activities.title: Box solar cooker (lesson page 160)
need: a shoebox or cardboard carton with a flap lid
clear plastic sheet, cling film or a glass pane (parent handles glass)
a stick to prop the lid
a small black or steel bowl
soaked poha, tomato slices, or a cube of butter or chocolate
steps: Stick black paper on the inside (and outside if you like) of the box.
Stick foil, smooth side out, on the inside of the lid flap to make a reflector.
Put the bowl of food inside the box.
Cover the open top of the box tightly with clear plastic, cling film or glass.
Prop the foil flap open with the stick so sunlight reflects off the foil, through the plastic, into the box.
Place it in strong sun around noon, turning it every 20 minutes to face the Sun. Check after an hour.
activities.outcome: A working solar cooker that heats or cooks food with no fuel, showing how black surfaces absorb heat, shiny surfaces reflect light, and a clear cover traps the heat.

voices.who: M. King Hubbert (1903–1989), USA, and the debate about when oil will run out
voices.idea: Hubbert, an American geologist working for an oil company, predicted in 1956 that oil production in the mainland USA would rise to a peak around 1970 and then fall, because oil fields run down as they are emptied. This idea became known as 'peak oil'.
voices.then: Many in the oil industry dismissed his prediction. But US production did peak around 1970 and fall for decades, and he became famous. Since then many others have predicted that world oil would run out or peak soon, much like the book's 'Do you know?' box saying oil and gas will finish in 30–35 years.
voices.now: From around 2010 new methods of drilling (fracking) pushed US oil output above its 1970 level, and new oil fields keep being found, so many earlier forecast dates have passed. Scientists agree that oil, gas and coal are limited and will not form again in human time, but when production will peak or run short is debated, because it depends on new discoveries, technology, prices and how fast the world switches to other energy.
voices.ask: A forecast said oil would run out by a certain year, and that year passed. Does that mean the forecast was useless, or that something changed? What would you need to know to make a better forecast?

voices.who: Augustin Mouchot (1825–1911), France
voices.idea: Mouchot, a French mathematics teacher, worried that France's coal would one day run out. From the 1860s he built solar machines with large curved mirrors that focused sunlight onto a boiler, making steam to run a small engine. At the 1878 World's Fair in Paris his large solar concentrator was shown working and won a gold medal; it was even used to run a small printing press.
voices.then: After the French government had his machines tested, it decided that coal, which had become cheaper and easier to transport, was more practical than solar power. His funding stopped and his inventions were largely forgotten.
voices.now: His central idea, that sunlight can be focused or captured to make useful power and could replace coal, is now accepted and used across the world in solar thermal plants and solar cookers, and solar panels are now among the cheapest ways to make electricity in many countries, including India.
voices.ask: Mouchot's machine worked, but coal won because it was cheaper. Is the 'best' energy source always the cheapest one? What else should we count?

voices.who: Eunice Newton Foote (1819–1888), USA
voices.idea: In 1856 Foote put thermometers in glass cylinders filled with different gases and placed them in sunlight. She found that the cylinder filled with carbon dioxide ('carbonic acid gas') got hotter than the one with ordinary air, and stayed hot longer. She suggested that more of this gas in the air would make the Earth warmer.
voices.then: Her paper was read at a scientific meeting in 1856 by a male scientist, Joseph Henry, and printed in a journal, but it got little attention. Three years later the Irish scientist John Tyndall published more detailed experiments on how gases absorb heat and became known as the pioneer of this science.
voices.now: Her work was rediscovered around 2010, and she is now recognised as one of the first people to show that carbon dioxide traps heat. Scientists today agree that burning coal, oil and gas has added carbon dioxide to the air and is warming the Earth, one reason why solar, wind and water power matter.
voices.ask: Foote did a simple test with jars in the sun. What would you need to add to her experiment to be sure the carbon dioxide, and not something else, made the jar hotter?

check.q: What is energy, and why do we need it even when sleeping?
check.a: Energy is the power to do work. While we sleep our heart, lungs and brain keep working and the body stays warm, which all need energy.

check.q: What is the difference between renewable and non-renewable sources? Give two examples of each.
check.a: Non-renewable sources get used up and cannot be replaced in our lifetime, like coal and petrol. Renewable sources keep coming back, like sunlight and wind (also flowing water and food).

check.q: Name the seven kinds of energy in the book.
check.a: Food energy, solar energy, wind energy, hydro energy, organic (biogas) energy, electrical energy and magnetic energy.

check.q: Why does a pinwheel spin faster when you run with it?
check.a: More air pushes on the blades, so the wind energy is greater and more work of spinning is done.

check.q: How is electricity made in a hydro power station?
check.a: Water stored behind a dam falls through pipes and spins turbines, which turn generators that make electricity.

check.q: What goes into a biogas plant and what comes out?
check.a: Animal dung, dead plants, dry leaves and crop waste go in; bacteria break them down without air and give a gas (mostly methane) for cooking and light, and the leftover is manure.

check.q: Give four ways to save energy at home.
check.a: Any four: switch off lights and fans when not needed, don't leave taps running, cover pots while cooking, use only as much water as needed, soak dal and rice before cooking, use a pressure cooker, use LED or CFL bulbs, take public transport.

c.covers: Planets of the solar system and Earth; planets vs satellites; phases of the Moon; natural and man-made satellites; latitude and longitude; time zones

p.title: Solar System and Earth
p.source: NIOS Open Basic Education, Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 11 (lesson pages 161–173)
p.summary: The Sun is a star with eight planets going round it, and our Earth spins on a tilted axis while it travels round the Sun. Your child models day and night, the phases of the Moon (and the Indian Shukla and Krishna Paksha), natural and artificial satellites, the lines of latitude and longitude, why India keeps one standard time, and why the tilt of the Earth (not its distance from the Sun) gives us long and short days and seasons. Along the way they meet Aryabhata, Galileo and the live argument about Pluto, and learn to spot two mistakes in the book's own revision page.
goals: By the end your child can name the eight planets in order from the Sun and explain what makes something a planet, a star or a satellite.
By the end your child can show with a torch and a ball how rotation gives day and night and how revolution makes a year of about 365¼ days.
By the end your child can explain why the Moon shows phases, name purnima and amavasya, and say what Shukla Paksha and Krishna Paksha are.
By the end your child can find the equator, the tropics, the polar circles and the prime meridian on a globe or map, and locate India by latitude and longitude.
By the end your child can explain why time is different in different places, and why India uses one Indian Standard Time based on 82½° East.

By the end your child can explain that seasons and long and short days are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis, and use the dates of perihelion and aphelion as evidence that distance from the Sun is not the cause.
words: a huge ball of very hot glowing gas that makes its own light and heat; the Sun is our nearest star
a large round body that travels round a star in its own path; the Sun has eight
the fixed path in which a planet moves round the Sun, or a satellite moves round a planet
a body that moves round a planet; the Moon is Earth's natural satellite, and man-made satellites are machines put into orbit
an imaginary line through the Earth from the North Pole to the South Pole, around which the Earth spins; it is tilted about 23½°
the spinning of the Earth on its axis; one full turn takes about 24 hours and gives us day and night
the movement of the Earth round the Sun; one full trip takes about 365 days and 6 hours, which is one year
the changing shapes of the lit part of the Moon that we see, from new moon (amavasya) to full moon (purnima) and back, in about 29½ days
imaginary circles running east–west round the Earth, measuring how far north or south a place is from the equator (0° to 90°)
imaginary half-circles running from the North Pole to the South Pole, measuring how far east or west a place is from Greenwich (0° to 180°)
the 0° line of latitude, halfway between the poles, which divides the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres
one clock time agreed for a whole country or region; Indian Standard Time is set by the sun time at 82½° East

days.title: Watching the sky
days.goal: Start from what we see in our own sky, learn how people in India studied it from ancient times, and begin a Moon diary that runs all lesson.

steps.title: What did you see in the sky?
steps.do: Ask your child: 'Where does the Sun rise from our home? Which window or which building?' (East.) 'Where does it set?' (West.) 'Did you see the Moon last night? What shape was it?' 'Is the Moon always the same shape?' (No.) 'Why do you think that is?' Let them guess freely and write their guesses in the notebook; do not correct them yet. Tell them: 'This week we will test every one of these guesses.'

steps.title: The opening of Lesson 11 (lesson page 161)
steps.do: Read the opening of Lesson 11 on lesson page 161 aloud. Ask: 'What did people in ancient times try to understand?' (The sky, Sun, Moon, stars, day and night, the waxing and waning Moon, seasons.) 'What did learned men in India make using the phases of the Moon?' (The Indian calendar and dates, called tithis.) Parent note: the book says horoscopes are made from the zodiac signs. Tell your child honestly: 'Watching the stars to make calendars and to track time is astronomy, a science, and it works. Using the stars to predict a person's future is astrology; when scientists have tested it carefully, it has not been shown to work.' Keep this calm and respectful; many families follow such traditions.

steps.title: Start the Moon diary
steps.do: Start Activity a1. Make a Moon diary page with 7 boxes, one per lesson day, each with space for the date, time, the Moon's shape (drawn and shaded) and where in the sky it was (above which building or tree). Check today's Moon phase on a wall calendar (panchang) or any calendar that shows purnima and amavasya, and write the tithi if you can. Tonight, or in the early morning if the Moon is up then, go out together and draw it. If clouds hide it, write 'cloudy' and look again tomorrow.

steps.title: How big is the Sun?
steps.do: Read the start of 11.1 on lesson page 162: 'The Sun is also a star... the star closest to the earth. This is why it looks bigger than other stars.' Then show the size difference. Put a peppercorn or a mustard seed (Earth) next to a large football or a big round watermelon, and explain: 'If the Earth were this tiny seed, the Sun would be about as wide as a person is tall. More than a million Earths could fit inside the Sun.' Then show why far things look small: your child holds a one-rupee coin at arm's length and covers your face with it from across the room. Ask: 'Is the coin bigger than my face? Why does it cover it?' (It is closer.) 'So why do stars look like dots?' (They are suns too, but very, very far away.)

steps.title: Never look at the Sun
steps.do: Explain an important safety rule: never look straight at the Sun, even with sunglasses, and never through binoculars or a camera lens, because it can permanently damage the eyes. Then make a safe Sun viewer: make a pinhole in a card, stand with your back to the Sun, and hold the card so sunlight passes through the hole onto a sheet of white paper held a little away. Your child sees a small bright circle: that is an image of the Sun. Ask: 'What shape is the Sun's image?' (Round.) Write 'The Sun is a star. It is our nearest star' in the notebook.

need: NIOS Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 11 (lesson pages 161–162)
a calendar or panchang showing purnima and amavasya
a peppercorn or mustard seed, a football or big watermelon
a card, a pin, a white sheet of paper

prep.task: Check on a calendar or online at what time the Moon is visible tonight or early tomorrow morning

days.title: The Sun's family of planets
days.goal: Learn the eight planets in order, build a walking scale model of the solar system, and weigh the argument over Pluto.

steps.title: 11.1 Our solar system and its planets (lesson pages 162–163)
steps.do: Read 11.1 on lesson page 162 aloud and look at the 'Solar System' picture. Ask: 'What are planets?' (Celestial bodies that go round the Sun.) 'How many does the Sun have?' (Eight.) Note: the book lists the planets ending 'Neptune and Uranus', but the correct order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune; Uranus is seventh and Neptune eighth. Teach a memory sentence: 'My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles.' Ask: 'Why is Earth the only planet with life, as far as we know?' (It has air and liquid water, and is not too hot or too cold.)

steps.title: Walk the solar system
steps.do: Do Activity a2 in a long corridor, terrace or park. Place a ball or a big round fruit as the Sun at one end. Your child walks heel-to-toe steps (about 25 cm each, call them 'paces') and drops a labelled paper chit at each planet: Mercury 1 pace, Venus 2, Earth 3, Mars 4½, Jupiter 15, Saturn 28, Uranus 57, Neptune 90 paces. If space runs out, stop at Saturn and point far away for Uranus and Neptune. At each planet, tell one fact: Mercury is closest and fastest; Venus is the hottest because of its thick cloudy air; Mars looks red because of rusty dust; Jupiter is the biggest; Saturn has bright rings. Ask at the end: 'What is between the planets?' (Mostly empty space.)

steps.title: Is Pluto a planet? A live argument
steps.do: Tell your child Voice v3: when you (the parent) were young, many books said there were nine planets, the ninth being Pluto. In 2006 astronomers voted that Pluto is a 'dwarf planet', and some scientists still disagree. Explain the three rules from the 2006 vote: a planet goes round the Sun, is big enough to be pulled into a round shape, and has cleared its path of other objects. Pluto passes the first two but not the third. Then ask the voice question and let your child argue a side.

steps.title: Let's see 11.1, first part (lesson page 163)
steps.do: Ask questions I and III of 'Let's see, what you have learnt 11.1' on lesson page 163 aloud: 'What are planets?' and 'Write the names of the eight planets.' Your child writes the eight names in the correct order using the memory sentence. Answers are on lesson page 173 (remember Uranus comes before Neptune).

steps.title: Moon diary
steps.do: Add today's box to the Moon diary (Activity a1): date, time, shape drawn and shaded, position in the sky. Ask: 'Is the lit part bigger or smaller than last time? Is it on the same side?'

need: a ball or big round fruit for the Sun
8 paper chits with planet names and a marker
a long corridor, terrace or park

days.title: Spinning Earth: day, night and the year
days.goal: Understand rotation and revolution with a torch and a ball, see why the Earth's tilt matters, and meet Aryabhata, who said the Earth spins.

steps.title: Earth, its poles, rotation and revolution (lesson page 162)
steps.do: Read the second half of lesson page 162 aloud, from 'Our earth is a planet of the sun' to the 365 days and 6 hours. Ask: 'What is rotation and how long does it take?' (Spinning on its axis; about 24 hours.) 'What is revolution and how long does it take?' (Going round the Sun; about 365 days and 6 hours.) Ask: 'What do we do with those extra 6 hours each year?' (Every 4 years they add up to about a day, so we add 29 February: a leap year.) Note: the book says the Earth is 'geoid/spherical'; geoid means almost a sphere but slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator.

steps.title: Torch, ball and a tiny India
steps.do: Do Experiment e1 in a darkened room. Push a knitting needle or long pencil through a ball (or use a globe) as the axis, and stick a small paper dot on it for India. Your child holds a torch steady as the Sun. You tilt the axis slightly and slowly spin the ball from west to east (anticlockwise when looked at from above the North Pole). Ask your child to call out 'sunrise', 'noon', 'sunset' and 'midnight' as the India dot moves. Ask them to predict first: 'Is it day everywhere at once?' Then ask: 'When India has noon, what does the other side of the ball have?' (Night.) Then walk the tilted ball slowly round the torch in a big circle to show revolution, keeping the axis pointing the same way all the time.

steps.title: Aryabhata: the Earth turns, not the sky
steps.do: Tell your child Voice v1: about 1,500 years ago in Kusumapura near Pataliputra (today's Patna), Aryabhata wrote that the Earth spins on its axis and that the stars only seem to move, like the trees seem to move backwards to a person in a moving boat. He also explained eclipses by the shadows of the Earth and Moon. Ask: 'When you sit in a moving train and look at the trees, what seems to move?' Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Shadow clock
steps.do: Stand a pencil upright in a lump of atta dough or clay on a sheet of paper in a sunny spot (balcony or terrace). Your child marks the tip of the shadow and writes the time. They will mark it again two more times today, an hour or more apart (ask them to set an alarm). Ask: 'Which way will the shadow move? Will it get longer or shorter towards noon?' Explain: 'The Sun seems to cross the sky because the Earth is turning. The shadow moves because we are moving.' Before sundials and clocks, people used shadows like this to tell time.

steps.title: Fill-ins and Moon diary
steps.do: Ask question II of 'Let's see 11.1' on lesson page 163 aloud (rotation, 24 hours, revolution, 365 days and 6 hours). Then add today's box to the Moon diary (Activity a1).

need: a ball (or globe) and a knitting needle or long pencil
a small paper dot for India
a pencil, atta dough or clay, a sheet of paper, a sunny spot

days.title: The Moon and other satellites
days.goal: Understand what a satellite is, model the phases of the Moon and the two pakshas, learn what man-made satellites do, and meet Galileo, who saw moons round another planet.

steps.title: 11.2 Planets and satellites, and the phases of the Moon (lesson pages 163–164)
steps.do: Read 11.2 and 11.2.1 on lesson pages 163–164 aloud and look at the 'Phases of the Moon' picture. Ask: 'What is the difference between a planet and a satellite?' (A planet goes round a star; a satellite goes round a planet.) 'Does the Moon make its own light?' (No, it reflects sunlight.) 'What is purnima? Amavasya?' (Full moon; new moon, when we cannot see it.) 'What are Shukla Paksha and Krishna Paksha?' (Shukla Paksha is the bright fortnight from amavasya to purnima, when the Moon grows; Krishna Paksha is the dark fortnight from purnima to amavasya, when it shrinks.) Ask: 'Which festivals fall on amavasya or purnima?' (Diwali on an amavasya; Holi, Raksha Bandhan and Guru Purnima on a purnima.)

steps.title: Phases with a lamp and a ball
steps.do: Do Experiment e2 in a dark room. Put a lamp without a shade (or a bright torch on a table) at one side of the room as the Sun. Your child is the Earth and holds a white ball or an orange on a pencil at arm's length, a little above their head, as the Moon. They turn slowly on the spot, anticlockwise, watching the ball. Ask them to predict first: 'Will the ball always look fully lit?' Stop at four places: ball towards the lamp (dark face, new moon), ball at the side (half lit), ball opposite the lamp behind your head (fully lit, full moon), ball at the other side (half lit on the other side). Ask: 'Did the ball's light ever change? What changed?' (Only how much of the lit half we could see.)

steps.title: 11.2.2 Natural and artificial satellites (lesson page 164)
steps.do: Read 11.2.2 on lesson page 164 aloud. Ask: 'What do artificial satellites do for us?' (Take pictures of the Earth for weather forecasts and forest fires, carry television and phone signals across the world, help maps and GPS find places.) Tell them: India's first satellite, named Aryabhata after the astronomer, went into orbit on 19 April 1975. ISRO, the Indian Space Research Organisation, now builds satellites for weather, TV and maps, and its Chandrayaan-3 mission landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023. Ask: 'When Dadi watches tomorrow's rain forecast on TV, which satellite work is helping her?'

steps.title: Galileo sees moons round Jupiter
steps.do: Tell your child Voice v2: in 1610 Galileo pointed his new telescope at Jupiter and saw four tiny 'stars' beside it that moved night after night. He worked out that they were going round Jupiter: moons of another planet. Ask: 'Why was that a big surprise for people who believed everything in the sky went round the Earth?' (It showed that not everything goes round the Earth.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Let's see 11.2 and Moon diary
steps.do: Ask 'Let's see, what you have learnt 11.2' on lesson pages 164–165 aloud: the four true-or-false statements and the three fill-in-the-blanks (artificial, information, 29½). Statement i is false: bodies that move round stars are planets, not satellites; statement iii is false: the bright full moon night is purnima, not amavasya. Then add today's box to the Moon diary (Activity a1) and ask: 'Are we in Shukla Paksha or Krishna Paksha now? How do you know?' (Growing Moon: Shukla; shrinking Moon: Krishna.)

need: a lamp without a shade or a bright torch
a white ball or an orange on a pencil

days.title: Lines on the globe
days.goal: Learn latitudes and longitudes, the equator, tropics, polar circles and the prime meridian, and use them to find India and other places.

steps.title: 11.3 Latitudinal and longitudinal lines (lesson pages 165–166)
steps.do: Read 11.3 and 11.3.1 on lesson pages 165–166 aloud and look at the 'Lines of Latitude and Longitude' picture. Ask: 'Why do we need imaginary lines on the Earth?' (About 196 countries and countless towns; the lines make a grid so any place can be found.) 'What is a globe? A map?' (A model of the Earth; a globe printed flat on paper.) Make the directions clear, because the book's wording can confuse: latitude lines run across from east to west, like the rungs of a ladder, and tell you how far north or south a place is. Longitude lines run from pole to pole and tell you how far east or west a place is. Note: the book says 180 latitudes; counting each whole degree, there are 90 north, 90 south and the equator itself.

steps.title: Draw the grid on an orange
steps.do: Do Activity a3. Take an orange (or a ball) and mark a dot at the top (North Pole) and bottom (South Pole). Your child draws with a marker: the equator round the middle; the Tropic of Cancer a little above (23½° N) and the Tropic of Capricorn a little below (23½° S); the Arctic Circle near the top (66½° N) and the Antarctic Circle near the bottom (66½° S). Then draw 6–8 longitude lines from pole to pole, like the segment lines inside a peeled orange (lesson page 166). Ask: 'Where are the longitude lines furthest apart? Where do they meet?' (Widest at the equator; they meet at the poles.) Colour the strip between the tropics and call it the hot belt.

steps.title: 11.3.2 Longitudes and the prime meridian (lesson page 166)
steps.do: Read 11.3.2 on lesson page 166 aloud. Ask: 'Where does the 0° longitude pass?' (Greenwich, in London, England.) 'How many longitudes are there?' (360: 180 east and 180 west of Greenwich.) 'What do the 0° and 180° longitudes together divide the Earth into?' (Eastern and Western Hemispheres.)

steps.title: Find India on the grid
steps.do: Open an atlas or a world map (or a map on the phone). Your child finds: the equator (it passes south of India, near Sri Lanka); the Tropic of Cancer (it passes through the middle of India, through states like Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram); the 0° line through England. Ask: 'Is India in the Northern or Southern Hemisphere? Eastern or Western?' (Northern and Eastern.) Find your own city on the map and read its latitude and longitude from the map edges or a phone map, and write them in the notebook: for example, Mumbai is about 19° N, 73° E; Kolkata about 22½° N, 88° E.

steps.title: Moon diary
steps.do: Add today's box to the Moon diary (Activity a1). Ask your child to compare all the boxes so far and say whether the Moon has been growing or shrinking, and roughly how many days until the next purnima or amavasya.

need: an orange or a ball and markers
an atlas, a world map or a phone map

days.title: Different times and long and short days
days.goal: Understand why clocks differ across the world and why India uses one standard time, and test why the Earth's tilt gives long and short days and seasons.

steps.title: 11.3.3 Different times at different places (lesson page 167)
steps.do: Read 11.3.3 on lesson page 167 aloud. Ask: 'How many minutes of time difference are there between two longitude lines one degree apart?' (4 minutes, because the Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so 1° in 4 minutes.) Work it out together for India: India stretches from about 68° E to 97° E, about 29°, so 29 × 4 = 116 minutes, nearly 2 hours. Ask: 'So does the Sun rise in Arunachal Pradesh before or after Gujarat?' (Almost 2 hours before.) Explain that India uses one clock time, Indian Standard Time, set by the 82½° E line, which passes near Prayagraj (Allahabad) and Mirzapur, so that trains, offices and TV all run on one time. It is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich time. Tell them some people in the North-East argue for a separate time zone because the Sun rises there so early.

steps.title: Call a cousin abroad
steps.do: Ask your child: 'If it is 8 pm in India, what time is it in London, which is 5½ hours behind?' (2:30 pm.) 'In Dubai, 1½ hours behind?' (6:30 pm.) If you have relatives or friends abroad, look up their city's time on the phone clock and work out together whether it is a good time to call them. Finish the shadow-clock idea from Day 3: ask why a clock-time agreement is needed at all when the Sun 'tells' time. (Because sun-time is different at each longitude; trains and planes need one shared time.)

steps.title: 11.4 Day and night becoming long and short (lesson pages 167–168)
steps.do: Read 11.4 on lesson pages 167–168 aloud and look at the picture. Ask: 'Why are days and nights not equal everywhere?' (The Earth's axis is tilted, so sunlight does not fall evenly.) 'What happens on 21 June?' (Sun's rays fall straight on the Tropic of Cancer; longest day and hottest time in the Northern Hemisphere.) 'On 22 December?' (Straight on the Tropic of Capricorn; shortest day in the north.) 'On 21 March and 23 September?' (Straight on the equator; day and night equal everywhere: the equinoxes.) 'Why is it always cold at the poles?' (Sun's rays fall slanting.)

steps.title: Straight rays and slanting rays
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. On a sheet of squared paper (or draw a grid of 1 cm squares), your child holds a torch straight down from 20 cm above and you trace the bright patch with a pencil. Then they tilt the torch at a slant from the same distance and you trace again. Ask them to predict first: 'Which patch will be brighter? Which will be bigger?' Count the squares in each patch. Ask: 'The same torch gives the same light. When it is spread over more squares, does each square get more or less?' (Less, so it heats less.) Explain that near the tropics in summer the Sun's rays fall nearly straight down and heat strongly; at the poles they slant and spread out, so it stays cold.

steps.title: Catch the book's mistake
steps.do: Read the four lines in 'Let's Revise' on lesson page 169 beginning 'When the Earth is close to the sun it is hot...'. Ask your child: 'The book says the Earth is closest to the Sun on 3 January and farthest on 4 July. In India, is January hot or cold? Is July colder than January?' (January is winter; it is not colder in July.) 'So can closeness to the Sun be what makes summer?' (No.) Explain: the Earth's distance from the Sun changes only a little through the year. Seasons are caused by the tilt, as section 11.4 says, which is why Australia has summer in December while we have winter. Praise your child for checking the evidence instead of just believing the page. Then add today's box to the Moon diary (Activity a1).

need: a phone clock showing world times
squared paper or a hand-drawn 1 cm grid
a torch, a pencil and a ruler

days.title: Let us revise, check and teach it back
days.goal: Review the whole lesson with the book's revision and exercises, finish the Moon diary, check understanding and have your child teach it back.

steps.title: Let's Revise with corrections (lesson pages 169–170)
steps.do: Read 'Let's Revise' on lesson pages 169–170 together. For each point your child says 'true' and names the model that showed it, or 'needs fixing'. Points to fix: the seasons line (tilt, not distance); the line saying horoscopes are made from Moon phases (calendars and tithis are; horoscopes are astrology, not science). Then finish the Moon diary (Activity a1): look at all the boxes and ask, 'What pattern do you see? Did the lit side switch sides?'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws1 (core) on their own; it covers the book's exercise ideas on lesson pages 170–172. Check it together. For any mistake, re-do the torch and ball model for 1 minute.

steps.title: Stretch and challenge worksheets
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 (stretch) and then Worksheet ws3 (challenge) section A together; keep ws3 section B for a quiet talk at dinner tonight. Let your child think aloud; you only ask 'How do you know?'. Note: the book's answer key on lesson pages 172–173 has some slips (for example it gives 'oval' for the Earth being tilted, and swaps latitude and longitude in Exercise I); trust the lesson text and your models.

steps.title: Lesson check
steps.do: Ask the 8 check questions aloud one at a time without the book. Tick each answer given well. For a missed one, use the matching model again for one minute (planet walk, torch and ball, lamp and Moon ball, orange grid, torch on squares) and ask again in other words. Six or more right is good; fewer than five means repeat Days 3 and 4 next week.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the teacher and the family are the students. In 5–7 minutes, using the ball and torch, the Moon ball, the orange grid and the Moon diary, they explain: the Sun and its eight planets; rotation (day and night) and revolution (the year); why the Moon has phases and what the two pakshas are; latitude, longitude and Indian Standard Time; and why the tilt causes seasons. The 'students' ask: 'Is it the Earth's shadow that makes the Moon's phases?' (No; that is an eclipse. Phases are how much of the lit half we see.) and 'Why don't we feel the Earth spinning?' (We move along with it smoothly, like in a smooth train.)

need: ball, torch, Moon ball, orange grid and Moon diary from the week

sections.p: The Sun is a ____.
Celestial bodies that go around the Sun are called ____.
Write the eight planets in order from the Sun.
Why is the Earth the only known planet with life?
opts: It has air and liquid water and is not too hot or cold
It is closest to the Sun

sections.p: Match.
pairs: Spinning on its axis in about 24 hours
Going round the Sun in about 365 days 6 hours
The fixed path round the Sun
Imaginary line from North Pole to South Pole

sections.p: Day and night happen because the Earth ____ on its axis.
The full moon night is called ____.
The fortnight from amavasya to purnima, when the Moon grows, is called ____ Paksha.
The Moon shines because:
opts: It reflects light from the Sun

sections.p: Sort these.
Match each line to where it is.
Which line passes through the middle of India?
Draw a globe. Mark the poles, the equator, both tropics and two longitude lines. Mark roughly where India is.
The Earth turns 1° of longitude in ____ minutes.
Two towns are 10° of longitude apart. How different is their sun time? Show your working.
Itanagar is far east of Ahmedabad. Why does the Sun rise much earlier there, though both clocks show the same Indian Standard Time?
On 21 June, which has the longest day?
The Earth is closest to the Sun on about 3 January, yet that is winter in India. Use this to explain what really causes seasons.
What if the Earth's axis were not tilted at all? What would happen to seasons and to the length of days?
A friend says the Moon's phases are the Earth's shadow falling on it. How would you use the lamp-and-ball model to show them why that is wrong?
In Australia, which month is usually hottest?
Aryabhata said the Earth spins, but even some later Indian astronomers like Brahmagupta disagreed. Why is it hard to believe the Earth moves when it feels still?
Galileo's moons of Jupiter changed people's minds. Why does seeing something with your own eyes (or a telescope) count as strong evidence?
Should Pluto be called a planet? Give one reason for and one against, then your own decision.

experiments.title: Torch, ball and a tiny India
experiments.question: How does the spinning of the Earth make day and night, and its trip round the Sun make a year?
need: a knitting needle or long pencil pushed through it as the axis
a small paper dot for India
steps: Stick the India dot on the ball a little above the middle.
Your child holds the torch steady and shines it at the ball from about 1 metre away.
Tilt the axis slightly and spin the ball slowly from west to east (anticlockwise seen from above the North Pole).
Your child calls out 'sunrise' when India enters the light, 'noon' when it faces the torch, 'sunset' when it leaves the light and 'midnight' when it is furthest in the dark.
Now carry the tilted ball slowly round the torch in a big circle, keeping the axis pointing the same way, to show one year.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: is it day everywhere on the Earth at the same time? When India has noon, what does the far side have?
experiments.observe: Half the ball is always lit and half dark. Each place passes from light to dark as the ball spins. During the walk round the torch, the North Pole half leans towards the torch at one side of the circle and away at the other.
experiments.why: The Sun lights only the half of the Earth facing it. As the Earth rotates once in about 24 hours, each place is carried into the light (day) and then into the dark (night). The Sun looks as if it rises in the east and sets in the west because the Earth spins from west to east. While spinning, the Earth also revolves round the Sun once in about 365¼ days. Because the axis stays tilted the same way in space, the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun for half the year (summer, long days) and away for the other half (winter, short days).
experiments.safety: Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes. Take care with the knitting needle point.

experiments.title: Moon phases with a lamp and a ball
experiments.question: Why does the Moon look a different shape on different nights?
need: a lamp without a shade or a bright torch on a table
a white ball or an orange stuck on a pencil
steps: Put the lamp at one side of the room at about head height.
Your child stands a few steps away, holding the ball on the pencil at arm's length, slightly above the head.
They turn slowly on the spot anticlockwise, keeping the ball in front of the face.
Stop and look at four positions: ball towards the lamp, ball to the side, ball opposite the lamp, ball to the other side.
Draw the shape of the lit part seen at each position.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: will the ball always look fully lit? Will the lit part ever disappear?
experiments.observe: Towards the lamp, the side you see is dark (new moon). At the sides, half is lit (half moon, on opposite sides each time). Opposite the lamp, the whole face is lit (full moon). In between you see thin crescents and fat 'gibbous' shapes.
experiments.why: The Moon has no light of its own. The Sun always lights the half of the Moon facing it. As the Moon goes round the Earth, about once every 29½ days from one full moon to the next, we see different amounts of that lit half. When the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, the lit half faces away from us: amavasya. When the Earth is between, we see the whole lit half: purnima. The Indian lunar calendar counts the tithis of the bright fortnight (Shukla Paksha) and the dark fortnight (Krishna Paksha) from these phases. The Earth's shadow does not cause the phases; it falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse.
experiments.safety: Do not look straight into the bulb. Keep the lamp cord out of the way while turning.

experiments.title: Straight rays and slanting rays
experiments.question: Why do places where sunlight falls at a slant stay cooler?
need: squared paper or a hand-drawn grid of 1 cm squares
steps: Lay the squared paper flat on a table in a slightly dark room.
Your child holds the torch straight down, 20 cm above the paper.
The parent traces round the bright patch.
Keeping the torch 20 cm away, tilt it to a steep slant and trace the patch again.
Count the squares inside each patch and compare how bright each looked.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which patch will be bigger, and which will look brighter?
experiments.observe: The straight-down patch is small, round and bright. The slanting patch is a stretched oval, covers many more squares and looks dimmer.
experiments.why: The torch gives the same amount of light both times. Straight down, it is packed into a few squares, so each square gets a lot of light and heat. At a slant, the same light is spread over many more squares, so each gets less. The Sun works the same way. Because the Earth's axis is tilted, the half of the Earth leaning towards the Sun gets more direct rays and longer days, so it has summer. The poles always get slanting rays, so they stay cold. This is why seasons are caused by the tilt, not by the small change in the Earth's distance from the Sun.
experiments.safety: Do not shine the torch into eyes.

activities.title: Moon diary
need: a calendar or panchang showing purnima and amavasya
steps: Draw 7 boxes, one for each lesson day, with space for date, time, shape and position.
Each evening (or early morning, if the Moon is up then), go out with your child and find the Moon.
Draw its shape and shade the dark part.
Note where it is: above which building or tree, and how high.
Write the tithi from the calendar if you can, and whether it is Shukla Paksha or Krishna Paksha.
At the end, look at all the boxes together and describe the pattern.
activities.outcome: A week of real Moon observations that shows the Moon growing or shrinking and the lit side, matched to the Indian calendar; your child sees the phases with their own eyes instead of only reading about them.

activities.title: Walk the solar system
need: a ball or big round fruit for the Sun
8 paper chits labelled with the planets
a long corridor, terrace or park
steps: Place the Sun at one end.
Use heel-to-toe steps (about 25 cm) as 'paces'.
Drop the chits at: Mercury 1 pace, Venus 2, Earth 3, Mars 4½, Jupiter 15, Saturn 28, Uranus 57, Neptune 90.
At each planet, say one true fact about it.
Stand at Earth and look back at the Sun and forward to Neptune.
Talk about how much empty space there is between the planets.
activities.outcome: A walking model that shows the planets in the correct order and how the outer planets are much further apart than the inner ones.

activities.title: Grid on an orange
steps: Mark the North Pole at the top and the South Pole at the bottom.
Draw the equator round the middle in one colour.
Draw the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn a little above and below it.
Draw the Arctic and Antarctic Circles near the poles.
Draw 6–8 longitude lines from pole to pole in another colour, one of them marked 0° (Greenwich).
Colour the strip between the tropics as the hot belt and mark roughly where India is.
activities.outcome: A hand-made globe that shows how latitude lines run round the Earth and longitude lines meet at the poles, and where India sits on the grid.

voices.who: Aryabhata (476–about 550 CE), India
voices.idea: In his book the Aryabhatiya, written in 499 CE in Kusumapura (near Pataliputra, today's Patna), Aryabhata stated that the Earth spins on its axis, and that the stars only seem to move westward, just as a person in a boat moving forward sees the trees on the bank seem to move backward. He explained lunar and solar eclipses by the shadows of the Earth and the Moon, not by demons, and gave the length of the year very accurately.
voices.then: Several later Indian astronomers, including Varahamihira and Brahmagupta, did not accept that the Earth rotates, and some commentators even changed his words to say the opposite. His eclipse explanations and calculations, however, were widely used.
voices.now: His view that the Earth rotates is correct and is accepted by all scientists. India named its first satellite, launched in 1975, Aryabhata in his honour.
voices.ask: Aryabhata could not see the Earth spin from space. What everyday evidence could make you believe the Earth turns, even though it feels perfectly still?

voices.who: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), Italy
voices.idea: In January 1610 Galileo looked at Jupiter through a telescope he had improved himself and saw four small points of light next to it that changed position night after night. He concluded they were moons going round Jupiter. He also saw that Venus shows phases like our Moon. He argued this supported Copernicus's idea that the planets, including the Earth, go round the Sun.
voices.then: Many scholars of his time held that everything in the heavens went round the Earth, and some refused even to look through his telescope. The Church authorities put him on trial in 1633, forced him to take back his views, and kept him under house arrest for the rest of his life.
voices.now: His observations are fully accepted. The four moons he found, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, are called the Galilean moons, and scientists now know Jupiter has dozens of moons. The Sun-centred solar system is the basis of all space travel, including ISRO's missions.
voices.ask: Some people would not look through Galileo's telescope. If someone refuses to look at the evidence, can they still be right? What would you have said to them?

voices.who: The Pluto debate: the International Astronomical Union vote (2006) and critics such as Alan Stern
voices.idea: Pluto was discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh and called the ninth planet. From the 1990s astronomers found many similar icy bodies beyond Neptune, one (Eris, found in 2005) about as big as Pluto. In August 2006 the International Astronomical Union voted that a planet must orbit the Sun, be round from its own gravity, and have cleared its orbit of other objects. Pluto fails the third rule, so it was renamed a 'dwarf planet', leaving eight planets, as in the book.
voices.then: The vote was close and only a few hundred of the thousands of astronomers in the union took part. Alan Stern, who later led NASA's New Horizons mission that flew past Pluto in 2015, and others objected that the 'cleared its orbit' rule is unclear and that Pluto, with mountains, glaciers and moons, behaves like a planet.
voices.now: The official list has eight planets and most textbooks use it.
