But some planetary scientists still argue for a definition based only on whether a body is round, which would make Pluto and many moons 'planets'. The facts about Pluto are not in doubt; how to name and group it is still debated.
voices.ask: Pluto did not change in 2006; only the definition did. Is this argument about evidence or about words? Does it matter what we call it?

check.q: What is the difference between a star, a planet and a satellite?
check.a: A star, like the Sun, makes its own light and heat. A planet goes round a star. A satellite goes round a planet, like the Moon round the Earth.

check.q: Name the eight planets in order from the Sun.
check.a: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

check.q: What are rotation and revolution, and how long does each take?
check.a: Rotation is the Earth spinning on its axis, in about 24 hours, giving day and night. Revolution is the Earth going round the Sun, in about 365 days and 6 hours, giving a year.

check.q: Why does the Moon show phases?
check.a: The Sun lights half of the Moon. As the Moon goes round the Earth we see different amounts of the lit half, from none (amavasya) to all (purnima), in about 29½ days.

check.q: What are Shukla Paksha and Krishna Paksha?
check.a: Shukla Paksha is the bright fortnight from new moon to full moon, when the Moon grows; Krishna Paksha is the dark fortnight from full moon to new moon, when it shrinks.

check.q: Name two uses of artificial satellites.
check.a: Any two: weather forecasting, spotting forest fires, carrying TV and phone signals, GPS and maps, studying the Moon and planets.

check.q: Why is time different in different places, and what is Indian Standard Time based on?
check.a: As the Earth turns, the Sun reaches each longitude at a different time, 4 minutes later per degree. India uses one time, set by the 82½° East longitude near Prayagraj (Allahabad).

check.q: What causes the seasons and long and short days?
check.a: The tilt of the Earth's axis: the half leaning towards the Sun gets straighter rays and longer days. It is not the distance from the Sun; the Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.

c.covers: Deficiency diseases and how to prevent them; when to take extra care with food; cheap nutritious foods; storing food

p.title: Food and Health
p.source: NIOS Open Basic Education, Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 12 (lesson pages 174–187)
p.summary: Food gives us energy, helps us grow and protects us from disease through its nutrients, and when a nutrient is missing for a long time the body shows it. Your child learns the deficiency diseases in the book (anaemia, kwashiorkor, marasmus, night blindness, rickets, goitre and beriberi), how to prevent them with ordinary Indian foods and iodised salt, who needs extra care with food, how to make cheap meals more nutritious, and eight ways of storing food so fungus and bacteria cannot spoil it. Mould and drying experiments make the storage science visible, and stories of the doctors who solved beriberi, kwashiorkor and goitre show how this knowledge was won.
goals: By the end your child can name the main nutrients (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals) and the job of each.
By the end your child can match each deficiency disease in the lesson to the missing nutrient, describe one or two signs, and name Indian foods that prevent it.
By the end your child can explain why iodised salt, sunlight, green leafy vegetables and iron-rich foods matter, and why vitamin pills and iron tablets are taken only on a doctor's advice.
By the end your child can say who needs special attention to food (babies, growing children, teenagers, pregnant and breastfeeding mothers, sick people) and why.
By the end your child can suggest at least six ways to make cheap food more nutritious, such as mixing cereals and pulses, sprouting, cooking in less water and using iron kadhais.
By the end your child can explain how drying, cooling, salting, sugaring, oil and spices, cooking, freezing, canning and fermenting stop fungus and bacteria, using our own mould test as evidence.
words: a substance in food that the body needs to work, grow and stay healthy: carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals (and water and fibre)
not having enough of something; a deficiency disease happens when the body lacks a nutrient for a long time
a condition in which the blood has too little haemoglobin, the iron-containing part of red blood cells that carries oxygen; it makes a person pale, weak and tired
poor health from not getting the right food: too little food, too little of a nutrient, or the wrong balance
a serious kind of malnutrition in young children, with swelling of the face, feet and legs, linked to a diet very low in protein and other nutrients
a serious kind of malnutrition from too little food of every kind, in which the child becomes extremely thin; the book calls it 'dry malnutrition'
not being able to see well in dim light, the first sign of too little vitamin A
a disease in which a child's bones become soft and bend, caused by too little vitamin D (made by the skin in sunlight) and calcium
a swelling in the front of the neck from the thyroid gland growing bigger, usually because of too little iodine in food
ordinary salt with a small amount of iodine added, so that everyone gets enough iodine
a disease caused by too little vitamin B1 (thiamine), which harms nerves and the heart, causing weakness, numbness and pain in the legs; common where people ate mainly polished white rice
a process in which helpful microbes such as yeast and bacteria change food, as when milk becomes curd or rice and urad batter rises for idli

days.title: What is in our food?
days.goal: Start from our own meals, learn the main nutrients and their jobs, and set up a mould test that we will watch all week.

steps.title: Why do we eat?
steps.do: Ask your child: 'Why do we eat? Give me three reasons.' Listen for: 'because we are hungry', 'for energy to play', 'to grow taller', 'to stay strong and not fall sick'. Then ask: 'If someone ate only white rice every day for a year, what might go wrong?' Let them guess. Tell them: 'This week we find out what each food gives us, what happens when something is missing, and how to keep food from spoiling.'

steps.title: Opening and 12.1 nutrients (lesson pages 174–175)
steps.do: Read the opening of Lesson 12 on lesson page 174 and the start of 12.1 on lesson pages 174–175 aloud. Ask: 'What three jobs does food do?' (Helps the body develop, gives strength for work, protects from disease.) 'Which nutrients give strength or energy?' (Carbohydrates and fats.) 'Which help us grow?' (Proteins.) 'Which protect us from disease?' (Vitamins and mineral salts.) Add: water and fibre are needed too; fibre in whole grains, vegetables and fruit keeps the gut working well.

steps.title: Kitchen nutrient sort
steps.do: Put out small bowls or packets of: rice, atta, potato, sugar or jaggery, ghee or oil, groundnuts, dal, an egg or paneer, milk, spinach or methi, a carrot, an orange or guava, a banana, salt. Make three labels on paper: 'Energy food (carbohydrates and fats)', 'Body-building food (proteins)', 'Protective food (vitamins and minerals)'. Your child places each food under the label for its main nutrient. Good sort: rice, atta, potato, sugar, ghee and oil are energy; dal, egg, paneer, milk, groundnuts are body-building; spinach, carrot, orange, guava, banana are protective. Point out that many foods belong to more than one group (milk has protein, fat and calcium; groundnuts have fat and protein).

steps.title: Set up the mould test
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Take four equal pieces of bread or a leftover roti torn in four. Piece 1: leave it dry on an open plate. Pieces 2, 3 and 4: sprinkle each with a few drops of water and put each in its own small zip-bag or closed steel dabba. Rub a thick layer of salt all over piece 4 before closing. Keep pieces 1, 2 and 4 on the kitchen shelf and piece 3 in the fridge. Label everything with the date. Ask your child to predict which pieces will grow mould and which will stay fresh, and write the guesses in the notebook. Ask: 'Why do we use the same bread for all four?' (So that only one thing changes in each, which makes it fair.)

steps.title: What was on my plate today?
steps.do: Your child draws today's lunch or dinner thali in the notebook and labels each item energy, body-building or protective. Ask: 'Did our plate have all three? What could we add?' Good answers: 'a bowl of dal for protein', 'a slice of guava or a raw salad for vitamins'.

need: NIOS Environmental Studies Level B, Lesson 12 (lesson pages 174–175)
small amounts of rice, atta, potato, sugar or jaggery, oil or ghee, groundnuts, dal, egg or paneer, milk, spinach or methi, carrot, orange or guava, banana, salt
3 zip-bags or small dabbas, a plate, salt, water

days.title: Iron, protein and serious malnutrition
days.goal: Learn about anaemia and how iron-rich food prevents it, understand kwashiorkor and marasmus with care and compassion, and start sprouting moong.

steps.title: 12.1.1 Anaemia (lesson page 175)
steps.do: Read 12.1.1 on lesson page 175 aloud. Explain properly: red blood cells carry oxygen to every part of the body using haemoglobin, which needs iron. With too little iron, less oxygen reaches the body, so a person feels weak and tired and looks pale. Ask: 'What are some signs?' (Pale skin, pale gums, pale inside of the eyelids, pale nails, tiredness; when severe, fast heartbeat, breathlessness and swelling.) Note for you: the book says 'yellowness in the eyes', but in anaemia the inner eyelid looks pale, not yellow; yellow eyes are a sign of jaundice, a liver problem. Ask: 'Which foods prevent anaemia?' (Bajra, ragi, jaggery, green leafy vegetables like spinach, dals, meat, fish, chicken and eggs.)

steps.title: Pink check and iron hunt
steps.do: In daylight, both of you gently pull down the lower eyelid in a mirror and look at the inside: healthy is pink or red. Press a fingernail for 2 seconds and watch it turn white and then pink again. Explain: 'Pink means blood is flowing with plenty of red cells. A doctor uses a blood test to know for sure; we cannot diagnose anaemia at home.' Then hunt in the kitchen for iron foods from the book: ragi, bajra, jaggery, spinach, chana, rajma, eggs. Tell them a useful trick: eating vitamin C foods like lemon, amla or guava with iron foods helps the body take in the iron, while tea with meals reduces it.

steps.title: Kwashiorkor and 'dry malnutrition' (lesson pages 175–176)
steps.do: Parent note: these pages describe very sick children and have pictures. Talk calmly; stress that these illnesses are preventable and treatable, that they happen because of poverty and lack of food, not because of anything a child did, and that we never tease anyone for being thin or small. Read 12.1.2 and 12.1.3 aloud. Kwashiorkor: swollen face, hands and feet, growth stops, skin and hair lose colour, thin upper arms. It is linked to too little protein and other nutrients. Treatment: extra dals, peas, soya, nuts, green leafy vegetables, milk, paneer, eggs, meat and fish, meals at least three times a day with snacks. Correct the book: the second disease, which the book calls 'Rickets (Dry Malnutrition)', is really called marasmus. It comes from too little food of every kind, and the child becomes extremely thin. Real rickets, a bone disease, comes on Day 3.

steps.title: Cicely Williams names kwashiorkor
steps.do: Tell your child Voice v2: in the 1930s a woman doctor working in the Gold Coast (now Ghana) in West Africa noticed swollen, sick young children, often just after a new baby had arrived and they had stopped breastfeeding. She used the local Ga word 'kwashiorkor' for the illness and showed that it came from diet. Scientists still argue today about exactly why some starving children swell and others become thin. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Start the sprouts
steps.do: Start Activity a1. Your child washes 1 cup of whole green moong (and, if you have it, a handful of whole chana) in three changes of water, picks out any stones, and soaks it in plenty of clean water in a steel bowl overnight. Read the line on lesson page 179: 'If these are germinated, then the amount of protein and vitamins will further increase.' Explain: 'When a seed sprouts, it starts using its stored food and making new vitamins, especially vitamin C, and becomes easier to digest.' Plan: tomorrow morning drain it, wrap it in a damp clean muslin cloth or keep it in a closed sprout-maker, and rinse once or twice a day.

need: ragi, bajra, jaggery, spinach, chana, rajma or eggs from the kitchen
1 cup whole green moong, a handful of whole chana (optional)
a steel bowl, clean water, a clean muslin cloth

days.title: Vitamins A and D, sunlight and iodine
days.goal: Learn about night blindness, rickets, other vitamin-linked problems and goitre, find vitamin A foods by colour, check our salt for iodine, and meet the doctor whose village study helped iodise India's salt.

steps.title: 12.1.4 Night blindness and 12.1.5 Rickets (lesson pages 176–177)
steps.do: Read 12.1.4 and 12.1.5 on lesson pages 176–177 aloud. Ask: 'What is the first sign of too little vitamin A?' (Not seeing well in dim light or at night; later the eyes become dry, and without treatment a child can go blind.) 'Which foods have vitamin A?' (Green leafy vegetables, yellow and orange fruits and vegetables such as carrot, pumpkin, papaya and mango, milk, eggs, liver.) Read the caution aloud: too much vitamin A is harmful, so capsules are given only on a doctor's advice; in India health workers give children vitamin A doses through a government programme. For rickets ask: 'What does the body need for strong bones?' (Calcium from milk, curd, ragi, sesame, and vitamin D, which our skin makes in sunlight.) Read the next lines about cracked lips, mouth corners and bleeding gums: tell them bleeding gums can come from too little vitamin C (scurvy), found in amla, guava, lemon and oranges.

steps.title: Colour plate hunt
steps.do: Lay out whatever you have: carrot, pumpkin, papaya, mango, tomato, spinach, methi, drumstick leaves (moringa), amla, guava, lemon, milk, ragi, an egg. Your child sorts them into four groups: 'Vitamin A (eyes)', 'Vitamin C (gums and healing)', 'Calcium (bones)', 'More than one'. Good sort: carrot, pumpkin, papaya, mango and spinach for vitamin A; amla, guava and lemon for vitamin C; milk and ragi for calcium; drumstick leaves and spinach fit in more than one (vitamin A, iron and calcium). Ask: 'Which of these can we grow or buy cheaply in season?'

steps.title: 12.1.6 Goitre and 12.1.7 iodine in pregnancy (lesson page 177)
steps.do: Read 12.1.6 and 12.1.7 on lesson page 177 aloud. Explain: the thyroid is a small gland in the front of the neck that makes a hormone controlling how the body uses energy and how a baby's brain grows. It needs iodine to do this. Too little iodine makes the thyroid swell into a goitre. If a pregnant mother lacks iodine, her baby's brain and body may not develop fully, so the baby may have learning difficulties, short height or deafness. Ask: 'Why is it more common in hilly areas?' (Rain and melting snow over thousands of years washed iodine out of the hill soils, so food grown there has little.) 'What is the simple prevention?' (Using iodised salt.)

steps.title: Read the salt packet
steps.do: Bring the salt packet from the kitchen. Your child finds the word 'iodised' and the small sign showing a smiling sun or the words 'iodised salt'. Ask: 'Why is iodine put into salt and not into, say, mangoes?' Good answer: 'Everyone, rich or poor, eats a little salt every day, all year, so adding iodine to salt reaches everyone.' Add: keep salt in a closed container away from heat and damp, because iodine slowly escapes from open, damp salt; and add salt near the end of cooking where you can. We still need only a little salt, not a lot.

steps.title: V. Ramalingaswami and the Kangra valley salt
steps.do: Tell your child Voice v3: in the 1950s Indian doctors led by V. Ramalingaswami tested iodised salt in the Kangra valley of Himachal Pradesh, where many people had goitre. Over the years goitre went down in the villages that got iodised salt but not in the villages that got ordinary salt. Ask: 'Why did the doctors need villages that got ordinary salt too?' (To compare; otherwise they could not be sure the iodine made the difference.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Check the mould test and sprouts
steps.do: Look at the four bread pieces from Experiment e1 without opening the bags. Ask your child to draw each and note any fuzzy spots, colour or smell. Then drain the soaked moong from Activity a1, wrap it in a damp muslin cloth, and keep it in a warm place; rinse it again in the evening.

need: carrot, pumpkin, papaya, mango, tomato, spinach, drumstick leaves, amla, guava, lemon, milk, ragi, egg (whatever you have)
the soaked moong and a muslin cloth

days.title: Polished rice and the vitamin B puzzle
days.goal: Learn about beriberi and vitamin B, compare polished and unpolished rice, hear how doctors found that something was missing from white rice, and check what we have learnt so far.

steps.title: 12.1.8 Beriberi (lesson page 177)
steps.do: Read 12.1.8 on lesson page 177 aloud. Explain more exactly: beriberi is caused by too little vitamin B1 (thiamine). It damages nerves and the heart, causing weakness, numbness and pain in the legs, loss of appetite and, in some people, swelling and heart trouble. The cracked corners of the mouth and red, sore tongue that the book also lists are signs of too little of other B vitamins, such as B2 (riboflavin). Ask: 'Where is vitamin B1 found?' (In the outer layers and germ of grains, in whole wheat atta, unpolished or parboiled rice, dals, groundnuts, eggs and meat.)

steps.title: Polished and unpolished rice side by side
steps.do: Put a spoon of ordinary white (polished) rice beside a spoon of brown, red, unpolished or hand-pounded rice (or parboiled rice) on a white plate. Your child looks with a magnifying glass. Ask: 'What is different?' (The unpolished grain has a brownish or reddish skin, the bran, and sometimes a small bump at one end, the germ.) Explain: 'Polishing rubs off the bran and germ to make rice white and soft. But most of the vitamin B1, fibre and some minerals are in those outer parts.' Also compare maida with whole wheat atta, and read the line on lesson page 179: 'Unpolished rice and wheat bran flour contain more vitamins.'

steps.title: Takaki, Eijkman and the white-rice chickens
steps.do: Tell your child Voice v1: in the 1880s many Japanese navy sailors got beriberi. A navy doctor, Kanehiro Takaki, changed their diet to include barley, meat and vegetables, and beriberi nearly disappeared. A few years later in Java, Christiaan Eijkman noticed that chickens fed leftover polished white rice got a beriberi-like illness, and got better on unpolished rice. Ask: 'At first many doctors thought beriberi was caused by a germ. How did these results point to something missing in food instead?' Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Let's see 12.1, with a corrected answer key (lesson page 178)
steps.do: Ask the four questions in 'Let's see, what you have learnt 12.1' on lesson page 178 aloud. For the matching question, the correct pairs are: kwashiorkor with deficiency of protein; rickets with no sunlight on the body; beriberi with deficiency of vitamin B; night blindness with deficiency of vitamin A. Tell your child that the book's answer key on lesson page 186 mixes up the beriberi and night blindness answers, and praise them if they noticed. Goitre and 'mental slowness' (from iodine lack in pregnancy) are the two iodine diseases.

steps.title: Core worksheet: nutrients and deficiency diseases
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws1 (core) on their own. Then check together; for any wrong answer, find the matching part on lesson pages 175–177 and read it again.

steps.title: Mould test check
steps.do: Check Experiment e1 again without opening the bags. Ask: 'Which piece has the most mould? Which has none? Is that what you guessed?' Draw them. Rinse the sprouting moong from Activity a1 and look at the little white tails. Ask: 'How long are they now?'

need: a spoon each of polished white rice and brown, red, unpolished or parboiled rice
a little maida and whole wheat atta
a white plate and a magnifying glass

prep.task: Buy or borrow a small amount of brown, red or unpolished rice if you do not have any

days.title: Who needs extra care, and cheap nutritious food
days.goal: Learn who needs special attention to food and why, learn the book's tricks for making cheap food nutritious, and cook a sprouts chaat and a mixed khichdi plan together.

steps.title: 12.2 When should more attention be paid to food? (lesson pages 178–179)
steps.do: Read 12.2 on lesson pages 178–179 aloud. Ask: 'Why do babies over six months need more than milk?' (They are growing fast and need extra energy, protein and iron; soft foods like rice-dal khichdi, mashed vegetables and fruit are started alongside breast milk.) 'Why do teenagers need extra care?' (Their bodies grow very fast.) Parent note: the book says that when girls start their monthly periods (menstruation), they need more iron-rich food. Say simply and calmly: 'When girls grow up, their body has a monthly cycle in which a little blood leaves the body, so they need extra iron to make new blood.' Answer any questions honestly and briefly. Also ask: 'Why should a pregnant or breastfeeding mother eat well?' (The baby gets everything from her food; she needs extra calcium and iron.) 'Why do sick people need good food?' (A weak body catches other illnesses more easily.)

steps.title: Food for the whole family (Let's see 12.2, lesson page 180)
steps.do: Do question I of 'Let's see, what you have learnt 12.2' on lesson page 180: match the family members in the pictures to their food needs (baby and children: milk and protein; teenage girl: more iron; pregnant woman: balanced food with calcium and iron; sick person: food that gives strength and protects). Then do question II aloud: mother's milk is complete food for a baby (true); unpolished rice has fewer vitamins (false: it has more); wash vegetables before cutting (true); jaggery has more iron than sugar (true, although it is still only a small amount, so it does not replace greens and dals).

steps.title: 12.2.1 Inexpensive nutritious food (lesson pages 179–180)
steps.do: Read 12.2.1 on lesson pages 179–180 aloud. After each tip, ask your child 'Why does this help?' Key reasons: mixing cereals and pulses gives a more complete protein; sprouting adds vitamins; vitamins B and C dissolve in water and are destroyed by long heat, so cook in less water, do not throw away the cooking water, and do not overcook; washing after cutting washes vitamins away; seasonal food is cheaper and fresher; whole dals keep their skin with fibre and vitamins; an iron kadhai adds some iron to food. Explain the 'lime' line: it means chuna (slaked lime), not lemon; soaking maize in it, as people in Mexico have done for thousands of years, frees a B vitamin called niacin. Do not try it at home without an adult who knows how; chuna burns skin and eyes.

steps.title: Sprouts chaat and a mixed khichdi plan
steps.do: Do Activity a2 using the sprouts from Activity a1. Your child washes the sprouted moong and puts it in a bowl. You chop half an onion, a tomato and a cucumber (washed before cutting, as the book says); your child adds them, squeezes half a lemon over it, and adds a pinch of iodised salt, roasted jeera powder and chopped coriander. While eating, ask: 'Which nutrients are in this bowl?' (Protein from moong, vitamin C from lemon, tomato and sprouts, fibre from everything, iron from moong helped by the lemon.) Then plan tomorrow's khichdi: your child chooses two cereals (rice, broken wheat dalia, bajra or millet) and two pulses (moong, masoor, toor) and two vegetables, and writes the recipe card.

steps.title: Mould test check
steps.do: Check Experiment e1 again and draw the four pieces. Ask: 'Which condition is the mould's favourite? Damp and warm, cold, dry or salty?'

need: onion, tomato, cucumber, lemon, iodised salt, roasted jeera powder, coriander

prep.task: Check the sprouts have tails at least 0.5 cm long; rinse them well

days.title: Keeping food safe: storage and preservation
days.goal: Learn the eight ways of storing food in the book, see why each stops fungus and bacteria, finish the mould test and start a sun-drying test.

steps.title: 12.3 Storage of food items, methods 1–4 (lesson pages 181–182)
steps.do: Read 12.3 on lesson pages 181–182 aloud: why we store food, and methods 1 to 4 (drying, refrigerating, oil and spices, chemicals, plus salting, sugar, vinegar and lemon). Explain the one idea under all of them: 'Fungus (mould) and bacteria are tiny living things. To grow they need water, warmth and food. Every method takes away one of these: drying takes away water; the fridge takes away warmth; lots of salt or sugar pulls water out of the microbes; the oil layer on pickle keeps air and microbes out.' Ask: 'Which of these does Nani use for mango pickle?' (Salt, oil and spices, and sun.) 'For papad and badiyan (vadi)?' (Drying in the sun.) Also mention the matka or a cloth-wrapped earthen pot, which cools by evaporation.

steps.title: Open the mould test
steps.do: Finish Experiment e1. Look at all four pieces through the closed bags first; then open them outdoors, away from your faces, and do not sniff closely. Your child completes the results table: dry and open, damp and warm, damp in fridge, damp with salt. Usually the damp warm piece has fuzzy green, black or white mould; the fridge and salted pieces have little or none; the dry piece is hard but not mouldy. Ask: 'Which of the book's storage methods did each piece test?' (Drying, refrigerating, salting.) Throw all the pieces away in the dustbin, seal the bags, and wash hands with soap.

steps.title: Methods 5–8: cooking, freezing, canning, fermenting (lesson pages 182–183)
steps.do: Read methods 5 to 8 on lesson pages 182–183 aloud. Ask: 'Why does boiling milk keep it longer?' (High heat kills most bacteria.) 'What is food poisoning?' (Illness with vomiting or diarrhoea from food spoiled by bacteria, for example food not cooked well or left warm for many hours.) 'Why should melted frozen food not be frozen again?' (Bacteria start growing while it is thawed, and refreezing does not kill them.) For fermenting, the book's examples are wine and vinegar; give your child Indian home examples: curd from milk, idli and dosa batter, dhokla, kanji, and some pickles. Explain: 'Here we let helpful microbes grow on purpose; they make the food sour, which stops harmful microbes.'

steps.title: Start the sun-drying test
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Slice one tomato (or an apple) into thin rounds. Weigh 4 slices together on a kitchen scale (or count them and draw their size on paper). Put 4 slices on a plate covered with thin muslin in direct sun; put 4 slices in a closed dabba on the kitchen shelf. Ask your child to predict: 'What will happen to each in two days? Will the sun slices weigh more or less?' Take the sun plate inside in the evening. Check and weigh again on Day 7.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws2 (stretch) on their own; it asks them to plan meals and choose storage methods for new cases. Check it together, asking 'Why?' for each choice.

need: a tomato or apple, a knife (parent), a kitchen scale if you have one

days.title: Let us revise, check and teach it back
days.goal: Review the lesson with the book's revision and exercises, finish the drying test, try the challenge worksheet, check understanding and have your child teach it back.

steps.title: Weigh the dried slices
steps.do: Finish Experiment e2. Weigh the sun-dried slices and compare with the start. Look at the dabba slices. Ask: 'Which have mould or a sour smell? Which are lighter and leathery? Where did the weight go?' (Water evaporated in the sun.) 'Why does that stop mould?' (No water, no mould.) Connect it to the book's line on lesson page 181: drying makes things small and light, easy to store.

steps.title: Let's Revise and Let's see 12.3 (lesson pages 183–184)
steps.do: Read 'Let's Revise' on lesson pages 183–184 together. Correct one line: the third point says 'Malnutrition causes rickets'; that disease is marasmus. Then ask the three questions of 'Let's see, what you have learnt 12.3' on lesson page 183 aloud: advantage of removing moisture (fungus cannot grow, food does not rot, and it becomes light to store); four methods; and the table (papad: drying; butter and milk: refrigerating; vinegar: fermenting; pickle: oil and spices).

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 (challenge) together. Let your child think and write; you ask only 'How do you know?' and 'What evidence?'. The last section brings in the voices of Takaki and Eijkman, Cicely Williams and Ramalingaswami.

steps.title: Lesson check
steps.do: Ask the 8 check questions aloud one at a time without the book. Tick each one answered well. For a missed answer, open the matching lesson page (diseases pages 175–177, special needs pages 178–179, cheap food pages 179–180, storage pages 181–183) and read the part together for a minute, then ask again in different words. Six or more right is good; fewer than five means revisit the colour plate hunt and the storage pages next week.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the teacher for the family. In 5–7 minutes, using the kitchen foods, the salt packet, the rice comparison and the photos or drawings of the mould and drying tests, they explain: the nutrients and their jobs; three deficiency diseases and how to prevent each; two ways to make cheap food more nutritious; and three ways to store food and why they work. The 'students' ask: 'If I feel tired, should I just take iron tablets?' (No; see a doctor and get a blood test first; too much iron or vitamin A can harm.) and 'Why don't pickles go mouldy?' (Salt, oil, spices and sun-drying keep microbes out.) End by cooking the mixed khichdi from the recipe card together.

need: the drying test slices and kitchen scale
the kitchen foods, salt packet and rice samples from the week
khichdi ingredients from the recipe card

pairs: Help the body grow and repair

sections.p: Sort these foods by their main nutrient.
Match each disease to its cause.
pairs: Too little vitamin D (sunlight) and calcium

sections.p: To prevent goitre, always use ____ salt.
The best natural way to get vitamin D is:

Write two signs of anaemia.

Rahul cuts the vegetables at 8 am, washes them under the tap, and cooks them for lunch in lots of water which he throws away. What is wrong?

pairs: Pickle in salt, oil and spices
Murabba in sugar, or salting and drying

sections.p: In our mould test, which piece of bread had the most mould? Use the result to explain why a fridge keeps food longer.
Making curd from milk is an example of ____.
Polishing rice makes it look whiter and cook faster. Why did beriberi become more common when machine-polished rice spread in Asia?
Salt and sugar both keep food from spoiling, though one is salty and one is sweet. What do they have in common that stops microbes?
Plan a fair test to find out whether lemon juice helps cut apple slices stay fresh longer.
prefill: What will I keep the same?

sections.p: Which is the best evidence that iodised salt prevents goitre?
opts: Villages given iodised salt had less goitre over years than villages given ordinary salt

sections.p: Takaki fixed beriberi in the navy but thought the cause was too little protein. Can someone solve a problem with the wrong explanation? Why does the right explanation still matter?

experiments.title: The mould test
experiments.question: What does mould need to grow, and which ways of storing food stop it?
need: 4 equal pieces of bread or one roti torn in four
space on a kitchen shelf and in the fridge
steps: Piece 1: leave it dry on an open plate on the shelf.
Piece 2: sprinkle with a few drops of water and close it in a bag on the shelf (damp and warm).
Piece 3: sprinkle with water, close it in a bag, and put it in the fridge (damp and cold).
Piece 4: sprinkle with water, coat thickly with salt, and close it in a bag on the shelf (damp and salty).
Look every day or two without opening the bags, and draw what you see.
After 5–6 days, open the bags outdoors, record results, then throw everything away and wash hands.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: which piece will grow mould first, and which will stay clean? Write the guesses down.
experiments.observe: Record for each piece: any fuzzy spots, their colour (white, green, black), how much of the piece is covered, and the day they first appeared. Usually the damp warm piece goes mouldy within 3–6 days; the fridge piece slowly or not at all; the salty piece little or not at all; the dry open piece goes hard but not mouldy.
experiments.why: Mould is a fungus. Its tiny spores float in the air everywhere and land on food. To grow, they need water, warmth and food. The damp warm bread gives all three. In the fridge the cold slows the mould's growth almost to a stop. Thick salt pulls water out of the mould and bacteria by osmosis, so they cannot grow. Dry bread has too little water. These are exactly the book's storage methods: drying, refrigerating and salting. Bacteria behave in a similar way, which is why cooked food left warm for many hours can cause food poisoning.
experiments.safety: Do not open the mouldy bags indoors or sniff them closely; mould spores can cause sneezing and breathing problems, especially for anyone with asthma. Never eat the test bread. Throw it away sealed and wash hands with soap.
experiments.time: 16 min to set up + 4 min checks + 9 min to finish after 5–6 days

experiments.title: Sun-drying slices
experiments.question: How does drying in the sun keep food from spoiling?
need: a kitchen scale if you have one
steps: The parent cuts 8 thin slices of the same size.
Weigh 4 slices together (or count and trace their size on paper).
Lay 4 slices on a plate, cover with muslin to keep flies and dust off, and put it in direct sun. Bring it inside in the evening.
Put the other 4 slices in a closed dabba on the kitchen shelf.
After 1–2 days, weigh the sun slices again and compare both sets.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: will the sun slices be heavier, lighter or the same? Which set might grow mould?
experiments.observe: Record the weight (or size) of the sun slices before and after, their colour and texture, and any mould or sour smell in the dabba set. The sun slices usually shrink, turn leathery and lose much of their weight; the dabba slices go soft, wet and may grow mould.
experiments.why: Fresh tomato and apple are mostly water. The Sun's heat and moving air evaporate that water, so the slices shrink and get lighter. With very little water left, mould and bacteria cannot grow, so dried food keeps for months, as with sun-dried papad, vadi, kokum, amchur (dried raw mango) and dried red chillies. Drying also makes food small and light, so it is easier to store and carry. The closed dabba kept the slices damp, which is exactly what microbes like.
experiments.safety: Only the parent uses the knife. Keep the plate covered against flies. Do not eat slices that show any mould.
experiments.time: 12 min to set up + 6 min to weigh after 1–2 days

activities.title: Sprouting moong
need: a clean muslin cloth or a sprout-maker
steps: Wash the moong in three changes of water and remove stones.
Soak it in plenty of clean water overnight.
Next morning, drain and rinse it.
Wrap it in a damp muslin cloth or put it in a sprout-maker, and keep it in a warm place.
Rinse it once or twice a day so it stays fresh and does not smell.
Use it in 1–2 days, when the tails are about 0.5–1 cm long.
activities.outcome: A bowl of fresh sprouts for the sprouts chaat, showing the book's tip that germinated pulses give more vitamins and are a cheap source of protein.

activities.title: Sprouts chaat and a mixed khichdi recipe card
need: iodised salt, roasted jeera powder, chopped coriander
card or paper for the recipe
steps: Wash the vegetables before cutting them.
The parent chops the onion, tomato and cucumber; the child mixes them with the sprouts.
Add lemon juice, a pinch of iodised salt, jeera powder and coriander.
Eat it fresh and name the nutrients in it.
Write a recipe card for a mixed khichdi: two cereals, two pulses, two vegetables, cooked in just enough water, with a little ghee.
Cook the khichdi together on Day 7.
activities.outcome: A cheap, tasty, nutritious snack made by your child, and a family recipe that puts the book's advice (mixed cereals and pulses, sprouts, vegetables cut just before cooking, not throwing away cooking water) into practice.

voices.who: Kanehiro Takaki (1849–1920), Japan, and Christiaan Eijkman (1858–1930), Netherlands
voices.idea: In the early 1880s beriberi struck many sailors of the Japanese navy, who ate mostly polished white rice. Takaki, a navy doctor, changed their diet to include barley, meat, milk and vegetables; in 1884 a training ship's crew on the new diet had almost no beriberi. In the 1890s in Java (then a Dutch colony), Eijkman found that chickens fed polished white rice developed a nerve illness like beriberi and recovered when fed unpolished rice.
voices.then: Most doctors of the time believed diseases were caused by germs or poisons, and Eijkman himself first thought white rice contained a poison that the bran cancelled out. Takaki believed the cause was too little protein. In 1901 Eijkman's colleague Gerrit Grijns argued that the bran contained something essential that the body needed.
voices.now: Scientists now know beriberi is caused by too little thiamine (vitamin B1), found in the bran and germ of grains. Eijkman shared the 1929 Nobel Prize for this discovery, which helped start the science of vitamins. Takaki's diet worked, though his explanation was wrong.
voices.ask: Takaki got the cure right but the reason wrong. Eijkman's chickens gave a clue nobody expected. What would you need to test to be sure it was something missing from white rice, not a poison in it?

voices.who: Cicely Williams (1893–1992), Jamaica and Britain, and the kwashiorkor debate
voices.idea: Williams, a Jamaican-born doctor working in the Gold Coast (now Ghana) in the early 1930s, described a disease of young children with swelling, skin changes and pale hair, often appearing after they were weaned from the breast when a new baby arrived. In 1935 she named it kwashiorkor, a Ga word often explained as the illness of the child displaced by the next baby, and argued that it was caused by a poor diet, mainly maize gruel, not by infection.
voices.then: Some doctors thought it was pellagra, another nutrition disease, and challenged her. Over the next decades it became widely accepted as a separate disease linked to a diet low in protein.
voices.now: That kwashiorkor is a form of severe malnutrition, preventable with a good diet and treatable with special feeding, is accepted. But why some starving children swell while others become thin (marasmus) on similar diets is still debated. Researchers are studying the roles of infections, damage to cells from oxidation, and the bacteria in the gut, for example in a 2013 study of Malawian twins.
voices.ask: Two children in the same poor village eat nearly the same food; one swells and one becomes very thin. What would you want to measure about them to find the reason?

voices.who: Vulimiri Ramalingaswami (1921–2001), India
voices.idea: Ramalingaswami, an Indian pathologist, led a long study in the Kangra valley of Himachal Pradesh starting in the 1950s, where goitre was very common. Some areas were given iodised salt and comparison areas got ordinary salt. Over the following years goitre fell sharply where iodised salt was used, but not elsewhere.
voices.then: The study showed that cheap iodised salt could prevent goitre in India's own conditions. It led India to start a national goitre control programme in 1962, which later became the iodine deficiency disorders programme, and India moved towards iodising all edible salt.
voices.now: Iodised salt is accepted worldwide as the simplest way to prevent goitre and the brain damage in babies caused by iodine lack. Ramalingaswami later became Director of AIIMS and Director-General of the Indian Council of Medical Research.
voices.ask: The doctors compared villages with and without iodised salt. Why was the comparison more convincing than just giving everyone iodised salt and seeing what happened?

check.q: Name the main nutrients and say what each does.
check.a: Carbohydrates and fats give energy; proteins help the body grow and repair; vitamins and minerals protect from disease and keep the body working. Water and fibre are also needed.

check.q: What is anaemia, and how can it be prevented?
check.a: Blood with too little haemoglobin, usually from too little iron, making a person pale, weak and tired. Eat iron foods like ragi, bajra, green leafy vegetables, dals, eggs or meat, with vitamin C foods; take iron tablets only if a doctor advises.

check.q: Which vitamin prevents night blindness, and which foods have it?
check.a: Vitamin A: green leafy vegetables, yellow and orange fruits and vegetables like carrot, papaya and mango, milk, eggs and liver.

check.q: What causes rickets and how is it prevented?
check.a: Too little vitamin D and calcium, which makes children's bones soft and bent. Some sunlight on the skin, plus milk and other calcium foods, prevents it.

check.q: Why do we use iodised salt?
check.a: Iodine prevents goitre (swelling of the thyroid in the neck) and protects babies' brains during pregnancy; everyone eats salt, so adding iodine to it reaches everyone.

check.q: What causes beriberi, and why is unpolished rice better?
check.a: Too little vitamin B1 (thiamine). Polishing removes the bran and germ where most vitamin B1 is, so unpolished or parboiled rice keeps more of it.

check.q: Give four ways to make cheap food more nutritious.
check.a: Any four: mix cereals and pulses, sprout pulses, eat unpolished grains and whole dals, eat seasonal fruit and vegetables, wash before cutting, cut just before cooking, cook in less water and do not throw it away, do not overcook, use an iron kadhai, eat dark green leafy vegetables.

check.q: How do drying, refrigerating and salting stop food from spoiling?
check.a: Mould and bacteria need water and warmth to grow. Drying removes water, the fridge takes away warmth, and lots of salt (or sugar) pulls water out of the microbes.

topics.name: Living & non-living: is the distinction real?
sub: The usual 'signs of life': moves, breathes, eats, grows, responds, makes babies, gets rid of waste
Tricky cases that break the list: fire (eats, breathes oxygen, grows, spreads), a 100-year-old dormant seed, growing crystals, a plucked flower, a dead leaf, a virus
J.C. Bose: plants respond to touch, injury and poison; he claimed metals also 'tire' and 'recover'
Everything is made of elements forged in stars
Is a handful of soil living or non-living?
topics.summary: We start by sorting things at home into 'alive' and 'not alive' and writing down why. Then we test those reasons on tricky cases. Fire eats, breathes and grows; is it alive? A seed can sit still for 100 years and then sprout; was it alive all that time? Crystals grow. Then we meet J.C. Bose, who built machines sensitive enough to show plants reacting, and who argued that even metals show tiredness and recovery. We end with the honest truth: scientists still do not have one agreed definition of life. NASA's working definition is 'a self-sustaining chemical system capable of evolution', and even that is argued over.
topics.oneness: If the same atoms move from stars to rocks to plants to me, at what moment does something become 'alive'? Is aliveness a line, or a gradient?

res.title: A Seed Is Sleepy, Dianna Hutts Aston
Acharya J.C. Bose Indian Botanic Garden, Howrah
The Private Life of Plants (BBC, David Attenborough)
The King's Doubt: full game (cards + parent guide)

topics.name: How did life begin?
sub: Earth began hot, with no life
The oldest evidence of life is about 3.5 billion years old (stromatolites: layered rocks built by microbes)
First life was tiny single cells in water
Ideas: Darwin's 'warm little pond', deep-sea hot vents, life arriving from space (panspermia), the 'RNA world'
Miller–Urey experiment (1952): gases + electric sparks made amino acids
Nobody has made life from scratch yet
topics.summary: We tell Earth's story on a long rope or saree: Earth forms, it is too hot for life, then early on the first tiny cells appear in water, and humans arrive only in the last few millimetres. We look at photos of stromatolites, rocks built layer by layer by microbes over billions of years, some still growing in Australia today. Then we lay out the main ideas scientists have about how life started, and the one honest answer: nobody knows yet. Scientists have made some building blocks of life in a lab, but never life itself.
topics.oneness: If life came from non-living chemicals, was it ever really separate from them?

res.title: The Story of Life: Evolution, Catherine Barr & Steve Williams
NASA Space Place: life in the universe

topics.name: What's common between living and non-living?
sub: Everything is made of atoms; about 90 kinds occur naturally (elements)
The body is mostly oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen
The same carbon is in pencil lead, diamond, bread and you
Atoms are recycled: the water you drink has passed through clouds, rivers, plants and animals
Stars made most elements: 'we are star stuff'
topics.summary: We ask what a rock, a tree and a child have in common, and find that underneath they are built from the same tiny pieces: atoms. Your body is mostly oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen, the same elements found in air, water and coal. Carbon in a pencil and carbon in a diamond are the same atom arranged differently. Atoms never wear out; they keep moving between rocks, air, plants and people. Most of them were made inside stars long before Earth existed. So the difference between living and non-living is not in what they are made of, but in how those pieces are arranged and behave.
topics.oneness: If my atoms were once a star and will one day be soil, which part of the journey is 'me'?

res.title: Older Than the Stars, Karen C. Fox
PhET: Build an Atom (simulation)

topics.name: Materials around me & their properties
sub: Properties: hard/soft, rough/smooth, heavy/light, bendy/stiff, strong/brittle, see-through/opaque, magnetic/not
Float or sink: not about heavy vs light but about how tightly packed (Archimedes)
Microscope views: salt crystals, sugar, cloth threads, hair, soil
Soil & rocks: sand, clay, loam; soil layers; soil is full of life (a teaspoon holds billions of microbes)
Surprising 'materials': is water a material? Tears? Shadow? Sound? Fire?
topics.summary: Children become material detectives: touching, bending, dropping and floating everyday things and describing them with exact words. Float-or-sink predictions surprise them: a heavy steel plate floats when shaped like a bowl, while a tiny pebble sinks. We look closer with a magnifier or phone microscope: salt is little cubes, cloth is woven threads. We dig into soil, see its layers settle in a jar, and learn that one spoonful of good soil contains more living microbes than there are people on Earth, so is soil living? Finally the big puzzle: water and tears are matter, but a shadow is only missing light, sound is a shaking that travels through matter, and fire is hot glowing gas. What counts as 'stuff'?
topics.oneness: Is soil a thing, or a crowd of living beings? Where does the material end and the living begin?

res.title: Arvind Gupta Toys: science from everyday junk
PhET: Density (float or sink)

topics.name: Kinds of living things
sub: Plants: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed; what plants need (water, light, air, soil nutrients); grow-a-seed
Fungi: mushrooms, mould, yeast; neither plant nor animal, closer to animals than to plants
Animals: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, insects and other invertebrates
Microbes (links to B3)
Humans are animals: mammals and primates
Groups are made by humans, and they keep changing
topics.summary: We meet the big families of life. Plants: we find the parts on a real plant and discover which parts we eat (carrot is a root, potato is a stem, spinach a leaf, cauliflower a flower, rice a seed), then start growing seeds in light and dark to see what plants need. Fungi surprise everyone: mushrooms are not plants, and DNA shows fungi are closer relatives of animals. We sort animals by features (fur, feathers, scales, backbone or not) and place humans honestly among them: we are mammals, we are animals. Finally we see that these groups are human-made boxes: scientists used to call fungi plants, and today most scientists say birds are living dinosaurs.
topics.oneness: Who drew these boxes, and does nature know about them? If a mushroom is more like me than a plant, what does 'like me' mean?

res.title: A Seed Is Sleepy, Dianna Hutts Aston
StoryWeaver (Pratham Books): free picture books on plants and animals
Any botanical garden, e.g. Lalbagh, Bengaluru

topics.name: Big Bang & the universe
sub: About 13.8 billion years ago the universe was tiny, hot and dense, and began expanding
First atoms: hydrogen and helium
Mass and gravity: gravity pulls matter into clumps → stars, planets, galaxies, clusters
Stars make heavier elements and scatter them when they explode
Black holes; dark matter and dark energy (about 95% of the universe is something we cannot see)
Our planet: about 71% water, 29% land
topics.summary: We tell the biggest story there is. Long ago everything was squeezed into an unimaginably small, hot speck, which grew and is still growing, like dots on a balloon moving apart as it inflates. As it cooled, the first atoms appeared. Mass pulls on mass; that pull is gravity, and gravity gathered gas into stars and stars into galaxies. Stars cook new elements and scatter them when they explode; our Earth, and we, are made from that dust. Then the mysteries: black holes so strong that light cannot escape, and the shocking fact that most of the universe is 'dark' stuff no one has ever seen. We also learn how ideas about gravity changed: Newton said it is a pulling force, and it worked for 200 years; Einstein showed mass bends space and time itself; and today some scientists think even Einstein's idea needs fixing.
topics.oneness: If everything came from one tiny point, is the universe one thing that became many?

res.title: NASA Space Place
Me and My Place in Space, Joan Sweeney
Nehru Planetarium (Delhi / Mumbai)

topics.name: My world: how humans live, and why
sub: My world: home, food, transport, money, work, school, festivals
The chain of people behind my breakfast
Humans are social animals: families, groups, rules, sharing, trade
Why we live like this: biology (we bond, cooperate, compete), environment, history, culture
Different people live in different worlds: village, city, forest, another country
Money: from barter to coins to digital
topics.summary: We begin with the child's own world: list everything used in one day and trace where it came from. A single breakfast needs farmers, drivers, shopkeepers and cooks; no human lives alone. We ask why humans live in families and groups: like elephants, wolves and ants, we survive by cooperating, and our bodies are wired to bond (a hug really changes brain chemicals). We see that a child in a forest village, a fishing town or a city in another country lives in a different 'world' with different food, work and rules. We play a barter market to see why money was invented. And we ask the old question honestly: are humans naturally selfish or naturally kind? Thinkers disagree.
topics.oneness: If my breakfast needs a hundred people, where do 'I' end and 'we' begin?

res.title: StoryWeaver: stories of children across India

topics.name: The world of microorganisms
sub: Too small to see: bacteria, yeast and other fungi, amoebas, algae; viruses (alive or not?)
Everywhere: soil, air, water, skin, gut
Helpers: curd, idli/dosa batter, bread, compost; ocean plankton make about half of Earth's oxygen
Some make us sick (links to C10)
Leeuwenhoek first saw them in the 1670s with a home-made lens
topics.summary: There is a whole hidden world all around and inside us. We hear how a Dutch cloth-seller, Leeuwenhoek, ground tiny lenses and was the first person to see 'little animals' swimming in a drop of water. Microbes turn milk into curd, make idli batter rise, rot leaves into soil and, through tiny ocean plankton, make about half the oxygen we breathe. Only a few make us sick. We make curd at home and watch yeast blow up a balloon. And we ask whether viruses are alive: they cannot do anything outside a living cell, so scientists still disagree.
topics.oneness: If tiny beings make my curd, my soil and my oxygen, how separate is my life from theirs?

res.title: Microcosmos (1996 film)
Arvind Gupta Toys: simple magnifiers

topics.name: Other beings' worlds: how a bird sees the world
sub: Every creature lives in its own world of senses (umwelt, Jakob von Uexküll, 1909)
Birds see ultraviolet and have 4 kinds of colour cones (we have 3)
Many birds sense Earth's magnetic field to migrate; Amur falcons fly from East Asia through Nagaland to Africa
Bird societies: flocks, nests, parents, songs with local 'dialects', crows remember faces and use tools
Seeing time: many birds and insects see fast movements we miss
(Series can continue: an ant's world, a dog's world, a fish's world…)
topics.summary: Our world of cars, money and roads is only one world. A crow on the same street lives in a different one. Birds see colours we cannot even imagine, including ultraviolet patterns on flowers and feathers. Many feel the Earth's magnetism and use it like a compass to fly thousands of kilometres; the Amur falcon crosses the Arabian Sea on its way from Asia to Africa. Birds have families, neighbours, quarrels and songs, and crows can remember a human face for years. We try to imagine life in a bird's world, and meet a famous question: can we ever truly know what it is like to be another creature?
topics.oneness: If each being lives in its own world, is there one 'real' world, or many?

res.title: Planet Earth: Birds of Paradise episode (BBC)
Salim Ali Bird Sanctuary, Thattekad (Kerala) or a local lake

topics.name: Cycles in the sky & weather
sub: Day and night: Earth spins
A year: Earth goes around the Sun; seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun
Moon phases: we see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half; the Moon makes no light of its own
India's six ritus and the monsoon
Clouds and rain: water evaporates, cools and condenses
Planets you can see (Venus, Jupiter, Mars, Saturn) and stars as distant suns
topics.summary: With a torch and a ball we discover why day and night happen: the Earth spins, so our side faces the Sun and then turns away. Seasons come from Earth's tilt; most people wrongly think it is about being closer to the Sun. The Moon makes no light of its own; its shape changes because we see different amounts of its sunlit half, and the child keeps a moon diary for a month. We learn India's six ritus, why the monsoon comes, and make a cloud in a jar. We hear how ideas changed: people once believed the Sun went around the Earth; Aryabhata proposed in 499 CE that the Earth spins; Copernicus and Galileo argued the Earth goes around the Sun, and Galileo was put on trial for it.
topics.oneness: Sun, Moon, seasons and my sleep all move in cycles. Am I part of the sky's rhythm?

res.title: NASA Space Place: Moon phases
Shadow-stick sundial

topics.name: Forces, vibrations & sound
sub: Push and pull; gravity pulls everything down
The floor pushes back up (normal force); friction; air resistance; water pushes up (buoyancy); magnets
Contact forces are, at heart, electric pushes between electrons; your hand never truly 'touches' the table
Gravity is the exception, a different force
Sound is vibration travelling through air, water and solids; no sound in space
Loud/soft and high/low (pitch); echoes
topics.summary: Children push, pull, drop and float things to feel forces. The surprise: when you sit on a chair, the chair pushes back up, and when you 'touch' anything, its electrons and yours push each other away; atoms never really touch. Air pushes against a falling sheet of paper; water pushes up on a boat. We retell the history of falling: Aristotle said heavy things fall faster, and people believed him for nearly 2000 years until Galileo tested it; Newton explained gravity as a pull; Einstein explained it as bent space. Sound is also a push travelling along: we feel our throat buzz when humming Om, watch rice jump on a drum, and build a cup telephone.
topics.oneness: If nothing ever truly touches, how are we all still connected?

res.title: The Way Things Work Now, David Macaulay
PhET: Forces and Motion Basics
Arvind Gupta Toys: sound and force toys

topics.name: Light, colour & shadows
sub: Light sources: Sun, fire, bulbs, fireflies (living light)
We see when light bounces off things into our eyes
Light travels in straight lines → shadows; shadow size changes with distance
Reflection: mirrors, still water
White light holds all colours (rainbow, prism); objects show the colours they bounce back
Mixing paint vs mixing light: paints get darker; red, green and blue light make white
Darkness is the absence of light; light and shade in painting
topics.summary: Darkness is not a thing; it is what is left when light is missing. We make shadow puppets and discover shadows grow as hands move closer to the torch. We bounce torchlight off mirrors to hit a target, make rainbows with a glass of water, and learn that white light is all colours mixed, as Newton showed with a prism. A red apple looks red because it bounces red light and swallows the rest. Then the painting surprise: mixing paints makes colours darker, while mixing coloured light makes white. We paint a ball with one light source to see light, shade and shadow. And the deep puzzle: is light a wave or a particle? Scientists argued for centuries and now say it behaves as both, which still puzzles them.
topics.oneness: Is colour in the apple, in the light, or in my mind?

res.title: PhET: Color Vision
Shadow puppet show (Tholu Bommalata / Togalu Gombeyaata)

topics.name: Nature's events
sub: Rain and the water cycle
Floods, droughts and dry spells
Wind, storms and cyclones (countries around the Indian Ocean take turns naming them)
Thunder and lightning (light arrives before sound)
Earthquakes and tsunamis (2004 Indian Ocean tsunami)
Snow in the Himalayas
Why the monsoon happens: land heats faster than sea
topics.summary: Nature is always moving water, air and land around. We follow a raindrop through the water cycle, then see what happens when there is too much (flood) or too little (drought). The monsoon happens because land heats faster than the sea, so moist sea air rushes in. We count the seconds between lightning and thunder to tell how far away a storm is. We learn how earthquakes shake the ground and how in 2004 some Andaman island communities reportedly escaped the tsunami using traditional knowledge of the sea. And we ask whether 'natural disasters' are fully natural: building on riverbeds or cutting forests can make floods far worse.
topics.oneness: Rain, rivers and my body's water are the same water. Is a flood something happening to us or with us?

res.title: India Meteorological Department: today's weather
A stepwell (e.g. Chand Baori, Rajasthan) or a local lake

topics.name: Human impact on the environment
sub: Humans change land (forests → farms and cities), air (smoke), water (plastic, sewage) and climate (burning coal and petrol adds carbon dioxide)
Other animals change environments too (elephants, termites, earthworms, beavers), but humans at a huge scale
Good changes: Jadav Payeng planted a whole forest on a river island; the Chipko movement
Are humans part of nature or outside it?
topics.summary: Every living thing changes its surroundings: earthworms make soil, elephants clear paths, termites build towers. Humans do the same, but at a scale that now changes the whole planet's air, water and weather. We walk the neighbourhood spotting human-made changes, catch dust from the air on a sticky card, and feel how a road is hotter than a tree's shade. We meet people who changed things for the better: Jadav Payeng, the 'Forest Man of India', planted a forest bigger than many towns, and the women of the Chipko movement hugged trees to save them. We discuss honestly that people disagree about how fast to change things and which solutions are best.
topics.oneness: If I am part of nature, is damaging nature damaging myself?

res.title: StoryWeaver: Jadav and the Tree-Place
The Elephant Whisperers (2022)
Our Planet (2019)

topics.name: Waste: reduce & manage
sub: Nature has no waste: a fallen leaf becomes soil
Kinds of waste: wet, dry, hazardous, e-waste
Where waste goes: landfills, burning, recycling, oceans
Plastic can last hundreds of years
Refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle; composting
India's kabadiwala recycling system
topics.summary: In a forest nothing is wasted: leaves, dead animals and dung all become food for something else. Only humans make things nature cannot easily take back, like plastic that lasts for centuries. We find out what our own family throws away in a week, sort it into wet, dry and hazardous, and bury a banana peel, a paper and a plastic bag to dig up after 3 weeks. We meet India's kabadiwalas, who quietly recycle huge amounts, and old habits like turning sarees into quilts. We also learn an uncomfortable fact: only a small part of all plastic ever made has been recycled, and experts argue about whether recycling is the real answer.
topics.oneness: If nature has no waste, is waste a human idea? Can we live like a forest?

res.title: Arvind Gupta Toys: toys from trash

topics.name: Other life inside me
sub: Trillions of microbes live in and on us: roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells
Gut, skin and mouth each have their own communities
They help digest food, make some vitamins and train our defences
Mitochondria, the energy-makers in our cells, were once free-living bacteria
About 8% of our DNA is left over from ancient viruses
topics.summary: You are not just you: you are a walking city. About as many bacterial cells live in and on your body as your own cells (scientists used to say 10 times more, until a 2016 study corrected it). Your gut microbes help digest food and make vitamins; skin microbes guard against germs. Deeper still, the tiny power stations inside every cell, mitochondria, were once separate bacteria that moved in and never left. Lynn Margulis proposed this and was ridiculed for years before scientists accepted it. Even our DNA carries leftover pieces of ancient viruses. So which part is 'me'?
topics.oneness: If half the cells in my body are not 'mine', and my energy comes from ancient bacteria, what is 'I'?

res.title: Khan Academy: cells and microbes (older kids, parent prep)

topics.name: My genes
sub: Every cell carries instructions (DNA), like a recipe book
Half from each biological parent; why siblings differ
All life uses the same DNA 'letters'; we share many genes with bananas, flies and mice
Genes are not destiny: food, care and surroundings switch genes on and off
History: Mendel's peas; Rosalind Franklin's photo; Har Gobind Khorana and the genetic code
topics.summary: Inside almost every cell is a long coded message called DNA, a recipe book for building and running a body. We extract real DNA from strawberries and see the white strands. Half our recipes come from each biological parent, mixed in a new way, which is why siblings look alike but different. All living things use the same four DNA letters, so we share many genes even with bananas. We meet Mendel, a monk whose pea experiments were ignored for 34 years; Rosalind Franklin, whose photo revealed DNA's shape but who got little credit; and Har Gobind Khorana, born in Punjab, who won a Nobel Prize for cracking how DNA's code works. And we learn that genes are not destiny: what we eat, how we live and how we are cared for changes which genes are used.
topics.oneness: If a banana and I share the same code, are we written in the same language by the same author?

res.title: Strawberry DNA extraction (lesson card)

topics.name: Where humans came from
sub: Life changed over billions of years (evolution): fish → amphibians → reptiles → mammals → primates → humans, a branching tree, not a ladder
Darwin and Wallace: natural selection
Other humans: Homo erectus, Neanderthals, Denisovans; Homo sapiens appear about 300,000 years ago in Africa
Many of us carry a little Neanderthal DNA
People reached India tens of thousands of years ago; Bhimbetka rock shelters
topics.summary: We follow our family line back through time: fish that crawled onto land, early mammals scurrying under dinosaurs, tree-climbing primates, and many kinds of humans, several of them alive at the same time. Darwin and Wallace explained how living things slowly change: those best suited to their surroundings survive and pass on their traits. We see that evolution is a branching bush, not a ladder, and that new fossils keep pushing dates back. We visit (in pictures or in person) Bhimbetka's rock paintings, among the oldest human art in India. Then we compare this with the Dashavatara: Matsya (fish), Kurma (tortoise), Varaha (boar), Narasimha (half-lion, half-human), Vamana (small human), then full humans. Many people see in this order a story that parallels evolution.
topics.oneness: If all life is one family tree, is there anyone who is not my relative?

res.title: The Story of Life: Evolution, Catherine Barr & Steve Williams
Bhimbetka rock shelters (Madhya Pradesh)

topics.name: What's common between me and other life?
sub: Me & a dog: mammals, backbone, the same organs, hair, milk, feelings
Me & a bird: backbone, lungs, a 4-chambered heart
Me & a fish: backbone; early embryos look alike
Me & a tree: cells, DNA, using energy, water
Me & a mushroom: closer relatives than plants
Me & bacteria: the same DNA code and energy molecule
Differences too
topics.summary: We play detective comparing ourselves with other beings, one at a time. A dog shares our skeleton plan, organs, fur-like hair, milk-feeding and clearly feels joy and fear. A bird has a 4-chambered heart like ours. A tree breathes at the level of its cells, carries DNA and is made of cells like us. Even bacteria run on the same genetic code and energy molecule. The deeper we look, the longer the 'same' list grows. We also hear the 2012 Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, in which scientists stated that many animals, including birds and octopuses, are conscious, and the 2024 New York Declaration, which says even insects might be.
topics.oneness: 'Tat tvam asi': you are that. When does 'same' become 'one'?

res.title: My Octopus Teacher (2020)

topics.name: Our closest cousins
sub: Great apes: chimpanzees and bonobos (closest; about 98–99% similar DNA), gorillas, orangutans
Monkeys and other primates
India's only ape: the hoolock gibbon (Northeast)
Shared: tools, emotions, play, laughter, culture
Jane Goodall: chimps use tools
topics.summary: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives; we shared an ancestor several million years ago. When Jane Goodall saw a chimp stripping a twig to fish for termites, scientists had believed tool-making was what made humans unique. Her mentor Louis Leakey said we must now 'redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.' Chimps laugh, mourn, make up after fights and have local traditions. India has its own ape, the hoolock gibbon, singing in northeastern forests. We tape our thumbs to see why our hands matter, and ask: what, if anything, makes humans special?
topics.oneness: Every 'only humans can…' claim has been challenged. Is the line between us and them real?

res.title: Jane Goodall documentaries (e.g. Jane, 2017)

topics.name: My family history
sub: Family tree (3 generations); 'family' = the people who raise and love me (inclusive of adopted, single-parent and other families)
Traits that run in families: face, height, hair, handedness
Fingerprints: unique, even for identical twins
Stories, languages, places, recipes
How long people lived then vs now
Blood groups and family illnesses: parent-led and kept light
topics.summary: Every child is the newest page in a very long story. We build a family tree, interview a grandparent or elder, collect photos and stories, and look at what is shared: a nose, a laugh, a love of cooking. We take fingerprints and discover that no two people, not even identical twins, have the same ones. We learn that in 1947 people in India lived on average only about 32 years and now about 70, and ask why. For families that wish to, parents can add blood groups and health stories. Families made by adoption or in other ways trace both their 'raised-by' and 'born-from' stories in whatever way feels right.
topics.oneness: My family tree joins every other family tree if I go back far enough. Where does my family end?

topics.name: My body parts
sub: Skin (the largest organ), bones (about 300 at birth, 206 in adults), muscles, heart, lungs, stomach and intestines, brain
How they work together
Why they evolved: forward eyes, gripping thumbs, sweating for long-distance running, goosebumps from furry ancestors, tailbone
The appendix: once called useless, now possibly a store of helpful microbes
topics.summary: We trace the child's body on a big sheet of paper and place cut-out organs inside. We listen to the heart with a home-made stethoscope before and after jumping, blow up a balloon to feel lung power, and build a moving finger from straws and string. Then we ask 'why do I have this?' Goosebumps are left over from furry ancestors whose hair stood up; sweating lets humans run for hours; babies are born with about 300 bones that fuse to 206. We learn that science changes its mind: the appendix was called useless for a century and now may be a safe house for helpful gut microbes. Finally we meet another way of seeing the body: Sushruta, an early surgeon who described nose reconstruction, and the yoga and Ayurveda traditions that describe the body differently.
topics.oneness: My heart beats without my asking. Is it 'my' heart, or is it doing its own thing?

res.title: Science centres: Nehru Science Centre Mumbai, Visvesvaraya Museum Bengaluru, National Science Centre Delhi

topics.name: My body's sensors
sub: Beyond the 'five senses': touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain, itch, balance, body position (eyes closed), hunger, thirst, full tummy, heartbeat, the urge to breathe
Conscious vs automatic sensing
Senses mix: flavour = taste + smell
Other beings: birds (UV, magnetic field), bees (UV), snakes (heat), sharks (electric fields), bats (echoes), dogs (smell)
Plants sense light, gravity and touch
topics.summary: Aristotle listed five senses over 2000 years ago, and people repeated the list ever since. But your body is covered in sensors: you know where your hand is with your eyes closed, you feel hot and cold, you stay balanced on one foot, you feel hungry, thirsty or that you need the toilet, and a hidden sensor makes you breathe faster when you run. Scientists today count anywhere from about 20 to over 30 senses and still disagree on how to count. We pinch our noses and find apple and potato taste almost the same, because most flavour is smell. Then we meet the superpowers of others: snakes 'see' heat, sharks feel electricity, bats hear their way in the dark, birds feel Earth's magnetism. Even plants sense: roots know which way is down and the touch-me-not folds when touched.
topics.oneness: If a plant senses touch and I sense touch, is sensing the beginning of awareness everywhere?

res.title: What If You Had Animal Eyes?, Sandra Markle

topics.name: How do I think?
sub: The brain: about 86 billion neurons sending signals
Thinking = patterns of signals; learning changes connections
Memory: short-term and long-term; sleep helps memory; memories change each time we recall them
Emotions affect thinking
Other thinkers: crows, octopuses; even brainless slime moulds solve mazes
The hard question: how does the brain make experience?
topics.summary: Your brain has about 86 billion nerve cells passing tiny electric and chemical signals; every time you learn something new, the connections change. We play memory games and discover tricks that help (stories, pictures, a 'memory palace' walk through the house) and learn that sleep is when the brain files memories. Surprisingly, a memory changes a little each time you remember it. Thinking isn't only human: crows plan, octopuses solve puzzles, and a slime mould with no brain at all can find the shortest path through a maze. Then the biggest mystery: nobody knows how signals in the brain become the feeling of being you. Some scientists say the mind is what the brain does; Vedanta says consciousness comes first and the brain is something that appears within it.
topics.oneness: Who is watching my thoughts? Is the watcher a thought too?

topics.name: Getting sick, getting hurt & getting well
sub: Why we get sick: germs (bacteria, viruses), not enough food or sleep, allergies
The body's defences: skin, mucus, fever, white blood cells, antibodies, immune memory (how vaccines work)
Hygiene habits: handwashing (20 seconds), teeth, bathing, clean water and food, covering coughs
Getting hurt: cuts, burns, falls, electric shock; electricity safety at home
Healing: scabs, rest
Are 'I' and 'my body' different?
topics.summary: We learn that the body is a fortress: skin is the wall, mucus is a sticky trap, fever is the body turning up the heat on germs, and white blood cells are guards who remember invaders so they can fight faster next time (which is how vaccines work). Glitter 'germs' show why handwashing matters, and bread touched by washed vs unwashed hands grows very different mould. We tell the story of Dr Semmelweis, who told doctors to wash their hands in the 1840s and was mocked; years later germ theory proved him right. We learn home safety, especially electricity: water and electricity never mix, never touch sockets or bare wires, and never touch someone being shocked; switch off first. Finally the question: we say 'help my body heal'. Who is helping whom? Am I my body, or something more?
topics.oneness: When I say 'my body', who is the 'I' that owns it?

res.title: Germs Make Me Sick!, Melvin Berger

topics.name: What is food?
sub: Food = building material + energy + helpers (vitamins, minerals) + water
Digestion breaks food down: proteins → amino acids, carbohydrates → sugars, fats → fatty acids
All life uses the same ~20 amino acids, DNA code and energy molecule (ATP)
So why so many foods? Different bodies have different tools (teeth, enzymes, gut microbes)
Plants make their own food from light; food chains
Food for different beings: cows (helped by microbes), spiders, plants, fungi
topics.summary: We chew a piece of plain roti for two minutes and it starts tasting sweet: saliva is already breaking starch into sugar. Digestion is a giant breaking-down factory: proteins become amino acids, carbohydrates become sugars, fats become fatty acids, and the body rebuilds them into itself. Amazingly, every living thing builds itself from the same 20 or so amino acids. So why does a cow eat grass, a spider eat flies and a plant eat sunlight? Because each has different tools: a cow's stomach is full of microbes that break down grass, which we cannot do. We also learn that nutrition science keeps changing its mind: fat was the villain, then sugar, and eggs went from bad to fine.
topics.oneness: 'Annam Brahma': food is the Absolute. When I eat a mango, does the mango become me, or do I become a little more mango?

res.title: StoryWeaver: food stories

topics.name: Energy beyond food
sub: Sunlight: plants make sugar from light (photosynthesis); we make vitamin D in sunlight; warmth
Air: oxygen helps cells release energy from food; we breathe out carbon dioxide
Water: most of the body is water; every cell works in it
Life without sunlight: deep-sea vents where bacteria make food from chemicals (chemosynthesis); tubeworms
Microbes that 'breathe' nitrate or sulphate instead of oxygen; life in boiling springs, ice and deep rock
Tardigrades survive extremes
topics.summary: Food is only one kind of fuel. Plants catch sunlight and turn it into sugar; that sugar feeds almost everything else, including us. Our cells use oxygen to release energy from food, like a slow fire, and we breathe out carbon dioxide. A plant left in a dark box turns pale, and a candle under a jar goes out when its oxygen runs low. Then we dive to the deep ocean floor, where no sunlight has ever reached, and find whole communities living on chemicals from hot volcanic vents. Some microbes breathe sulphate instead of oxygen, some live in boiling water or deep inside rocks, and tiny tardigrades can survive drying out and even the vacuum of space. Life is far stranger and more flexible than the textbook picture.
topics.oneness: If all my energy started as sunlight, am I a little bit of the Sun, walking around?
